articles.title: Poland is racing ahead with military spending – but will it help or damage its economic growth story?
articles.body:
A short distance north from Warsaw along the Vistula river, camouflaged missile launchers roll through the quiet village of Czosnów.
As recently as two years ago, their destination – a hi-tech weapons facility opened this month – had been a cornfield. Now, as Poland drives up defence investment at one of the fastest rates in the developed world, this rural spot has been transformed amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.
“Everyone has had to move twice as fast to meet the Polish needs,” says Jim Price, the managing director of MBDA Polska, the local subsidiary of the European multinational arms group. Based in the UK, the former Royal Marine says Poland is shifting from importing its weapons to manufacturing them at home.
“When it became clear there is a need to defend Nato’s eastern flank, in the event of a war itself, they needed to be able to do things in the blink of an eye. So we decided to invest in-the country to create a facility. We had to build up our Polish subsidiary – and that means Polish jobs.”
Poland’s defence budget has grown at a blistering pace. Since Vladimir Putin ordered Russian troops into Ukraine almost five years ago, spending as a share of Polish gross domestic product (GDP) has more than doubled from 2.2% to 4.8% this year. In cash terms, this equates to $53bn (£39.8bn), the fourth-highest in the EU after Germany, France and Italy.
Attention in Warsaw is clearly focused on the risk of an imminent Russian test of Nato resolve. However, there is also another motive: growing the economy.
Inside the soundproofed, airlock-style doors enclosing his office in Warsaw, Marcin Bosacki, Poland’s deputy foreign minister, says Russian aggression is heavily influencing the Polish government’s plans for economic development and cooperation with EU and Nato allies.
“[It] is clearly benefiting Polish security; Polish defence, and the Polish economy as well,” he says.
Strengthening economic ties in the pursuit of military readiness would discourage Putin (“a traditional Russian imperialist”) from attacking Nato, Bosacki adds.
“The only thing which Putin understands is solidarity and power. And so the more we are united and strong, the less likely the outcome of more aggressive Russian provocations against Nato member states is.”
Hope remains for a diplomatic solution. This month, Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks in Moscow with Putin and in Kyiv with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Next month, further negotiations are scheduled in Abu Dhabi.
However, diplomatic sources believe Russia is unlikely to cede ground – rendering Nato’s demonstrations of military readiness critical.
History shows defence and economics are closely intertwined. Statisticians first devised GDP as a metric in response to the 1930s Great Depression and needs of wartime planning to gauge the capacity of an economy.
Poland has been through an economic miracle since the Solidarność (solidarity) movement that arose from the Gdańsk shipyard strikes paved the way for its transition from communism almost four decades ago. Living standards have shot up from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.
Joining the EU in 2004 and securing catch-up funds from Brussels – which was spent on new roads, railways, and other productivity-enhancing infrastructure – also helped. Annual output surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, with Poland among the fastest-growing EU countries at an annualised rate of 3.9% in the second quarter despite the global headwinds caused by the Iran war.
However, Poland’s defence boom is not cost-free. Nor has economic development helped it avoid political polarisation.
The rising military budget is among the reasons why Poland is predicted to run the biggest fiscal deficit in the EU next year, at 7.1% of GDP. Last week, Moody’s downgraded the country’s long-term sovereign credit rating to the lowest level since 2002, amid an apparent lack of willingness to rebuild fiscal buffers.
Leszek Kąsek, a Warsaw-based economist at ING Bank, said: “This path is not sustainable. You should ask people if Poland can maintain its growth story and whether politicians will be ready to adjust?”
Wedged between larger neighbours it has been subjugated twice within living memory, Poles are uneasy about national security. But despite its economic turnaround under EU membership, and as it secures billions of euros in defence funds from Brussels, support for Eurosceptic politics remains.
In the run-up to the general election next year, the defence of the country, support for Ukraine and EU relations will be highly politically charged.
Outside the foreign ministry in Warsaw, protesters wave placards in a “Poles for peace” nationalist rally, organised by rightwing politicians opposed to the EU and its support for Ukraine.
Inside the building’s marble halls, where the Polish flag appears to be positioned next to those of Nato and the EU at almost every opportunity, Bosacki says divisions over the benefits to Poland of membership to both institutions has emerged for the first time.
This year, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who has backing from the rightwing Law and Justice party, attempted to block the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk’s liberal, pro-EU government from accessing €44bn (£38bn) of defence investment loans approved under the bloc’s security action for Europe (Safe) programme.
“I think our right is so eager to regain power they will use anything,” Bosacki says. “Here for the first time, the opposition was [against doing] something which, in my opinion – and the opinion of the majority of Poles – is clearly benefiting Polish security, Polish defence and the Polish economy as well.”
Through Safe, Warsaw secured the largest single disbursement in the loan programme. The government has pledged to channel almost 90% of it to domestic industry – led by Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa (PGZ), the state-owned defence conglomerate.
However, in the race to build up capacity, the tills are ringing for US-arms manufacturers supplying Patriot missiles, Abrams tanks and F-35 fighter jets.
In March, the International Monetary Fund cautioned that the positive economic spillovers from EU defence investment would not necessarily flow for the governments taking out their chequebooks.
However, Warsaw is doing defence deals with international partners, including the UK, to help develop its domestic manufacturing base at the same time as building military readiness.
The British defence group Babcock is working with PGZ to help build a fleet of new frigates. Known as the Miecznik, or swordfish, programme, the company has a shipyard at Gdynia on the Baltic coast. The first ship was launched this summer by Tusk.
“It’s a must for Poland, basically, to invest more. But they want to do it in a smart way,” says Andrzej Maciejewski, Babcock’s country director for Poland, who is based in Warsaw.
“We’re addressing this ambition – that these great investments in defence will bring greater value for money and, in the longer run, these capabilities.”
BAE Systems is partnering with the PGZ subsidiary Mesko, which makes ammunition and rockets, to build an artillery plant in Poland’s old southern industrial heartlands near Katowice.
By 2028, Poland plans three new munition factories. During a visit to the Mesko facility in August, Tusk said figures for 2023 showed Poland was capable of producing only 5,000 rounds of 155mm ammunition – a Nato-standard artillery shells. “More is used in one day on the Russian-Ukrainian front,” he said. This year, Poland will have increased production to 30,000 rounds, with a goal of 200,000 a year in the next two years.
This month, Luke Pollard, the UK minister for defence readiness, visited Czosnów for the opening of the MBDA facility. Pollard said it would help support jobs in both countries, including in Bristol, Stevenage and Bolton.
Despite this, Britain is increasing defence investment at a slower pace. The government has committed to increase spending from 2.3% of GDP last year to 3%, but has not spelled out precisely how or when this will be achieved.
In Poland, there are signs its investment spree is beginning to pay off for local contractors.
Maciej Klemm, the co-founder of Advanced Protection Systems (APS), which builds counter-drone systems in Gdynia, has increased its headcount from about 150 staff to 200 this year.
Amid growing Russian drone incursions into Polish airspace, APS is playing a role in the Warsaw’s $4bn San programme to build an “anti-drone wall” to protect the country’s eastern flank.
“We are spending a lot of money as a nation, and we are almost a poster child for it,” Klemm says. Splitting his time between Poland and the UK, where he still lives with his family after graduating from the University of Bristol in the 2000s, Klemm also sums up Poland’s recent economic history.
“I was moving to Britain at the time there was a big wave of Poles coming over here. Now after Brexit, that wave partly receded and went the other way. Now, companies like ourselves and others are showing we have technical talent; we can build on this, and grow companies in Poland.”

articles.title: European statements about war with Russia could become a "self-fulfilling prophecy" – Russian foreign minister
articles.body:
European statements about war with Russia could become a "self-fulfilling prophecy" – Russian foreign minister
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has claimed that calls by European leaders to prepare for a possible armed confrontation with Russia could provoke a war.
Source: Lavrov speaking at a final press conference at the UN General Assembly in New York, as quoted by Russian Kremlin-aligned media outlets
Details: Lavrov dismissed warnings about a possible Russian attack on Europe as "nonsense". Meanwhile, he criticised European countries for investing heavily in arms production and preparing their defences.
Lavrov claimed that European investment in weapons could ultimately prompt an attack by Europe on Russia and said that, in such an event, this would provoke a completely different response which would be "short".
Lavrov completely ignored the fact that Europe's military build-up and preparations for self-defence are a direct response to the Kremlin's systematic nuclear threats and hybrid aggression in a number of EU countries. In particular, Russian military aircraft have repeatedly entered the airspace of NATO member states.
In addition, during large-scale attacks on Ukraine, Russian kamikaze drones and missiles have repeatedly crossed borders and fallen on Polish and Romanian territory.
Quote from Lavrov: "We have no intention to fight Europe, to engage in warfare with Europe; that is utter nonsense. But Europe is preparing for war with us... This could become a self-fulfilling prophecy, such a position, because they are investing enormous amounts of money in arms production.
And at a certain juncture, a certain individual engaged in misadventures (there are many of those right now) will say: 'We've accumulated so much, what should we do with it? Oh, yes, we promised to attack Russia.' And under that scenario, they would attack us. As the president [Putin] said, we will not do so and he also said that it would be a completely different war, and it would be short." [Ukrainska Pravda does not refer to Vladimir Putin as Russian president – ed.]
Details: Lavrov's assurances that Russia "does not want war" echo statements made by the Russian leadership before previous acts of aggression. Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Russian diplomats repeatedly denied plans to attack Ukraine before Russia's invasion in 2014 and immediately before the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
In particular, on 21 January 2022, a month before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Lavrov insisted at a press conference in Geneva following bilateral talks with then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken that Russia had "never threatened the Ukrainian people" and had no intention of attacking anyone, while troop movements were purely an "internal matter".
On 15 February, he described warnings from Western intelligence agencies and media reports as "information terrorism".
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov repeatedly insisted in February 2022 that Russia had "never attacked anyone first". In particular, on 15 February, he described reports that Russia was preparing an invasion as an "unprecedented information campaign aimed at escalating tensions".
"Throughout its entire history, Russia has never attacked anyone first. And Russia, which has lived through so many wars, is the last country in Europe that would even want to utter the word 'war'," Peskov said on the Rossiya 1 television channel four days before the full-scale invasion.
Putin himself said at an expanded meeting of the Russian Defence Ministry Board on 21 December 2021 that "armed conflicts and bloodshed are absolutely not our choice; we do not want events to develop in this way".
Six days before the full-scale invasion, on 18 February 2022, Putin said at a joint press conference with self-proclaimed Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko that large-scale Russian military exercises were "purely defensive in nature and pose no threat to anyone".
"I'm a little late. I was just double-checking whether we're invading or not. No, we're not invading," the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said sarcastically as she opened a regular briefing on 16 February 2022.
On the same day, she wrote on Telegram: "A request to the US and UK mass disinformation media... Please publish the schedule of our 'invasions' for the coming year. I'd like to plan my holiday."
Background:
- On 10 September, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev threatened to wipe Lithuania "off the map" if nuclear weapons were deployed on its territory, and claimed that its NATO allies would not dare invoke Article 5 on collective defence.
- On 11 September, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius, saying that if nuclear weapons were deployed in Lithuania, the country would come under the sights of Russian nuclear weapons.
- On 21 September, it was reported that intelligence officials from three EU countries believed Moscow was planning to step up provocations against NATO in the coming months.
- On 25 September, Russian state news agency RIA Novosti published a column headlined "Russia is in for another SVO. It will be very short", which threatened Lithuania with a nuclear strike. The article was subsequently deleted.
This news has been updated since publication.
	
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Foreign Affairs: World learning from Iran’s ‘precise mass’ warfare as costly Western systems falter
articles.body:
Foreign Affairs: World learning from Iran’s ‘precise mass’ warfare as costly Western systems falter
TEHRAN — In a stunning admission that challenges the foundations of modern Western military doctrine, the influential American journal Foreign Affairs has published a comprehensive analysis revealing how Iran has successfully dismantled the aggressive war plans of the United States and Israel.
The detailed report serves as a post-mortem on the hubris of the Pentagon, explicitly stating that the future of global warfare is being dictated by the very strategies pioneered by Tehran, and that the world is now actively learning from the Iranian model of endurance and precision.
Foreign Affairs recounts the initial phase of the conflict, noting that when the United States and Israel launched their aggression against Iran, they expected a swift and decisive victory. According to the article, American planners anticipated that they would quickly overwhelm the government. The publication details the sheer scale of the assault, stating that in the war’s first 24 hours, American and Israeli forces hit roughly 1,000 targets. Over the following 39 days, they struck 12,000 more, with the stated intent of laying waste to Iran’s military infrastructure and eliminating top leadership. Yet, Foreign Affairs acknowledges that more than six months later, Iran not only remains intact but is arguably stronger than before. The journal concedes that Tehran immediately replaced its lost officials, struck back at Washington, and successfully shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, thereby driving up global energy prices and securing newfound political leverage that has left US officials deeply frustrated.
At the core of the Foreign Affairs analysis is the concept of “precise mass,” which the journal defines as high-volume, low-cost, precision-guided weapons. The publication notes that the age of this doctrine is well underway, stating that it is no longer possible for the US military to win a full-blown war simply by using small numbers of expensive, exquisite weapons to dazzle opponents. Crucially, the journal admits that offense is currently cheaper than defense, observing that the price of effective interceptors has yet to fall to the level of attack drones and missiles. It points out that militaries cannot endlessly block salvos of 35,000 dollar Shahed-136 attack drones with 4-million-dollar Patriot missiles.
Foreign Affairs further notes that the world is learning from Iran, building on lessons that were already emerging in other conflicts. The journal provides an extensive list of nations that are now pivoting to adopt this Iranian-style strategy. The publication says six European states, including France, Germany, and the United Kingdom, have signed a letter of intent to jointly develop a one-way attack drone, and Saudi Arabia has unveiled its own attack drone modeled on the Shahed. Even Japan has requested a record 55.6 billion-dollar defense budget, largely to purchase vast quantities of attack drones.
The report by Foreign Affairs also addresses the failure of the American air campaign to neutralize Iran’s capabilities. It reveals that in the years before the war, Iran built a vast underground network of missile infrastructure spread across its territory that has proved impossible for US and Israeli forces to eliminate. The United States struggled significantly to destroy these dispersed production facilities, which Foreign Affairs notes inverted the assumptions that have guided American airpower campaigns since Operation Desert Storm in 1991.
Foreign Affairs provides a scathing critique of the organizational inertia within the US military. The article explains that the most powerful militaries are organized around small numbers of exquisite, expensive, and hard-to-produce platforms like Tomahawk missiles and F-35s. These units are trained to avoid wasting systems, whereas “precise mass” requires units to move quickly and prioritize volume over perfection. Because the US is locked into these legacy structures, it has struggled to adapt. Washington is now finding itself burning through its stockpiles of Tomahawks, SM-6 missiles, and other expensive systems to deal with the damage inflicted by Iran, leaving the US scrambling to resupply its own stocks and those of partners in places like Taiwan and Ukraine.
Regarding the role of technology, Foreign Affairs admits that while the US has utilized artificial intelligence systems to identify and recommend targets—even citing the use of the Maven Smart System—these advantages are not the deciding factor. The journal acknowledges that the current race to artificial general intelligence is not the primary driver of how AI is shaping warfare.
In its concluding remarks, Foreign Affairs issues a stark warning to the American defense establishment. It insists that the country’s reliance on exquisite, expensive, and hard-to-produce weapons is no longer sufficient to win wars or protect allies. The journal stresses that the United States must stop carrying on as if the Cold War just ended. It argues that if the US wants to maintain its military edge, it has no choice but to embrace the reality of “precise mass”—a strategy that Iran has already mastered and demonstrated to the world. Ultimately, Foreign Affairs admits that through indigenous resilience and the successful deployment of cost-effective strike capabilities, Iran has proven that a determined nation can stymie even the most conventionally powerful military in the world.

articles.title: The next war will be fought here. America and Europe will be enemies
articles.body:
The next war will be fought here. America and Europe will be enemies
This September, the Arctic quietly widened the rift between presumed transatlantic allies. Brussels’ attempts to mitigate growing US influence in the region have so far been unsystematic but intense. The Arctic Summit held in Finnish Lapland and the subsequent EU-Canada talks, where European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed granting Ottawa associate member status, should be viewed in the context of the new agreement between the US and Greenland.
The EU is using its usual competitive methods in the polar race, plunging into a de facto confrontation with the US. An alternative to this could have been attempts to find its own legitimate place among the major players; however, the window of opportunity for such initiatives has closed, which leaves the space no alternatives other than the prospects of a hybrid war in which Brussels and Washington are rivals.
The EU’s familiar patterns beyond the Arctic Circle
Twelve EU countries and the bloc’s leadership attended the Arctic Summit in Lapland this month, where they agreed upon a radical securitization of polar policy, officially recognizing the region as a “geopolitical hotspot.”
To understand the specifics of the bloc’s Arctic ambitions, it’s important to note that the union’s members lack any significant infrastructure of their own on the polar map. In the wake of Brexit, the EU no longer has its own sovereign Arctic borders directly connected to the Arctic Ocean. Norway and Iceland remain outside the union, Greenland remains an autonomous Danish overseas territory, and Finland and Sweden are geographically cut off from the ocean. Moreover, the EU as a single bloc completely lacks its own Arctic icebreaker fleet – the few national vessels of the Scandinavian countries are incapable of ensuring true strategic dominance.
Lacking either geographical rights or military hardware, Brussels has reduced its Arctic strategy solely to environmental concerns, climate monitoring, and the protection of indigenous peoples. In 2008, the EU formally designated the Arctic as a zone of its strategic interests, and in 2016 and 2021, key EU Arctic strategies were adopted.
This approach began to change in 2022–2025, when, against the backdrop of a rapidly shifting geopolitical situation in the world, US claims to Greenland triggered the performative landing of European troops on the island. The Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi this month, which was informal in nature, confirmed the shift in the focus of the EU’s interests.
The final agreement formalized the shift from an environmental agenda to a “hard power” strategy: the parties pledged to sharply increase investment in military mobility, satellite surveillance, and cross-border infrastructure in the north, as well as coordinate the blocking of Russia’s “shadow fleet” under the pretext of environmental protection. These decisions, reinforced by the leaders’ demonstrative visit to the Finnish Lapland Air Wing military airbase, formed the basis of the new EU Arctic Strategy, which Foreign Minister Kaja Kallas promised to present in October 2026.
After the summit, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen went on to invite Canada to become an associate member of the EU in the context of trade and tariff disagreements between Ottawa and Washington. The mere suggestion of such an alliance has maximized the politicization of the Arctic agenda, making the outcome highly unpredictable.
It’s worth noting that Brussels’ aspirations for leadership are always specific. It’s enough to recall Francois Duchene’s concepts of “civic” power and Jan Manners’ idea of “normative” power, which explain that Brussels projects its influence on the international stage through its economic model, diplomacy, and the export of legal and ethical standards. This approach has been further developed by Mark Leonard, who called the EU an expanding “invisible empire” and argued that the EU’s influence is based on the mechanism of attracting and integrating its neighbors, and Ana Bradford, who described the phenomenon of the “Brussels effect” – a mechanism by which the EU’s vast internal market allows it to unilaterally dictate regulatory rules to transnational corporations and governments around the world.
It is precisely in this vein that we should understand what is happening. Brussels is employing its standard, decades-old methods of supranational control. Unable to compete in the realm of real icebreaker technology and innovative logistics, the EU is attempting to redirect the race to its familiar channel of bureaucratic regulations, climate quotas, and virtual budget allocations, all while cloaking it in the most anti-Russian, defensive rhetoric possible.
Its urgent proposal to pursue a “unique” alliance with Canada is a classic attempt at normatively co-opting another country’s sovereignty. Brussels seeks to act as an “environmental and technological sponsor” and thus gain access to Canadian resources, thereby legitimizing its presence in the high north through the use of foreign geography.
It is for this reason that seemingly unrelated countries, including some of Moscow’s most committed foes, were invited to the summit in Lapland: a crowd had to be assembled to give the story a larger scope. It included Mediterranean Greece and Black Sea Romania, as well as the Baltic states, which were simply counting on participating in the new EU “polar” grants.
Why doesn’t this work?
Until recently, European activity has served as a mere backdrop for US policy in the Arctic. Washington has spent decades building an Arctic empire of steel, radar arrays, and military bases, relying on a strategy of strict deterrence. In Alaska, the US has deployed a powerful air force hub of fifth-generation F-35 and F-22 fighter jets, and American nuclear submarines have learned to maneuver under the ice. In September 2026, the White House and Ottawa began the practical phase of deploying Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radars (A-OTHR) as part of the modernization of NORAD, which will allow US command to monitor airspace all the way to the Arctic Circle in real time.
At the same time, Washington is accelerating the elimination of its main vulnerability – its backlog of icebreakers: the Bollinger shipyards are assembling the first heavy polar ship in half a century, the USCGC Polar Sentinel. Washington’s plans by 2030 include the launch of two more heavy icebreakers and the construction of the deep-water military port of Nome near the Bering Strait. Furthermore, active lobbying is underway to promote the concept of “freedom of navigation” to allow unimpeded passage through the Northwest Passage, significantly shortening the sea route from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean.
The US’s greatest geopolitical victory, however, was the signing of a trilateral agreement with Denmark and Greenland in September. Under the agreement, the Pentagon takes permanent military control of Greenland’s security, urgently reopening the bases in Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig and expanding and modernizing the Pituffik air force base in the north. This document imposed a direct veto on major investments by non-NATO and non-European countries, turning the island into a closed American bastion and blocking European businesses from accessing local rare earth metals.
In the European press, attitudes toward the trilateral defense agreement range from irony to muted relief, but the key leitmotif is the thesis of Donald Trump’s “defeat” and concessions. However, an analysis of the benefits to both sides reveals something else. The United States, having expanded its defense rights on the island and gained complete control over its economic resources, skillfully left any social obligations outside the agreement.
American strategists magnanimously left the obligation to provide benefits, subsidies, and social guarantees for the local Greenlandic population of fewer than 60,000 people out of the state budget, as it was the “sovereign right” of Copenhagen. Washington pocketed all the geostrategic and raw material dividends while shifting the maintenance of the depressed territory to weakening European taxpayers. It turns out that Trump’s European allies were willing to sign what he wanted, while publicly declaring that they had won.
This episode aptly characterizes the nature of the escalating standoff between the allies, in which the US, with its aggressiveness, puts the Europeans on the defensive, leaving them unable to maintain their positions. What makes this standoff unique is that there is no direct military clash between the US and the EU in the Arctic – they ostensibly remain NATO allies facing Russia and China. However, the region has de facto become a zone of intense geoeconomic espionage, trade wars, competition for ports, and the monopolization of polar resources, with the US securing military control of Greenland and the EU attempting to maintain its economic position through Canada and the Scandinavian countries. Interesting developments in the struggle for the Northwest Passage are likely to emerge.
The EU is extremely vulnerable in this standoff. This is due to its geographic isolation, a complete lack of hard power instruments, and a critical defense dependence on its main competitor. The attempt by European “hawks” to turn Article 42.7 of the Lisbon Treaty into a political shield and send symbolic contingents to Greenland in January turned out to be a bluff, which Donald Trump simply ignored, blackmailing countries with the threat of 25% tariffs. In the context of harsh American neo-mercantilism, under pressure from competition with China, Anu Bradford’s vaunted “Brussels effect” has collapsed: by establishing strict “green” standards at the Lapland summit, Europe had hoped to regulate the polar market. But the US, acting on the principle of “like it or not,” is hijacking the agenda, proving that in this polar race, Brussels’ old models simply will not work.
Prospects and Alternatives: Effects for Russia and China
As political scientist and Valdai Club program director Timofey Bordachev rightly notes, historical experience shows that conflicts among the Western elites have typically led to the large-scale restructuring of the international order, helping to keep the global system under the control of a narrow group of states. However, today, in the changed historical context, the results of the polar confrontation between Washington and Brussels are completely unpredictable. On the world stage, the number of sovereign players has radically expanded, and the West’s influence over them is either completely absent or negligible.
The growing transatlantic rift is opening up crucial strategic advantages for the Arctic’s major players – Moscow and Beijing. Russia is systematically developing the Northern Sea Route (NSR) as a key, protected, year-round global artery. While Washington is still attempting to complete its first heavy icebreaker in half a century, Russia possesses the world’s only and absolutely unparalleled nuclear icebreaker fleet.
For China, Brussels’ polar impasse serves as a direct call to action. Under American pressure, Beijing is pushing forward with its “Ice Silk Road” doctrine. Chinese businesses are freely redirecting investments into Russia’s Arctic LNG megaprojects, bypassing vulnerable southern routes. The EU states, having maneuvered but failed to escape American traps, are leaving the region with nothing, cementing the absolute geopolitical dominance of Moscow and Beijing in the ice.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Russia Not Ready To End War, Cites Spending On Jet-Powered Drones
articles.body:
Russian drone strikes killed at least four people in Ukraine overnight and into September 27, including one person in the capital, Kyiv, and three in the southeastern Zaporizhzhya region, Ukrainian officials said.
In Kyiv, a man was killed when a Russian drone struck a nonresidential building in the Solomyansky district, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
A fire broke out at a car-repair facility in the same district, while another nonresidential building was hit, the agency said.
It shared images showing firefighters battling fires at the damaged buildings.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a Russian strike on the Shevchenkivsky district injured a woman and two 16-year-old children. The three were hospitalized, he said.
In the Zaporizhzhya region in the country's southeast , three people were killed in Russian strikes, according to the regional military administration.
A man was killed in the village of Komyshuvakha, where one house was destroyed and several others damaged, it said. Two more people, a man and a woman, were killed when a Russian strike hit their car in the village of Novotavriyske.
Four people were also wounded in the attack on Komyshuvakha, the administration said.
Trump Tells Kyiv To 'Settle' War
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has declined to confirm that he had agreed to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's statement on September 25 that Trump had made a “final decision” to grant Kyiv a license to produce the air-defense missiles.
Asked about the Patriot agreement on September 26, Trump said he wanted Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin to “settle” their war.
Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on September 22.
“We talked about a lot of different subjects, and many of those subjects...very strong agreement,” Trump told reporters about the meeting.
“But you know what I want him to do? Make a deal. I want him to settle with Putin, and I want Putin to settle with him.”
Zelenskyy said after the meeting that he hoped Washington would help end the war “as soon as possible.” He has also called on Trump to maintain pressure on Moscow, including through new sanctions.
Zelenskyy: Putin Seeks Excuses To Keep Fighting
In his latest nightly video address, Zelenskyy said Moscow is showing no signs it is ready to end its war on its neighbor and he called on the West to remain united in efforts to force the Kremlin to the negotiating table.
“Obviously, the Russians are not preparing to stop their war, at least for now,” Zelenskyy said, citing intelligence reports that Moscow is intending to hike spending on deadly jet-powered drones and other munitions.
Putin “always finds some lame excuse -- not to meet, not to hold a trilateral, not to talk, not to end it, not to stop the killing.”
“It has been the same with him for years – and all our partners feel it. He is looking for excuses to keep waging the war. It always sounds the same -- and our recent meeting with the US president showed that,” Zelenskyy added in the September 26 address.
'Expand Their War'
The Ukrainian leader claimed that Russia plans to spend $12 billion in the upcoming year on the production of “jet-powered drones and loitering munitions alone -- just on this one category of weapons.”
“This directly concerns our partners as well. Many intelligence services have information that the Russians want to expand their war, their activities, to more countries. Perhaps to other regions. That is why we need to build our defense together. That is why we need to defend ourselves together, preventively.”
He said Ukrainian air defenses have been able to intercept 55 percent of jet-powered drones launched by Russia as overnight attacks on Kyiv and other cities have become increasingly frequent as cold weather starts to set in.
“We are working on this together -- with America, with Europe, with Canada, with Japan, and with many others around the world who are helping us, helping Ukraine, helping our people,” he added.
Zelenskyy wrote on social media that “we ask President Trump to implement the Lindsey Graham Act against Russia and everyone who props up its war financially."
The law, signed by Trump a week ago, gives the president sweeping new authority to impose sanctions and tariffs on Russia, its energy sector, and foreign governments and entities that help Moscow evade existing restrictions.
The Ukrainian president told journalists in New York that Washington had proposed holding what would be the first Ukraine-Russia-US meeting in many months at a relatively low "technical level," with the United Arab Emirates serving as host.
While there was no immediate confirmation from the United States, Putin said that all peace proposals were "on the table" but added that Moscow had to weigh its interests.
More Infrastructure Hit
French news agency AFP said an analysis of data from a leading conflict monitor indicate a significant increase in strikes against Ukraine's infrastructure over recent months.
It said figures compiled by the Armed Conflict Location and Event (ACLED) show Russia has struck twice as many warehouses in the Kyiv region over the past three months as in all previous years of the war combined.
ACLED recorded some 100 strikes or series of strikes on civilian storage facilities in the Kyiv region since mid-June, up from just 50 between February 2022 and mid-June of of this year.

articles.title: What Germany’s Wingcopter 262 Means for Ukraine’s Drone War
articles.body:
For years, the German startup Wingcopter built its reputation on civilian logistics. The company engineered autonomous aircraft to deliver life-saving vaccines and medical supplies to isolated communities in Africa and the Pacific. Today, it is making a direct jump into the military sector.
On Sept. 14 Wingcopter unveiled the Wingcopter 262, an all-electric tactical reconnaissance drone equipped with AI. Through a joint venture with Ukrainian manufacturer TAF Industries, these drones are headed straight to the front lines.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The move marks two critical developments in the war: commercial tech companies repurposing their civilian tools for military use, and European allies moving Ukrainian defense manufacturing into NATO territory to protect factories from Russian airstrikes.
Hybrid design
The Wingcopter 262 fills a vital tactical gap for Ukrainian forces. It uses a tilt-rotor design, meaning it can take off and land vertically in tight spaces just like a helicopter, but once airborne, it tilts its motors to fly fast and efficiently like a traditional airplane.
This design gets rid of the need for long runways or heavy catapult launchers. A single soldier can carry the 10-kilogram drone into rugged terrain and launch it in just a few minutes.
Zelensky Says Putin Keeps Finding Excuses to Continue the War
Once in the air, the drone can cover a tactical range of 150 kilometers and stay aloft for up to six hours. It carries high-resolution visual and thermal cameras backed by built-in AI, which helps operators spot targets, track movements and process imagery instantly.
Beating signal jamming
One of the drone’s biggest selling points for the front line is its ability to operate when GPS signals are completely cut off.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Russian electronic warfare units continuously flood the front lines with heavy jamming signals. Standard commercial drones that rely entirely on satellite navigation often lose control, drift off course, or crash the moment they hit a jammed sector. Wingcopter built the 262’s navigation system to stay on course even when GPS is blocked, using software fixes shaped directly by feedback from combat operations in Ukraine.
The German-Ukrainian deal
The partnership behind the drone represents a new approach to European defense. Wingcopter and TAF Industries, Ukraine’s largest drone producer, launched a joint venture under the “Build with Ukraine” initiative.
This arrangement fixes a major security issue for Kyiv. Domestic military factories inside Ukraine face constant threats from Russian long-range missile and drone attacks. By partnering with Wingcopter, TAF Industries can mass-produce its battle-tested designs inside secure facilities in Germany. In return, Ukrainian troops get priority access to the new Wingcopter 262 platform.
This partnership creates a shared defense pipeline, which is Ukrainian battle experience combined with German manufacturing power and funding.
Commercial tech reshaping defense
The Wingcopter 262 shows how fast commercial technology can adapt to battlefield realities. The engineering needed to deliver emergency medical packages in harsh weather over long distances turns out to be almost identical to what a military drone needs, with long battery life, reliable navigation and tough airframes that resist signal interference.
As European countries increase their defense spending, military procurement teams are turning away from slow-moving traditional defense contractors. Building a new military aircraft from scratch often takes years. Commercial startups like Wingcopter, which have spent a decade perfecting light electric flight and autonomous software, can deliver proven systems in a fraction of that time.
A high-stakes test for NATO’s future
The deployment of the Wingcopter 262 in Ukraine will act as a real-world stress test. If the aircraft holds up against Russian air defenses and electronic warfare, it will likely capture the attention of other NATO militaries looking to upgrade their tactical reconnaissance gear.
More importantly, the partnership between Wingcopter and TAF Industries proves that it is by moving past one-off weapon donations and fully linking Ukrainian tech into the broader European defense industry, that Western nations can sustain Ukraine over the long haul.

articles.title: German foreign minister sees no readiness for peace during first meeting with Russian counterpart since 2022
articles.body:
German foreign minister sees no readiness for peace during first meeting with Russian counterpart since 2022
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said that during a meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov, he saw no willingness on the part of the Russian delegation to refrain from further escalation.
Source: Deutsche Welle, citing Wadephul speaking on German TV channel ZDF; Tagesschau
Details: The officials met on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. Wadephul said he had used the conversation to urge Russia to abandon its path of escalation.
He said he had made it clear to the Russian delegation that actions such as the attempted sabotage involving drones at Leipzig/Halle Airport were unacceptable.
Wadephul said he had made it clear to Lavrov that "a line had been crossed, we expect this not to happen again, and we are ready to respond at any time".
Meanwhile, Wadephul stressed that he had not conducted any negotiations with Lavrov concerning Ukraine's future. The minister emphasised that such negotiations were a matter solely for the Ukrainians themselves.
Quote from Wadephul: "There are indeed fundamental differences between the positions of our governments, and these also need to be discussed. During the Cold War, exchanges of views and contacts between the two sides never ceased. And I thought it was right, particularly now, to try to find an initial opportunity for such dialogue."
Details: The German foreign minister warned the Russian representative that Berlin would continue its comprehensive support for Ukraine and maintain economic pressure on Russia.
"This support is absolutely unwavering, and Russia must now come to the negotiating table. There is no justification whatsoever for this war, which is claiming countless lives, including Russian lives, but above all those of Ukrainian civilians," Wadephul said.
However, the minister acknowledged that he had seen no willingness on the part of the Russian delegation to heed his call to begin negotiations on ending the war.
"To all those who keep saying that Germany needs to negotiate, that Germany needs to talk to Russia, I say now: we are doing so. And unfortunately, Russia is currently showing no willingness to adopt a constructive negotiating position," the foreign minister said.
According to Russian state propaganda agency TASS, the meeting lasted "just over 20 minutes" and covered "bilateral relations and the situation surrounding Ukraine". Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the meeting had taken place at the request of the German side.
The foreign ministers of Germany and Russia last met in Moscow on 18 January 2022. At the time, Annalena Baerbock travelled to the Russian capital amid Russia's rapid military build-up near Ukraine's borders and warnings from Western intelligence agencies that Moscow was preparing for a full-scale invasion.
Background:
- The resumption of diplomatic contacts at this level was preceded by a series of Russian nuclear threats against European countries.
- On 10 September, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev threatened to wipe Lithuania "off the map" if nuclear weapons were deployed on its territory, and claimed that its NATO allies would not dare invoke Article 5 on collective defence.
- On 11 September, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius, saying that if nuclear weapons were deployed in Lithuania, the country would come under the sights of Russian nuclear weapons.
- On 21 September, it was reported that intelligence officials from three EU countries believed Moscow was planning to step up provocations against NATO in the coming months.
- On 25 September, Russian state news agency RIA Novosti published a column headlined "Russia is in for another SVO. It will be very short", which threatened Lithuania with a nuclear strike. The article was subsequently deleted.
- On the same day, political scientist Sergei Karaganov, an adviser to Russian leader Vladimir Putin, called on television for preparations to use weapons of mass destruction.
- "Europe is the source of humanity's greatest troubles and Russia's greatest troubles. A nuclear war in Europe can easily be won... We would rather it did not come to that. But we must be prepared for it, and they must know that," Karaganov said.

articles.title: Iran insists on diplomatic solution after Trump rejects peace plan
articles.body:
Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel after U.S. President Donald Trump said he rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on social media. "Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock."
Iran announced a peace proposal last week at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators. Trump said on Saturday he rejected the plan and argued that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Despite Trump's public statements, mediators facilitating Iran's talks with the United States have not officially relayed a U.S. rejection of the plan, according to Araghchi.
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi posted.
The U.S. has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to stop Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, which have drastically reduced shipping through the area even as Trump repeatedly asserts that the U.S. controls the waterway.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
It said Trump was privately skeptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November U.S. midterm elections.
A U.S. official had said earlier that discussions with Iran through mediators were "positive and constructive."
Conflict has disrupted oil flows, harmed global economy
The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through a critical shipping lane and taken a toll on the global economy.
Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
"If there is seriousness on the U.S. side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," Araghchi said. If the U.S. were to agree, the warring parties could start wider talks "on mutually agreed subjects."
That could potentially include discussions of Iran's nuclear program. Trump has said Tehran must never acquire a nuclear bomb, while a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the U.S. accepted its peace deal.
Iran would grant no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, the official said.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation", said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion."
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that "we're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons."
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed to end the war, which began on February 28 with U.S. and Israeli attacks.
Since then, the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading the conventional forces of Iran and damaging its already ailing economy.
Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck U.S. allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests.
Yemen's Saudi-led coalition said early on Saturday it had intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by the Houthis toward the kingdom.

articles.title: How Australia's defence force is turning AI into a 'silicon commander'
articles.body:
How Australia's defence force is turning AI into a 'silicon commander'
In the weeks before Christmas last year, high over the remote desert of South Australia, a small slice of aviation and AI history was made.
The Ghost Bat — an Australian-made aircraft, about two-thirds the size of a regular fighter jet — shot down a target with an air-to-air missile.
What was remarkable was its pilot.
The Ghost Bat is autonomous. There is no human controlling it from a cockpit, nor a drone pilot on land behind a joystick.
It is a glimpse into the future of warfare, with artificial intelligence playing a far greater role in how militaries prepare, plan and carry out strikes.
And it's not unique — armed drones are being found in Ukraine with powerful "minicomputers" and no visible antennas, leading Ukrainian forces to conclude they were almost certainly piloted by AI.
And Ukraine has its own AI-piloted drones targeting key Russian supply routes.
Recently, Defence Minister Richard Marles flew to the United States to meet in person with representatives from firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google on where their models are heading.
Australia's defence force is one of many around the globe racing to work out how to best integrate AI into much of what it does, from quicker intelligence assessments to piloting platforms with lethal payloads.
And it is working out what guardrails need to be put in place, acknowledging that while AI has a role to play, humans need the final say when triggers are being pulled.
AI (sort of) takes flight
Aircraft like the Ghost Bat and its underwater counterpart, the Ghost Shark (an autonomous submarine), are the most visible signs of artificial intelligence being adopted within the Australian Defence Force (ADF).
The Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) describes the Ghost Bat as "a pathfinder for the integration of autonomous systems and artificial intelligence to create smart human-machine teams".
But Air Marshal Stephen Chappell, the chief of Air Force, points out that there are some deliberate limitations put on the brain of the Ghost Bat.
"AI has been involved in designing and developing the Ghost Bat, but it does not operate off AI. It operates off deterministic programming," he said.
"So, we have designed through digital twin testing with the support of AI, just thousands upon thousands upon thousands of options for the [Ghost Bat] to take.
"And it will choose one of those options, but we know exactly how that option plays out."
He said in the test-firing last year, an operator based in an E7 Wedgetail aircraft first told the Ghost Bat to engage the target, but the aircraft's system then worked out a plan as to how best to do so.
Still, the operator in the E7 gave a final authorisation before the missile was launched.
"It is not making up its own game plan itself. Therefore we have full confidence in what it will do and what it won't do,"
"And that's really important from a legal and ethical point of view."
AI already making a mark
While the ADF is still in many ways exploring the best use of AI, the technology is already being adopted to significant effect elsewhere.
Israel's use of artificial intelligence during its campaign in Gaza has attracted attention.
Analysis from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) says Israel's use of AI in warfare has increased "exponentially" since the October 7 terror attacks and the launch of its war in Gaza.
Reporting by progressive Israeli outlet +972 Magazine suggested that an AI-powered analysis tool known as Lavender was used in the first few weeks of the war to generate a list of 37,000 people, suspected to be military operatives with Hamas or the Palestinian Islamic Jihad, as possible targets for air strikes.
Israel has rejected suggestions it was using an AI tool "that identifies terrorist operatives or tries to predict whether a person is a terrorist", and said while information systems are used in target identification, analysts must conduct "independent examinations".
The IISS analysis suggests while the use of such systems has allowed for quicker decisions, it has also increased the risk for errors, as targets are identified faster than humans can possibly assess them.
Last month, the United Nations and International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) issued a joint call for a ban on autonomous weapons that are "unpredictable" or that target human beings.
The two bodies raised concerns that "life-and-death decisions will be taken by machines".
ICRC legal advisor Georgia Hinds said while advances like AI and autonomous weapons in warfare often came with promises that they would help limit civilian casualties, often it appeared that the opposite was true.
"We continue to see conflicts that cause unacceptable levels of civilian harm, and that's in some of the conflicts that have the most technologically sophisticated means of warfare," she said.
A seat at the command table
Concerns about human involvement in AI decision-making extend from those effectively holding the trigger, all the way up to those sitting around Defence's most powerful table.
While aircraft like the Ghost Bat are a physical sign of AI adoption within Defence, experts argue the bigger influence is actually largely unseen.
That is the use of AI to inform critical decision-making, analysing intelligence and making recommendations that go before those tasked with making the most important calls.
Aina Turillazzi from the Australian National University's Strategic and Defence Studies Centre said that was where the real leaps were being made.
"Most of what AI does in the military is upstream of any weapon," she said.
"It's more about assembling the picture of the situation that a human then makes a decision about."
She points to the ADF's adoption of technology such as Palantir's Maven Smart system, which has caused contention over the political links of its founders and concerns about data sovereignty.
Australian Strategic Policy Institute senior analyst Malcolm Davis described the role technology such as Maven Smart was already playing in conflicts, including the US-Iran war, as that of a "silicon commander".
"They're able to very rapidly assess the battle space, reduce the number of staff that they have to prepare orders and analysis and carry out that process much more rapidly than what would be possible without AI," he said.
The ADF has previously told parliament that Maven Smart was so far being used in a "sandbox" — that is, within a closed environment and not plugged into broader defence networks.
There are examples of artificial intelligence breaking out of "sandbox" environments, most notably the Hugging Face incident in which hundreds of AI agents worked together to break out of their environment and hack another company.
As AI enters the intelligence-assessing and decision-making picture, there are already concerns about an over-reliance on its enormous power.
What a Soviet-era nuclear scare can teach us about AI
Ms Turillazzi points to the story of Stanislav Petrov, a Soviet lieutenant colonel who in 1983 steered the globe away from a possible nuclear disaster.
When warning systems he was monitoring raised alerts about an imminent nuclear attack from the United States, Petrov's decision to pause and investigate a possible false alarm avoided the outbreak of accidental nuclear war.
As it turns out, sensors on a Soviet-era satellite mistook sunlight on clouds as the flaming trail of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
Ms Turillazzi said Petrov's momentous decision to pause and assess, rather than blindly accept automated warnings, was even more critical in an era of much more powerful artificial intelligence.
"Petrov was right. The risk with AI decision support isn't that the machine malfunctions, but it's that under pressure, people stop assessing the evidence and start simply confirming the recommendation or the evidence," she said.
She said it pointed to the risk of automation bias — that those interpreting AI-informed analysis place a greater weight on it than their own judgement, even subconsciously.
And she said the risks compounded in a conflict environment that moves faster than ever, where speed becomes a premium.
"The same compression that's an asset day-to-day becomes a liability in a crisis situation," she said.
"If alerts are moving faster than diplomats can absorb them, or decision-makers can absorb them, leaders end up making decisions about readiness before the intelligence picture is complete."
She said counterintuitively, when the stakes were higher, the decision-making process needed to be slowed down.
"Any AI decision support system used for planning or targeting should have a crisis mode that raises the evidentiary bar, surfaces uncertainty rather than smoothens it, and forces a pause at defined points," she said.
"Because speed is a feature but brakes, in my opinion, are the missing part here."
Staying on, or off, the loop
Defence's existing AI policies state clearly that a human operator will always be responsible, and accountable, for any action carried out by artificial intelligence.
"Human judgement and accountability is central to lawful, legitimate and responsible use of AI, and designated Defence personnel [Accountable Officers] will always be accountable for its use, decisions and outcomes," it states.
In practical terms, that means remaining "on the loop" and ensuring that someone maintains oversight of what AI is doing and intervenes at critical points (like using lethal force).
Dr Davis said while liberal democracies, including Australia, were likely to keep those policies in place, there was no guarantee that potential adversaries would adhere to the same standards.
"We simply don't know whether our authoritarian adversaries are going to do the same thing," he said.
"They may see it more to their advantage to have humans 'off the loop' and to allow the AI to have greater control.
"That will increase their ability to [make decisions] faster, and so that gives them a military advantage."
In an interview with the ABC, Mr Marles was asked if he was concerned about how AI might be adopted and employed by potential adversaries.
"The answer to that is the answer that we give a lot, that we live in the most complex and, in some ways, the most threatening strategic landscape that we have since the end of World War II," he said.
"We need to be advancing our own technology so that friends and partners and allies have the technological advantage here.
"We also need to be doing this within a set of guardrails, which means that what we are doing in terms of the development of our defence capability across our friends and partners is about making the world a safer place."

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian defense plant producing missile components, General Staff says
articles.body:
Russian Defence Ministry officials show off the Russia's 9M729 cruise missile at the military Patriot Park outside Moscow on January 23, 2019. (Vasily Maximov/AFP via Getty Images)
Ukrainian forces struck the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in Russia’s Rostov Oblast overnight on Sept. 26, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
A fire broke out at the plant’s foundry, while equipment in five production buildings was damaged, according to the military. The extent of the damage could not be immediately verified.
The plant, located in the city of Azov, is part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation and produces opto-mechanical and optoelectronic equipment, electronics for artillery, missile and anti-tank weapons, as well as radar homing systems for guided missiles. Ukraine’s military intelligence also lists the facility as part of Russia’s defense-industrial complex.
The General Staff said the plant produces equipment used by the Russian military and described the strike as an effort to reduce Russia’s military-industrial capabilities.
The strike on the Azov plant followed a separate Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Ilsky oil refinery in Krasnodar Krai overnight. Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said the refinery, located about 400 kilometers (250 miles) from the drone launch area, was targeted by the 1st Separate Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces, the 414th Unmanned Systems Brigade, known as "Madyar’s Birds," and other Ukrainian units.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point said the refinery was hit by FP-1 drones and subsequently halted operations. According to the company, three primary oil-processing units and a tank farm were damaged in the strike.

articles.title: Zelensky Urges China, India to Pressure Russia as Weekly Strikes Top 2,200 Drones
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky called on China, India and other major non-Western powers to take a stronger stance on Russia, saying Moscow had launched more than 2,200 attack drones, about 1,650 guided aerial bombs (KABs) and 38 missiles at Ukraine this week alone.
In a statement posted to Telegram on Sunday, Sept. 27, Zelensky said overnight Russian strikes killed three people in Zaporizhzhia region and a man in Kyiv, while Russian forces struck a data center twice in the morning of that same day.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, there is a lack of a consistently strong position from China and India, Brazil and South Africa, the G20 countries and the Global South,” Zelensky said, adding that “each of these countries has influence over Russia and can help make peace a reality.”
Ukraine continues working with its partners, including the US, EU, Canada, Japan and Australia, to strengthen its defense and pursue diplomacy.
“Building guaranteed, dignified security here in Ukraine means adding to security and stability globally,” he said.
Kyiv data center hit twice
According to Zelensky, a significant share of the 38 missiles Russia launched this week were ballistic.
Three people, including two children, were injured in the first of the two strikes on the Kyiv data center, he said, adding that overnight strikes also hit residential buildings, energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in the Odesa, Kharkiv, Sumy, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Zhytomyr and Kyiv regions.
Russian Attacks on Kyiv Kill 1, Injure at Least 10 Since Saturday
Earlier, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a woman and two 16-year-olds had been hospitalized after the strike in the capital’s Shevchenkivskyi district.
On Saturday, Russian forces struck Kyiv’s Cosmonova data centers, affecting local television broadcasts and overall civilian ability to receive critical information.
The attack followed an almost three-week campaign against data centers, with four already hit on Wednesday.
China’s leverage over Moscow
China and India are the two largest buyers of Russian crude oil globally, providing revenue that helps sustain Moscow’s war effort. Beijing also supplies Russia with weapons-making components, while India remains one of largest buyers of Russian arms.
Brazil and South Africa, along with China and India, are fellow members of the BRICS bloc with Russia, which is why they have largely avoided taking sides – at least publicly – in the war against Ukraine.
Although US President Donald Trump gained new legislative powers to target Russia’s major oil and gas buyers with tariffs of up to 100% after signing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, it remains unclear whether he will use them against China. Imposing such tariffs could potentially undermine the trade stability Washington is seeking to preserve with Beijing, despite the fact that cutting out Russia’s oil revenue would prove significantly meaningful to Ukraine.
Zelensky has repeatedly called on Trump to exercise his new rights as Russia increases its strikes on civilian infrastructure across Ukraine.
His latest remarks came only two days after Russian PresidentVladimir Putin revived claims that Russian speakers’ rights were being violated in the Baltic states – the same rhetoric the Kremlin used to justify its invasion of Ukraine.
While Zelensky continues to appeal to countries with significant economic ties to Russia, NATO faces a growing wave of Russian hybrid attacks, with the line between sabotage and direct aggression increasingly blurred.
Meanwhile, Kyiv and Washington continue working jointly on brokering an end to the war.
On Wednesday, 51 countries backed a joint statement at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations.
Washington has also invited Putin to the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December, with Trump urging him to “settle the war.”
Moscow, however, has shown no sign of backing down. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the Kremlin would not pause its “special military operation” even during negotiations, while Putin blamed Kyiv for stalled diplomacy and has so far rejected every proposal for a direct meeting.
“It has been the same with him for years – and all our partners feel it. He is looking for excuses to keep waging the war,” Zelensky said on Saturday, Sept. 26.
“It always sounds the same – and our recent meeting with the US President showed that.”

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1676: Zelenskyy offers NATO’s neighbors Ukraine’s drone-defense know-how
articles.body:
Military
Ukraine destroys record 76 Russian air-defense systems this month, losses analyst says Russia "will never be able to restore". The 76 systems destroyed this month beat a record from July 2023.
Russia's air defenses can't protect all its strategic sites once Ukraine's ballistic missiles are ready, expert says. Russia's best interceptors cluster around the capital.
Intelligence and technology
Combat shows speed alone can't catch Russia's jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers' assurances. So why can't they stop them?. Eight makers said their interceptors were ready last winter. They weren't.
Pentagon brings in Ukrainian jamming maker to do to its candidate drones what Russia does to Ukraine's, and see which survives. Unwave brought four electronic-warfare systems to a US base to jam the drones the Pentagon is choosing to buy.
War's next tech leap: Former Ukraine's defense minister behind "Army of Drones" is now creating new "Army of Robots". The architect of Ukraine's "Army of Drones" wants robots to do the deadliest work.
International
Asked if Ukraine would send troops to defend NATO, Zelenskyy offered something else: know-how to stop drones now reaching its neighbors. Zelenskyy says Ukraine will share its drone-defense experience with partners facing Russian attacks, NATO or not, through the Drone Deal pacts.
Built by Ukrainian officers from real combat, DWAC course is now "NATO Selected". It has trained officers from over 10 countries.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Neptune Missiles Hammer Russian Plant Supplying Missile and Artillery Components
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Neptune Missiles Hammer Russian Plant Supplying Missile and Artillery Components
Ukraine struck the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in Russia’s Rostov region overnight on September 26, damaging multiple production facilities at an enterprise that manufactures components for Russian missiles, artillery, and anti-tank weapons.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said the strike was carried out by its Alpha Special Operations Center together with the Ukrainian Navy using domestically produced Neptune cruise missiles and Ruta, Palianytsia, and Bars jet-powered drone missiles.
According to the SBU, preliminary assessments showed damage to the plant’s optical and foundry production facilities, an assembly area, an electroplating workshop, and a printed circuit board production facility.
Ukraine’s General Staff separately confirmed the strike on September 26, reporting a fire at the plant’s foundry and damage to equipment in five production buildings.
The Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant is part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation, a major state-owned weapons manufacturer. Ukrainian military intelligence lists the facility as a producer of electronic systems used in precision artillery, missile, and anti-tank weapons, as well as radar seekers for tactical guided missiles, thermal imaging equipment, and optoelectronic systems.
The plant has been subject to international sanctions. The European Union lists the facility as part of Tactical Missiles Corporation and has included it in restrictive measures against Russia since June 2022.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed the attack, saying Ukrainian long-range weapons had struck a plant in the Rostov region supplying Russian forces with components for missiles and artillery, as well as a Pantsir-S2 air defense system.
The Azov facility was one of several Russian military and energy-related targets hit during the overnight operation. Ukrainian forces also struck the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region, while a Russian ammunition depot was targeted in temporarily occupied Sievierodonetsk in Ukraine’s Luhansk region.
Ukraine’s General Staff also reported a strike on a Russian P-18 Terek radar near Semenivske in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region. The mobile two-dimensional radar is used to detect and track aerial targets and provide targeting information to air defense units.
