articles.title: Araghchi outlines Iran’s diplomatic conditions, and regional priorities at NY
articles.body:
Araghchi outlines Iran’s diplomatic conditions, and regional priorities at NY
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has used a series of meetings, diplomatic engagements and media appearances on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly to lay out Tehran’s positions on negotiations with Washington, the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s nuclear program, regional security, sanctions and the future of multilateral cooperation.
Across his remarks, Araghchi presented diplomacy as Iran’s preferred avenue for resolving disputes, while insisting that negotiations must be conducted on the basis of sovereign equality, international law and reciprocal commitments rather than military pressure or coercion.
His comments also linked the security of the Strait of Hormuz to the wider regional situation, while outlining a specific seven-day mechanism for restoring normal maritime traffic if the United States accepts Tehran's conditions previously conveyed to Washington.
Diplomacy remains open, but Iran rejects coercion
Speaking to reporters outside the UN Security Council, Araghchi said Iran remained committed to international law, the UN Charter and diplomacy, pointing to the negotiations that led to the 2015 nuclear agreement and Iran’s subsequent diplomatic efforts.
He said Tehran had repeatedly kept the door to negotiations open over the past two years, but argued that Washington had responded in bad faith and repeatedly chosen military action and pressure over diplomacy.
According to Araghchi, this history has created deep distrust in Tehran over the prospect of simply returning to negotiations without credible guarantees against a repetition of military action.
He said Iran would not accept threats, intimidation or pressure as a substitute for diplomacy.
“The UN Charter is not optional. Sovereignty is not conditional. Diplomacy does not mean surrender. And peace cannot be built through threats of destruction,” Araghchi said.
Iran sets out seven-day framework for reopening Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz emerged as one of the central issues in Araghchi’s discussions in New York.
The foreign minister said Iran had conveyed, through Qatar, a specific seven-day plan to the United States. Under the proposal, he said, the process of restoring normal maritime traffic could be completed within seven days if Washington accepted the necessary conditions.
Araghchi subsequently provided additional details, saying the seven-day period would begin immediately once the United States accepted the plan.
He said the technical implementation could be completed within four or five days, allowing the strait to reopen on the sixth day, followed by US entry into a final agreement on the seventh day.
The measures required from Washington, he said, had already been communicated to the United States and were incorporated into the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
“If there is sufficient seriousness on the American side, this will happen, and the Strait of Hormuz will reopen,” Araghchi said.
He stressed that Iran’s proposal should be understood within the framework of reciprocal commitments rather than as a unilateral concession.
Islamabad memorandum and the Oman track
Araghchi said that following mediation efforts by Pakistan and Qatar, Iran and the United States signed the Islamabad memorandum on June 17.
Under Article 5 of the memorandum, Iran committed to making the necessary arrangements to facilitate the safe passage of ships.
Iran, he said, immediately began technical discussions with Oman to implement that commitment and restore maritime traffic to pre-war levels.
According to Araghchi, maritime traffic reached approximately 60 percent of its pre-war level within two weeks of implementation.
He said subsequent unilateral US measures and military action halted the implementation of the memorandum, arguing that Washington had chosen military action instead of using the dispute-resolution mechanism contained in the agreement.
Iran, he emphasized, had nevertheless continued to keep diplomatic channels open.
Tehran links Hormuz security to regional stability
Araghchi reaffirmed Iran’s commitment to safe and secure shipping, but rejected the idea that maritime security could be restored through additional military deployments, threats, blockades or economic pressure.
He said the Strait of Hormuz had remained open until February 28, 2026, and argued that the subsequent disruption of maritime traffic was, from Tehran’s perspective, a consequence of the conflict and military actions against Iran.
“A country cannot be bombed, threatened with destruction, subjected to a naval blockade and coercive measures, and at the same time be expected to automatically restore security and shipping to normal,” he said.
Araghchi also criticized the role of certain regional states, arguing that some had allowed their territory, military bases, airspace, logistical infrastructure or intelligence facilities to be used in connection with military operations against Iran.
In his meetings with regional counterparts, however, he emphasized Iran’s preference for regional security mechanisms based on cooperation among neighboring states.
Iran and Saudi Arabia: Focus on regional security cooperation
In a meeting with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan, Araghchi emphasized Tehran’s determination to strengthen mutual trust and promote regional security through cooperation among countries in the region.
He briefed his Saudi counterpart on the understanding reached between Iran and Oman regarding safe maritime routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
The two ministers also discussed bilateral relations and ways of expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
Araghchi called for greater participation by influential regional states in security arrangements, while referring to the experience of the past seven months and the use of the territory and facilities of some regional countries in military operations against Iran.
The meeting underscored Tehran’s emphasis on the principle that regional security should be addressed collectively by regional states.
Iran briefs India on Hormuz and diplomatic efforts
Araghchi also held talks with Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in New York, discussing bilateral relations, regional developments and international issues.
The Iranian foreign minister briefed his Indian counterpart on Iran’s talks with Oman over establishing safe maritime routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
He also outlined Tehran’s position regarding US violations of previous commitments and military actions against Iran, including a maritime blockade and attacks on Iranian commercial shipping.
Araghchi said the international community had a responsibility to hold those responsible for aggression accountable.
The two ministers also discussed efforts by mediators to convey the conditions and essential elements required for a return to the diplomatic process.
They agreed on the importance of using available diplomatic capacities to prevent further escalation and discussed implementation of existing bilateral economic and trade understandings.
Tehran calls for greater Iran-Arab dialogue
In a separate meeting with Arab League Secretary General Nabil Fahmy, Araghchi called for increased dialogue and interaction between Iran and Arab countries.
He described regional security as an integrated and indivisible issue requiring shared responsibility and constructive engagement.
The two sides discussed regional developments, particularly the situation in Palestine and the escalation of Israeli military actions in Palestine and Lebanon.
Araghchi said stronger interaction among regional countries could help address misunderstandings and concerns that Tehran attributes, in part, to hostile propaganda.
He emphasized Iran’s determination to strengthen mutual trust with neighboring states and called for greater regional cooperation.
Iran defends its nuclear program and NPT commitments
Iran’s nuclear program was another major element of Araghchi’s diplomatic message in New York.
He rejected recent allegations concerning Iran’s nuclear activities as political rather than technical or legal in nature.
Araghchi described claims that Iran was on the verge of acquiring nuclear weapons as false, saying such allegations had been repeatedly raised by Israel and subsequently echoed by the United States and European countries.
He stressed that Iran has been a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty since 1970 and has been subject to extensive International Atomic Energy Agency monitoring for decades.
From Tehran’s perspective, Araghchi argued, it is contradictory for Washington to claim to support the international nonproliferation regime while targeting peaceful nuclear facilities operating under IAEA safeguards.
He characterized attacks on such facilities as inconsistent with international obligations and argued that technical and legal mechanisms, rather than military action, should determine the future of nuclear verification.
Iran accuses US of economic pressure and “economic terrorism”
Araghchi also devoted significant attention to the impact of unilateral sanctions on Iran.
He accused Washington of using economic deprivation as an instrument of political pressure and said sanctions had affected access to trade, financial resources, medicines, technology, education and scientific cooperation.
In his address to the Global Development Initiative, he argued that the consequences of such measures extend beyond governments and directly affect ordinary people.
He described the humanitarian consequences of sanctions as “economic terrorism” and called on the United Nations to oppose unilateral coercive measures and demand their complete and unconditional removal.
He also linked the sanctions issue to the broader question of sustainable development, arguing that developing countries require greater access to finance, technology, knowledge and international cooperation rather than additional economic restrictions.
Development, South-South cooperation and multilateralism
At the fifth anniversary meeting of the Global Development Initiative, Araghchi placed development at the center of Iran’s broader foreign-policy agenda.
He said developing countries continue to confront poverty, hunger, inequality, debt burdens, financing shortages, technology gaps and environmental challenges. These pressures have been exacerbated by conflicts, protectionism, unilateral coercive measures and the use of force.
Araghchi welcomed the initiative launched by Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2021 and highlighted its work in poverty reduction, food security, development financing, green development, industrialization and the digital economy.
Iran, he said, attaches particular importance to the initiative’s potential to strengthen South-South cooperation by mobilizing the knowledge, technology and capabilities of developing countries.
He called for international solidarity to be translated into concrete development outcomes and said the voices of developing countries should have a greater role in global development governance.
ECO as a platform for regional integration
Araghchi also addressed the 27th Informal Meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organization Council of Ministers in New York, calling for stronger regional cooperation and solidarity among ECO member states.
He said ECO could play a greater role in promoting peace, stability, connectivity and sustainable development.
The foreign minister highlighted recent progress within the organization, including the resumption of ministerial meetings, the five-year roadmap for mining cooperation, the ten-year strategy for sustainable and resilient transport, and efforts to amend the ECOTA trade agreement.
He also pointed to expanding transport corridors and links with major cargo and logistics hubs, including routes connected to China, as an important factor in strengthening the region’s role in international trade and transit.
Tourism, intra-regional trade, energy, agriculture, industry, human resources and environmental cooperation, he said, should remain among ECO’s key priorities.
Iran is scheduled to host the 18th ECO Summit in Tehran on December 3–4, 2026.
Iran’s account of the conflict and civilian impact
Across his statements in New York, Araghchi repeatedly referred to US and Israeli aggression against the country.
He said thousands of Iranians had been killed, including women and children, and accused the United States and Israel of targeting civilian and critical infrastructure.
Among the examples cited by the foreign minister were the killing of 168 students and teachers at a school in Minab, an attack on the Lamerd sports complex, damage to the Pasteur Institute of Iran and attacks on residential areas and other civilian facilities.
Araghchi argued that these incidents should be investigated within the framework of international law and that accountability should apply regardless of political alliances.
He also criticized efforts to portray the conflict in a manner that reverses the positions of victim and aggressor.
 
  
A consistent message from NY
Taken together, Araghchi’s meetings and public statements in New York presented several interconnected themes in Iran’s foreign-policy position.
At the diplomatic level, Tehran says it remains open to negotiations but wants guarantees against a recurrence of military action and insists that diplomacy cannot take place under coercion.
On the nuclear issue, Iran continues to emphasize its NPT membership, cooperation with international monitoring mechanisms and opposition to military action against nuclear facilities.
On the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has presented a concrete seven-day framework for restoring maritime traffic, linking implementation to conditions already communicated to Washington and incorporated into the Islamabad memorandum.
At the regional level, Iran is calling for security arrangements based on dialogue and cooperation among neighboring countries, while seeking closer engagement with Saudi Arabia, India, Arab states and other regional partners.
And at the global level, Araghchi has called for stronger multilateralism, sovereign equality, South-South cooperation and an international development agenda free from unilateral coercive measures.
The common thread running through his remarks was that Iran considers diplomacy and international law essential to resolving disputes, but rejects attempts to use military, economic or political pressure to dictate the terms of that diplomacy.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: German foreign minister urges Russia to abandon dangerous escalation in rare meeting
articles.body:
- 
  The foreign ministers of Russia and Germany met in New York on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, in the first such talks since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. But Russia’s top diplomat dismissed Germany’s calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” toward Europe, instead accusing Germany of being Ukraine’s main sponsor and seeking to be a leading military power in Europe. “Does Berlin understand what this could lead to?” the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, asked in his speech at the gathering of world leaders on Saturday. “Didn’t they learn the lessons of world war two?”
- 
  German foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, used the talks to call on Russia “to abandon the dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and Nato”, according to a delegation source. Wadephul said incidents such as the attempted drone attack in Leipzig would not shake Germany’s resolve to support Ukraine, according to sources.
- 
  Relations between Moscow and Berlin have been frozen since the Russian invasion, and tensions escalated further after the drone incident at Leipzig airport. In a sign of the continued frostiness, Lavrov told a press conference on Saturday “nothing new” came from the talks with his German counterpart.
- 
  “I told him that frankly … you could just have called me and said: ‘read my statement’,” Lavrov said. “He simply reiterated his official public position condemning Russia … you can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not.”
- 
  Still, the ministers discussed bilateral ties and the war in Ukraine, officials from both sides said. Wadephul urged Lavrov to do “everything possible to reach an agreement on grain exports via the Black Sea”, a German delegation source said.
- 
  In a sign of the sensitivities around meeting the Russian foreign minister, Wadephul notified his European allies of the meeting afterwards in a message seen by Reuters. “I used this opportunity to reiterate our position on Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and to call for an immediate and complete ceasefire, most pressingly with a focus on grain exports, and the energy infrastructure,” he wrote.
- 
  After the meeting Lavrov addressed world leaders at the assembly, where he defended Russia’s war in Ukraine and lobbed barbs at the west — including Germany – and criticised the militarisation of Japan. He made clear that Russia will veto any attempt by Germany and Japan for permanent seats on the UN security council. The two nations fought Russia, Britain and the US in the second world war. Writing on her personal Telegram channel, Maria Zakharova, a spokesperson for Russia’s foreign ministry, said that “tens of diplomats” had come to meet Lavrov to “shake his hand and thank Russia”.
- 
  An overwhelming majority of general assembly member nations have repeatedly condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, as Wadephul noted in his own address to the assembly Saturday. “Russia’s war targets the lives of millions of innocent people, the existence of the Ukrainian state and culture and the European peace order,” he said, urging Russia to negotiating toward ending the fighting.
- 
  The talks came amid an intensifying aerial war and as Donald Trump said he hoped the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, would “settle” with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. With frontline positions largely unchanged since last year, Russia has hammered Ukraine with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months, while Ukraine’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses.
- 
  “It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day,” Zelenskyy wrote on Saturday. “If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further.”
- 
  Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed four people on Saturday, as Russian authorities said a Ukrainian drone attack killed three.
- 
  Residents of Kyiv are preparing for power cuts, drone attacks and a bitter cold winter by stocking up on generators, food and “dry showers”, as the Ukrainian capital becomes a frontline city.
- 
  And Russia has opened a new front in its campaign against Ukraine, hitting several datacentres and internet providers in Kyiv this week in an apparent attempt to weaken the digital backbone of the economy.

articles.title: Russia ignores German de-escalation calls as strikes kill 2 in Kyiv
articles.body:
Hours after Moscow rejected German calls to ease its escalation toward NATO, Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least two people overnight into Sunday, officials said.
Russia’s top diplomat Saturday brushed off what’s believed to have been the first tete-a-tete with his German counterpart since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The meeting was held during the U.N. General Assembly’s annual gathering of world leaders, as an intensifying aerial war between Russia and Ukraine shows no sign of slowing.
Ties between Russia and Germany have soured in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack last month at Leipzig airport that Berlin blamed on the Kremlin.
With front-line positions largely unchanged since last year, Moscow has hammered its neighbor with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months. Meanwhile, Kyiv’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses.
In Kyiv, a man was found dead after a Russian drone hit a non-residential building overnight, according to Ukraine’s emergency service.
Another drone struck a single-story vehicle repair shop, leaving firefighters battling the blaze into early Sunday, the emergency service said.
Russian forces also struck Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, which surrounds the country’s main Black Sea port, multiple times overnight into Sunday, killing one person and injuring two others, according to the head of the local military administration, Oleh Kiper.
In Russian-occupied Ukraine, a strike by Kyiv's forces Sunday killed a civilian woman in Enerhodar, the town housing Europe's largest nuclear plant, according to its Kremlin-installed mayor. Maxim Pukhov said the Ukrainian drones also injured two others.
Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly blamed each other for damaging power lines supplying Enerhodar's Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, which Moscow captured early in the war. The plant is not in service, but needs power to keep cooling systems running and maintain safety.
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was dismissive after the meeting in New York, which was held at German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s request. Lavrov said that Wadephul "simply reiterated his official position condemning Russia.”
"You can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not,” he said.
Wadephul expressed openness to a better relationship but said it required a genuine willingness from Russia’s leadership to end the war in Ukraine, according to a German delegation official.
An overwhelming majority of U.N. member nations have repeatedly condemned Moscow’s invasion.
The Kremlin describes the war a "special military operation” intended to ensure Russia’s security and the rights of Russian speakers.

articles.title: IDF expands Personal Security Branch to protect troops, officials from global threats - interview
articles.body:
Over the past year, the Operations Directorate underwent a significant restructuring to update personal security policies for service members of all ranks, both domestically and abroad.
In recent months, the specialized branch's mandate expanded, taking responsibility for the security of IDF personnel both in Israel and abroad against a wide array of threats - ranging from active-duty soldiers to high-profile officials, major generals, and the Chief of Staff.
In an interview with Walla, the head of the expanding branch discussed the growing risks, active intelligence alerts, and the joint operational response across Israel's defense establishment.
"We are responsible for the entire spectrum of terrorist threats. This has hit home even more acutely since Operation Roaring Lion in Iran, driven by what the Iranians call 'settling scores' abroad, as well as the spike in antisemitic incidents we’ve been seeing," the branch head explained.
He added, "About a year and a half ago, it was published that we extracted a soldier from Thailand following public calls to harm him, along with various other antisemitic incidents in places like Amsterdam, as well as legal challenges."
An international incident mobilized the security establishment, changing it forever
On November 2, 2022, details were cleared for publication regarding a 19-year-old lone soldier serving on active duty. Flying on a commercial flight to visit family in Uzbekistan, she departed the capital, Tashkent, heading toward Dubai in the United Arab Emirates as a layover on her way back to Israel.
Due to a severe medical emergency involving one of the passengers that required immediate attention, the plane made an emergency landing at around 5:00 a.m. in Shiraz - one of Iran’s major cities.
The soldier immediately alerted her family, who quickly notified her commanders. The information reached the Mossad, senior IDF officials, and the prime minister quickly. The minutes that followed were tense and felt like an eternity, as everyone understood she could be detained by local authorities the moment her identity was discovered.
A few hours later, under a total blackout in Israel and with the Mossad guiding and monitoring the entire situation, the plane took off for the UAE and then returned to Israel. It was a high-stakes crisis, with every development reported directly to the prime minister, the Defense Minister, and the IDF Chief of Staff.
The incident marked a turning point in how the IDF views the safety of its service members worldwide. In its aftermath, the Personal Security Branch was established under the command of Lt.-Col. "A" within the Security Division of the General Staff’s Operations Directorate.
Once it became clear that this sensitive issue required multi-agency coordination beyond the military alone, the decision was made to establish the Security Division within the Operations Directorate under the command of Brig.-Gen. "T."
This created a single, centralized authority responsible for issuing policies and technical directives across all service branches, directorates, arms, and regional commands. "Another step was appointing a dedicated intelligence officer for this domain, alongside a specialized reorganization within the Intelligence Directorate that I cannot elaborate on," Lt.Col. A. explained.
Route analysis, location tracking at the press of a button
One of the branch's initial tasks was a comprehensive risk analysis of global flight paths and routes that could pose a hazard to IDF personnel (similar to the emergency landing in Iran). In collaboration with the National Security Council (NSC), clear rules were established detailing which flights are off-limits due to the risk of emergency landings or layovers in enemy or hostile nations.
"All of this painstakingly gathered data was made accessible to every soldier via a dedicated app, allowing them to easily check what is permitted and what is off-limits," Lt.-Col. A. said. "Service members enter their full itinerary, including transit flights, and receive real-time threat advisories - including operational security guidelines and cybersecurity protocols. That's why we call it 'personal security.'"
The attack on Maccabi Tel Aviv soccer fans in Amsterdam in November 2024 served as another major red flag. Pro-Palestinian groups carried out coordinated attacks against Israelis across several locations in the city against the backdrop of the "Swords of Iron" war, sharing real-time information and documenting the violence on social media. Parts of the media described the events as a pogrom, while Dutch authorities characterized them as an antisemitic attack.
"When it started, we got a call saying the Chief of Staff wanted to know if any active IDF personnel were there. We checked and discovered a significant number of soldiers we had no prior record of - either because they had landed in another country and traveled to Holland by land, or because they were moving between cities. That event proved we had to expand our tracking and oversight capabilities for all IDF soldiers worldwide.
"Today, if an earthquake strikes Venezuela, for instance, I can generate a report at the press of a button showing whether any soldiers are there or just passing through. We handle everything directly from the branch and no longer have to scramble for information after the fact."
One ongoing challenge involves instances where a soldier flies abroad, and civil-military systems fail to automatically flag them as active-duty or career personnel, though a solution has been developed to retrieve this data that remains classified.
"Another major concern is dual citizenship, especially given the rise in antisemitism - whether it's protests outside the homes of soldiers living abroad or service members facing mandatory draft requirements in foreign countries that they need to resolve legally," noted the head of the Personal Security Branch.
"Because of this, all soldiers are required to report dual citizenship so we can vet their situation and issue appropriate instructions. We want to avoid a scenario where a soldier flies overseas and is arrested by local authorities for unresolved paperwork. This happened to us at the start of the Russia-Ukraine war, and we later discovered that mandatory draft laws exist in several European countries as well."
Doxxing, legal warfare, and the exposure dilemma
An equally complex threat involves the public exposure of soldiers' personal details, doxxing campaigns, and global efforts to issue arrest warrants.
"I sign off on all exposure protocols for commanders and officials regarding whether their name and rank can be published," said Lt.-Col. A. "There is a clear military order that we enforce to protect the identities of IDF personnel. On one hand, we want to allow public visibility - and we work closely within the intelligence community alongside the Shin Bet and Mossad. But unlike them, while they are covert organizations, the IDF is a public-facing entity."
"I recently explained this at Shin Bet headquarters: 'The IDF is the people's army; it comes from the people and returns to the people.' That makes it difficult to enforce a total gag order on the identity of a brigade training base commander or a brigade commander. On the other hand, we have a vital interest in protecting them from arrest abroad or from being targeted.
"We manage this tension on a daily - almost hourly - basis in close coordination with the IDF Spokesperson’s Unit. We constantly balance the desire for public engagement with the necessity of keeping service members safe. Ultimately, we set the policy on who can be named publicly, and it escalates up to the Head of the Operations Directorate (Maj.-Gen. Itzik Cohen). That provides a major advantage, as he has a macro-level view of the entire IDF and access to intelligence that gives us the full picture. I can conduct a proper risk assessment and damage control evaluation even if information happens to leak."
However, the Security Division's responsibilities extend beyond mandatory and career soldiers. An equally complex issue involves reservists who have completed their service and travel the world as private citizens. The Personal Security Branch has limited authority and oversight over them, as civilians are not required to report their locations to the military.
Despite this, the Operations Directorate’s Security Division works in tight coordination with the Foreign Affairs Ministry and the Justice Ministry.
"If a complaint is filed against a reservist, or if there is an intent to file one, we bring in the Military Advocate General’s International Law Department, working alongside the Justice Ministry and handling operational coordination with the Foreign Ministry. We manage these cases jointly through a streamlined framework we established to tackle the issue," Lt.-Col. A. said.
"Most of these reports stem from content posted online during 2023–2024. We aren't seeing new cases emerge. However, it's crucial to highlight the risk posed by hostile groups using data-scraping techniques: the moment a service member lands in a country and posts about it online, these groups sometimes manage to track them down."
Recently, a specific fund published allegations targeting naval reservists who allegedly took part in intercepting a protest flotilla. Following an investigation by the Personal Security Branch, it turned out the claims were made solely because the individuals listed details about their naval service on LinkedIn.
"We are formulating policies for these scenarios to define what is permissible online, even for reservists who are civilians and not fully subject to IDF regulations. At this stage, our focus is primarily on public awareness so everyone understands the threat," Lt.-Col. A. emphasized, clarifying that the individuals in question had not actually participated in intercepting the flotilla, but were targeted simply for having served in the Navy. "
We also recently saw a social media campaign involving career officers. We called them in, presented the risks, and explained our recommendations."
Psychological warfare, espionage, and physical threats
Beyond direct threats abroad, the Personal Security Branch also navigates the evolving online landscape of public diplomacy and legal warfare, particularly surrounding public controversies.
For instance, regarding the film NAZA - which sparked intense public debate in Israel and within the military, raising concerns about a potential wave of media and legal attacks against IDF soldiers - the branch head noted that it is too early to gauge the long-term impact.
The Security Division is currently awaiting a formal legal assessment from international law experts in the Military Advocate General's Corps.
"It's important to emphasize that none of these threats have materialized into actual legal complaints or immediate physical danger so far. It concerns us primarily because the line between legal proceedings and someone attempting to cause physical harm is very thin, which is why I treat this as a personal security issue."
Beyond the media arena, the IDF is bracing for immediate physical threats: revenge efforts by Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas surrounding the sensitive High Holy Days, alongside warnings from the defense establishment regarding a fresh wave of espionage targeting IDF personnel and security officials - aimed in part at uncovering classified operational methods utilized during the war.
"This is the core purpose of the Security Division," Lt.-Col. A. explained. "Where we used to look strictly at VIP protection, today - when we sit down with partner agencies like the Shin Bet, Mossad, the Israel Police, and the Defense Ministry - we evaluate threats holistically with a completely different level of access.
"Take espionage cases, for example: I can immediately assess whether a threat impacts the Chief of Staff's immediate surroundings or affects someone traveling anywhere in the world. That is the Security Division's key advantage; previously, every security agency handled these matters in isolation."
According to the branch head, there are cases where the unit handles real-time threat mitigation regarding cyberattacks and mobile device security:
"We have significantly expanded our capabilities in executive protection. What has changed most is our capacity for intelligence monitoring - detecting a threat early and issuing an immediate alert and operational response. I cannot comment on specific operations, but we address these risks both through broad contingency plans and targeted interventions. We have encountered incidents - certainly involving senior officials, but also lower ranks - where we had to intervene, and we successfully protected our people. We have faced these threats continuously."
Asked whether there have been actual physical attempts on the lives of senior officials, Lt.-Col. A. replied, "Abroad, almost none - that falls largely under the Mossad's domain. But domestically, there were clear intentions that we identified early enough to prevent them from escalating into an attack. In other words, we never let it reach a 'near-miss' physical attempt."
He continued, saying, "We focus on identifying when something is brewing and deploying a response, supported by the Shin Bet and, for overseas matters, the Mossad. I am glad to say that our adversaries have had zero success so far, and I hope it stays that way. We work hand-in-hand with everyone - the Shin Bet, Mossad, and Police - because this is a challenge that affects us all."
Reflecting on the current threat environment and the enemy's motivation to target IDF soldiers and commanders at home and abroad, Lt.-Col. A. concluded: "There is far more focus on this now, and clear intent. Yes, their motivation is very high."

articles.title: Lavrov delivers Russia’s message to the UN
articles.body:
Lavrov warns UN over EU warmongering: As it happened
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has addressed the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York and set out Moscow’s position on the Ukraine conflict and global security while warning of the EU’s military buildup.
The top Russian diplomat arrived in New York earlier this week for a diplomatic marathon on the sidelines of the gathering, holding talks with senior officials from around the globe, including US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi, and many others.
His General Assembly address follows a heated UN Security Council meeting on Ukraine earlier in the week, during which he reiterated Moscow’s readiness for negotiations but rejected calls to halt military operations during talks, arguing that a pause would allow Kiev to regroup and rearm.
The key statements he made in the UNGA address and in the follow-up Q&A include:
- The EU is militarizing for war with Russia despite Moscow having no plans to attack Europe. The sheer scale of the EU buildup could eventually spark a conflict.
- Berlin’s goal of achieving military primacy in Europe can be construed as an attempt to create a Fourth Reich.
- Many EU ruling elites are “infected with the virus of racial superiority” and espouse extremist Russophobic ideas.
- Ukraine’s Western backers continue pumping it full of arms and helping it attack non-combatants and civilian infrastructure.
- Europe actively cultivates and supports Ukraine’s neo-Nazi lionization of WWII Nazi collaborators.
- Russia remains open to dialogue with Washington and is ready to return to the understandings reached at the August 2025 Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage.
Lavrov stressed that the Ukraine conflict has deeper roots in NATO expansion, the failure of the Minsk agreements, and the rejection of Russia’s security proposals to the US and NATO in 2021.
The week’s diplomacy extended well beyond Ukraine. Talks with Arab officials covered tensions in the Middle East, including the US war against Iran and Israel’s continued hostilities in Gaza. Other meetings focused on bilateral ties and coordination at the UN.
The General Debate is being held at UN Headquarters from September 22 to 28 as part of High-Level Week, with the theme: ‘Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all’.
This live feed has now ended.

Russian officials have long argued that the UK, France, and Germany undermined previous peace efforts, including in the 2014-2015 Minsk Agreements and the draft deal reached in Istanbul in 2022.

The European military buildup will eventually have to be put to use, he said. “In that case, they will attack us, because we are not planning to,” the top diplomat said, recalling Russian President Vladimir Putin’s warning that such a war would be a “short one.”
- 18:17 GMTRussia believes that Russia and the US reached an agreement at Putin-Trump in Alaska in August 2025, which focused on the Ukraine conflict, Lavrov has said, stressing that Moscow is ready to return to it.
- 18:07 GMTSome analysts believe that Berlin is attempting to create the Fourth Reich, Lavrov said, recalling that Chancellor Friedrich Merz has repeatedly stated his goal is to make Germany “the leading military power in Europe again.” “Does he understand the significance of the word ‘again’ in that statement?” the Russian top diplomat asked.
- 17:58 GMTMoscow and the Trump administration maintain “regular dialogue in different formats,” Lavrov has said, stressing that this fact alone speaks of “normalcy” in relations. While admitting the US often engages in hardball diplomacy, he stressed that it would be a mistake not to talk over issues on which the two powers are at odds. Lavrov added that he believes the Trump administration wants to remove the Ukraine conflict from among the issues affecting Russia-US relations.
- 17:48 GMTEU countries have helped return the remains of Nazi collaborators to Ukraine and are openly patronizing Vladimir Zelensky in his attempts to use them for building a “pantheon of heroes,” Lavrov has charged. The Zelensky government has moved to entomb the remains of WWII Nazi Collaborators in the Kiev Pechersk Lavra, Ukraine’s oldest monastery. It is run by the Ukrainian Orthodox Church, which has been subject to a state-backed crackdown since 2014.
- 17:41 GMTRussia supplied Türkiye with S-400 air defense systems under an end-user agreement requiring Moscow’s consent for any transfer abroad, Lavrov told a Turkish reporter, adding that Ankara has made no formal request to sell them.
- 17:28 GMTBerlin has failed to cite any examples of Western-linked commercial ships being attacked by Russia, Lavrov said, stressing that all strikes on civilian shipping in the conflict zone were carried out by Ukraine.
- 17:23 GMTGerman Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul requested a meeting at “the last hour,” Lavrov said, adding that while Russia remained open to diplomacy, Berlin’s overture contained nothing new and essentially contained demands for more concessions.

articles.title: A new flash point in the Iran war: The narrow strait called the 'Gate of Tears'
articles.body:
A new flash point in the Iran war: The narrow strait called the ‘Gate of Tears’
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Houthi rebels’ seizure of Yemen’s Red Sea coast gives them a strategic grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital route for global shipping.
- With the Strait of Hormuz mostly closed by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, Bab el-Mandeb has taken on even greater importance.
- Known as the ‘Gate of Tears’ for the dangers of navigating there, the straight links the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean.
BAB EL-MANDEB, Yemen — To visit Bab el-Mandeb is to understand that old adage about looks being deceiving. For this humble fishing village in Yemen, a tumbledown grouping of barely-there huts nestled between the water and an imposing mountain range, stands sentinel over one of the world’s most vital waterways.
The village shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow passageway connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea that’s become another flash point in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
“You hear so much about Bab el-Mandeb, you’d think we would be like New York, with skyscrapers and money,” said Saleh, a 58-year-old resident who, like all people interviewed here, refused to give their full name to avoid reprisals.
“So many ships pass near here. If the Yemeni government knew how to invest in it, we would be rich. We should be bringing in billions of dollars. Instead, look around you,” he said, pausing as his gaze took in the sorry-looking boats haphazardly laid on the beach.
“We have nothing.”
Saleh was interviewed in January, when Bab el-Mandeb was thrust into the power struggle between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the friendly-but-occasionally-fractious backers of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
That war of wills ended with the Emirates ceding control of Bab el-Mandeb — along with the nearby island of Perim, where the Emirates had built a drone airbase — to Saudi Arabia.
But this month, control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait switched once more, when the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, ousted government forces from the waterway in a blitzkrieg in which they seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The move grants the Houthis a valuable foothold in controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ribbon of Red Sea — known as the “Gate of Tears” for the dangers involving its navigation — between Yemen’s coast and Djibouti and Eritrea.
About 7% of global energy supplies and around 12% to 15% of all global shipping transit the strait. And in taking Perim Island, which lies in the middle the Red Sea at the strait’s narrowest point (a mere 12½ miles), the Houthis could harass ships with ease.
“We don’t need a drone or a missile,” one Houthi commander bragged in a social media video posted from the island. Instead, he added, all they had to do was place a few artillery units on Perim’s coast and they would be able to strike any ship crossing the strait.
The impact of any movement disruption through Bab el-Mandeb wouldn’t be limited to already skittish energy markets: To enter the Suez Canal’s southern entrance, ships must first transit through Bab el-Mandeb, meaning any trouble in the passageway would force freighters to circumnavigate the African continent — adding anywhere from 12 to 21 days to voyages and spiking fuel costs.
A shipping disaster in 2021 shows how blocking the strait — and thus severing a link to the Mediterranean Sea — could harm global commerce. A container ship in the Suez Canal ran aground and blocked the waterway for six days, delaying the delivery of billions of dollars of goods.
More recently, the Houthis sealed off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in 2023 to coerce Israel into stopping its campaign in Gaza; that pushed the U.S. to attack the Houthis, before the Trump administration agreed to a ceasefire of its own with the group.
These days, the Houthi advance comes at a particularly fraught moment, one in which Bab el-Mandeb has taken on outsize importance. With the Israeli-U.S. war on Iran prompting Tehran to seal the Strait of Hormuz — cutting off the world’s most important energy passageway — Persian Gulf oil powerhouses have been forced to divert crude exports to alternatives, including Bab el-Mandeb.
That’s especially true for Saudi Arabia, which turned to its East-West pipeline and exports through the Red Sea to sidestep the trouble in Hormuz. But it’s also the most vulnerable to the Houthi threat.
The Houthis have a long-running animus against the Saudis, which began in 2015, months after the Houthis overran the Yemeni capital of Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia, spooked about the notion of an Iranian ally on its border, led a coalition — with U.S. backing — to dislodge them. It started a blockade and a devastating air campaign that persisted until a 2022 truce.
But in July, the ceasefire broke after the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking Sanaa‘s airport in what appeared to be an attempt to stop Iranian flights from landing there. The Houthis began attacking Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and declared a naval blockade against the kingdom.
The rebels’ land grab this month stunned Saudi Arabia, which failed to launch airstrikes and stanch the rout of its allied forces from the coast. Saudi leaders reportedly reached out to President Trump to push the rebels back, but he appears disinclined to help.
Still, on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “We have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement.” He did not elaborate on what U.S. support that would entail.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia said its defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif, a manufacturing center, and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea. It responded with hundreds of strikes on the Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen.
For their part, the Houthis insist they have no plans to attack shipping on the Red Sea and that their blockade applies only to Saudi Arabia — a move calculated to prevent the rise of an international effort to dislodge them.
“They don’t want to attract international military operations,” said Mohammad al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory.
“They realize that when you do things in the Red Sea, you create panic in the world.”
But leaders in the internationally recognized Yemeni government say the Houthis are not to be trusted.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
He added that protecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the responsibility of “every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation.”
Using tribal power and rigorous detective work, a family of an army officer in Yemen tries to find out how he was abducted in broad daylight, and what happened to him afterward.
In the meantime, the Houthis have been consolidating their gains on Yemen’s coast, Basha said, setting up checkpoints and bringing loyalists to administer the regions now under their control.
In taking the coastal areas around Bab el-Mandeb village, they reap the benefit of Emirati investment, manifested in kilometers of paved highways that stand in stark contrast to much of Yemen’s road network. They also gain control of several airbases in the area, most crucially on Perim, where the Emirates spent years ferrying construction supplies to build out a roughly 6,000-foot runway along with three hangars.
Although such a runway could not be used by larger bombers, it still can accommodate attack and surveillance aircraft. Another area of the island, which lies roughly two miles off of Yemen’s coast, has what appears to be a helicopter landing area.
The U.S.-Israel campaign against Iran was billed as the final blow to Tehran’s ‘Axis of Resistance,’ but the alliance though bloodied is unexpectedly resilient.
One resident in Bab el-Mandeb village said much of that construction was done by the Emirates, whose contractors would ferry Southeast Asian construction workers to the island and provide them with food. It also built roughly 100 structures for Perim’s residents.
Government forces have since overcome their initial disarray and stopped further Houthi advances. But Basha warned any attempt to push out the Houthis from the coast will be difficult, especially with the group’s advances in manufacturing and fielding drones and ballistic missiles, not to mention the divisions and competing loyalties plaguing Yemeni government forces.
“It’s an uphill battle,” he said.
“You have a divided command-and-control; a divided Yemen; a divided society; a divided geography; and these divisions empower the Houthis.”

articles.title: Ukraine destroys record 76 Russian air-defense systems this month, losses analyst says Russia “will never be able to restore”
articles.body:
Ukraine has destroyed a record 76 Russian air-defense systems this month, and September is not over. The tally beats a record that had stood since July 2023 and reflects a systematic Ukrainian campaign to hunt down Russia's air defenses, opening the skies over occupied territory and inside Russia, the analyst Oleksandr Kovalenko said on Telegram.
Ukraine is methodically peeling apart Russia's layered air defense, and September has been its worst month yet: 76 systems destroyed, past the 73 lost in July 2023, by Kovalenko's count, with days still to go.
It is part of a campaign in which Ukrainian drones and special forces have hunted Russian radars and missile launchers across occupied territory and Crimea, and each one destroyed opens a corridor for the next strike.
The record falls with days to spare
Kovalenko credited Ukraine's Defense Forces' sustained hunt for Russian anti-air, which he said pays off twice: it clears the defenses that would otherwise stop Ukraine's strikes, making later attacks on occupied territory and on Russia itself more effective.
Each kill opens a corridor
Ukrainian drone and special-operations units have picked off Pantsir, Tor, Buk, and pieces of S-300 and S-400 systems across occupied territory and Crimea, sometimes several in a single night throughout 2026.
As Russia pulls its scarce long-range systems back to guard Moscow, fewer are left to cover occupied Ukraine, widening the openings for the next wave of Ukrainian strikes.
Russia cannot replace the losses
Over the full-scale war, Kovalenko said, Russia has lost more than 1,673 air-defense systems of every kind, from radars to surface-to-air missiles and self-propelled anti-aircraft guns.
That, he argued, is a level Moscow can no longer make good with a defense industry already stretched thin by the war.
"Such a quantity of equipment Russia will never be able to restore and compensate," he thinks.
He added that this means it would no longer be able to return to the pre-war level of closing the sky, neither technically nor technologically."

articles.title: British drone-killer startup heads to Japan with cheap interceptors
articles.body:
- Britain's Cambridge Aerospace plans to produce low-cost drone interceptor missiles in Japan and offer them to Japan's Ministry of Defense.
- Each round would cost several million yen, and the company already supplies its Skyhammer interceptor to British forces.
British startup Cambridge Aerospace plans to build its low-cost drone interceptor missiles in Japan and offer them to Japan’s Ministry of Defense, with each round priced at several million yen, or tens of thousands of dollars, the Nikkei business daily reported.
The company’s interceptors cost tens of times less than conventional air defense missiles, and it already has a contract with the British military, the newspaper said. Cambridge Aerospace plans to set up production in Japan before pitching the weapon to the ministry.
The company’s first missile, Skyhammer, is built to shoot down Shahed-type attack drones and slower cruise missiles. It has a range of more than 30 km (19 miles) and a top speed of 700 km/h (435 mph). Cambridge Aerospace has said it uses an X-band radar seeker, and The Register reported that it carries a blast-fragmentation warhead that detonates near its target. The company began developing Skyhammer in January 2025 and flew it within six weeks.
A Skyhammer prototype that crashed and washed up on a British beach in August, and was collected by the company after Reddit users identified it, appeared to be built largely from off-the-shelf parts, according to UAV engineer Chris Wheat, who analyzed photos of the wreckage and called his conclusions educated guesses. He said it seemed to be powered by a JetCat P250-Pro, a commercially sold small jet turbine costing about 4,000 euros ($4,560), and built around two aluminum box-section spars inside a 3D-printed outer shell whose material he put at about £150 ($203). Wheat estimated the airframe at roughly 1.5 m (4.9 feet) long with a similar wingspan, and said he could not find hardware for the radar seeker, suggesting it may not have been fitted to that prototype.
British Defence Secretary John Healey announced on April 10, 2026, that the Ministry of Defence would buy a “significant number” of Skyhammer interceptors and launchers for British forces and Gulf partners facing Iranian-designed drones, with deliveries starting in May. In July, the company won an award under the five-nation LEAP program, and in August it raised $300 million at a $3.4 billion valuation.
Cambridge Aerospace was founded in 2024 by Steven Barrett, a former MIT aeronautics professor who now holds the Regius Professorship of Engineering at the University of Cambridge, and Chris Sylvan, who previously led business in Europe, the Middle East and Africa for U.S. defense company Anduril Industries. Former British Defence Secretary Grant Shapps chairs the company. It has also shown a second interceptor, Starhammer, and builds solid rocket motors in Britain.
Its Nightstar rocket motor is one of seven finalists in the low-cost solid rocket motor category of the U.S. Army’s xTech|Apex Intercept competition, which is looking for cheaper interceptors to work alongside the Patriot air defense system. Finalists will demonstrate their technology in October and November.

articles.title: At least 10 people killed in Russian and Ukrainian attacks
articles.body:
At least 10 people killed in Russian and Ukrainian attacks
New strikes come as Russian FM accuses Europe of doing ‘everything it can to thwart peace talks’ with Ukraine.
Russia and Ukraine have traded attacks that have killed at least 10 people, while the United States pushes for talks to end the war and Moscow’s top diplomat blames Europe for hindering negotiations.
Russian attacks killed four people in Ukraine, while Ukrainian strikes killed six in Russia and Russian-occupied territory, officials on both sides said on Saturday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump invites Putin to Miami G20: Why that matters
- list 2 of 3US seeks to revive Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks as seven killed in Kyiv
- list 3 of 3Poland boosts air defence after ‘Russian provocations’ amid Ukraine war
In Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia, two women died under the rubble of their home, following an overnight Russian barrage of drones and missiles, the regional military administration said.
A separate Russian attack killed two people in the city of Sumy, according to local officials.
“It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X on Saturday.
“If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further.”
Ukraine has pressed on with long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and industrial sites.
In Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, a Ukrainian drone attack killed three people and wounded two, with Governor Veniamin Kondratyev writing on Telegram that it had also sparked fires at two industrial facilities.
Russian media later said an oil refinery was among the targets.
Moscow-installed regional head Yevgeny Balitsky said Ukrainian strikes overnight into Saturday killed three people in the Russian-occupied part of Zaporizhzhia region, according to Russian state media.
Russia’s Defence Ministry meanwhile said Russian forces struck a cargo vessel with military supplies near Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Odesa on Saturday. A logistics hub was also hit in Odesa, it added.
On Friday, Russian strikes on Kyiv killed seven people, injured 58 and forced a halt to production at Ukraine’s largest steelmaker.
ArcelorMittal said on Friday that a number of strikes in recent days had killed five workers and badly damaged one of their sites. Ukraine’s steel industry previously made up 15 percent of the country’s exports.
Ukrainian forces, for their part, hit oil refineries in Russia’s Perm and Novoshakhtinsk on Friday, causing a temporary halt to operations.
‘Awaiting a proposal’
The deadly strikes came after Zelenskyy said on Friday that Washington had proposed a meeting of Russian, Ukrainian and US officials in the United Arab Emirates.
“We are awaiting a proposal from the United States regarding the date, and the United States has suggested the Emirates as a possible location,” he said in a WhatsApp briefing.
He also said Egypt, India, Turkiye and representatives from the Middle East were taking part in talks on unblocking shipping in the Black Sea, while other nations had put forward proposals.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that every settlement proposal remained on the table, though Moscow was still weighing what served its interests, according to Russian news agencies.
He said Moscow was prepared to return to talks with Kyiv following last week’s parliamentary elections, but accused Ukraine of trying to strike the capital and attacking polling stations.
In Zelenskyy’s nightly video address on Saturday, the Ukrainian leader accused Russia of “not preparing to end the war – at least not at this point.”
“Putin always has some pretext ready – not to meet, not to hold a three-way meeting, not to talk, not to end these killings and not to stop them,” Zelenskyy said. “He is looking for pretexts to wage war.”
Meanwhile, Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Saturday, and accused Europe of hindering talks with Ukraine.
“Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the [Donald] Trump administration is interested,” he said, referring to the US government.
Lavrov also said Moscow would achieve its military aims in Ukraine “no matter the circumstances”.
“The aims of the special military operation will be achieved, the threat to Russian security will be eliminated and peaceful life will come back,” he said.

articles.title: Berlin’s ‘Russian House’ stayed open despite Russia’s war in Ukraine and EU sanctions, shielded by a reciprocal deal over Moscow’s Goethe-Institut. Germany’s sabotage accusation was the final straw.
articles.body:
Berlin’s ‘Russian House’ stayed open despite Russia’s war in Ukraine and EU sanctions, shielded by a reciprocal deal over Moscow’s Goethe-Institut. Germany’s sabotage accusation was the final straw.
In early September, Germany’s Foreign Ministry announced the closure of the Russian House in Berlin, Russia’s largest cultural center abroad. The center had operated in the heart of the German capital for more than 40 years. It remained open after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, even as similar institutions across Europe shut down. What finally brought it to an end was a drone attack on Leipzig Airport that German authorities described as Russian sabotage. Meduza tells the center’s story.
In early August, a DHL cargo plane approaching Leipzig Airport had to climb sharply when the airport unexpectedly closed. After the plane landed in Hanover, inspectors found minor damage caused by a collision with an unidentified flying object.
At Leipzig Airport, bomb disposal experts found and defused a drone fitted with explosives and a detonator near a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane. Ten days later, another drone bearing traces of explosives was found near the airport.
German authorities investigated for nearly a month before blaming Russia for the attempted sabotage. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced Germany’s response: the closure of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova criticized the decision. Speaking about the Russian House, she said:
The Russian House was obviously a thorn in their side. Why?.. Its first and foremost purpose is to teach Russian. Demand was enormous. […] That’s the Russian House’s main offense — the reason the German establishment disliked it so much.
There are more than 70 Russian Houses worldwide. The full-scale war has disrupted their work.
The worldwide network of Russian Houses took its present form in 2008, when President Dmitry Medvedev signed a decree creating Rossotrudnichestvo, a Russian federal agency for cultural outreach abroad. Officially overseen by the Foreign Ministry, the agency runs Russian language courses and promotes Russian culture, science, and education.
Before the war, Russian Houses operated in at least 77 countries. Their work became more difficult after the EU imposed sanctions on Rossotrudnichestvo following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In July 2022, the EU added the agency to its sanctions list, accusing it of promoting the ideas of the “Russian World,” funding propaganda projects, and spreading “Kremlin narratives” and historical revisionism.
After the EU’s decision, Russian Houses suspended operations in six European countries: Slovenia, Slovakia, Croatia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, and Romania. The Russian House in Baku also suspended operations in 2025 after a passenger plane crashed near Aktau. In July 2026, the Russian House in Chișinău closed indefinitely. Moldovan authorities called it a “tool of the Kremlin’s hybrid influence.”
In Berlin, however, the Russian House kept operating after the sanctions against Rossotrudnichestvo. Its seven-story modernist building on Friedrichstraße, within walking distance of the Russian embassy, opened in 1984 as the House of Soviet Culture and Science. It was the Soviet Union’s largest cultural center abroad. Russia later took ownership of the building, and the center became the Russian House of Culture and Science.
The Russian House’s activities changed little over more than 40 years. At its 20th anniversary celebration in 2004, then-director Anatoly Bogushevsky said the center drew about 300,000 visitors a year. Its main aim, he said, was to give people in Germany “as comprehensive a picture as possible of a new, reformed Russia seeking to strengthen democracy.” Its activities centered on a Russian language center, a Russian college, a Pushkin Library with more than 40,000 books, small clubs and workshops, concerts, and film screenings.
Decades later, the 29,000-square-meter building, which occupies an entire Berlin block, still housed children’s clubs and workshops — some free, others paid — as well as a movie theater, concert halls, and exhibition spaces. Rossotrudnichestvo says more than three million people attended events there over the past 15 years. Some events, however, were difficult to describe as purely cultural. After 2022, the theater sometimes screened RT material that called Ukrainians Nazis, and the center held photo exhibitions on similar themes.
Two agreements signed in 2011 and 2013 governed the Russian House’s operations. The first established its status as a cultural and information center; the second gave Russia the right to lease the building for 99 years. Throughout that period, Germany paid about 70,000 euros a year in property tax on the land beneath it. In return, Germany received the right to lease the Goethe-Institut building on Baumanskaya Street in Moscow on the same terms.
Berlin long resisted politicians’ calls to close the Russian House because terminating those agreements could put the Goethe-Institut in Russia at risk.
Even so, sanctions severely hampered the Russian House’s work. All its assets in the EU were frozen, and it could use its bank account only under Bundesbank supervision. Its ability to receive money was tightly restricted: EU legal entities were barred from providing it with funds or economic resources, directly or indirectly, while it could accept only enough from third parties to maintain the building.
The Russian House nevertheless continued collecting rent on apartments and offices in the building. Tagesschau.de found that 115 people lived there in June 2023. In 2018, for example, the Russian House earned about $2 million from rent. Meduza asked Rossotrudnichestvo what would happen to the apartment residents after the closure but had received no response by publication.
The Russian House has drawn espionage allegations
Once the invasion of Ukraine began, German authorities increasingly suspected that the building could be used for spying and to skirt sanctions. In January 2023, Berlin prosecutors launched a probe into possible violations of the country’s foreign trade law. It led nowhere. Prosecutors closed the investigation after Germany froze the Russian House’s accounts, and Moscow hit back by freezing the Goethe-Institut’s accounts there.
The allegations gained renewed attention in the summer of 2026, when German outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung and WDR reported on a French Interior Ministry document. According to the document, Russian intelligence services use the Russian House as a front, and the center’s mission is to influence the diaspora to support Moscow’s policies.
Green Party Bundestag member Robin Wagener called the allegations plausible, saying, “The center’s activities are not limited to harmless language courses.” Christian Democratic Union lawmaker Roderich Kiesewetter called it a “disinformation center” and an extension of the Kremlin. An investigation by CORRECTIV also found that the organization running the Russian House maintains a branch in Dresden called the German-Russian Cultural Institute.
In August 2026, Green Party Bundestag member Sara Nanni, who works on defense issues, pointed to unusual mobile phone and GPS “signal activity” near the building. She said it could indicate that powerful equipment for intercepting signals or communicating covertly was operating inside. Kiesewetter also said that although 100 people lived in the complex, the building used a disproportionate amount of electricity. He and Free Democratic Party member of the European Parliament Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann said the building might serve as a hub for technical intelligence gathering and the coordination of cyberattacks.
Many of the building’s business tenants, however, had no connection to Rossotrudnichestvo. They included the Samowar Hof restaurant and Mnogo Knig, one of Berlin’s few Russian-language bookstores. Businesses there may also have faced pressure from Russian authorities. Journalist Ilya Barabanov said that in 2024, a complaint from Rossotrudnichestvo led the bookstore to remove his book “Nash biznes — smert” (“Our Business Is Death”), about the Wagner private military company, from sale. Meduza published the book.
Hi, I’m N.
I report for Meduza from inside Russia. I could go to prison for my work. To stay safe, I have to follow strict security protocols. I know my lawyer’s phone number by heart. And, of course, my articles are published anonymously.
Working for an independent news outlet while still living in Russia feels like something out of a spy film. My friends know me by one name. My colleagues and sources know me by another. But sometimes there’s a glitch. At a close friend’s birthday party, someone I don’t know reaches out to shake my hand. “Hi, I’m Lyosha.” It takes me a few seconds to decide how to introduce myself. Do I use my real name or my pseudonym? I’m trying to figure out whether this is someone I might one day end up writing about.
What I do is journalism in exile, even though I’m not in exile myself. I have the rare opportunity to do uncensored, on-the-ground reporting in Russia. Please support Meduza so I can continue this work.
The closure led to deportations and cost dozens of people their jobs
Staff assigned from Russia to the Russian House and Rossotrudnichestvo were ordered to leave Germany within seven days. On September 10, they arrived in Belarus along with diplomats from the closed consulate in Bonn. According to Ekho, only about seven Russian House employees were specialists assigned from Russia; they were the ones who had to leave Germany. The rest had been hired locally, and some were German citizens.
Sabine Gimaeva, who owns the Samowar Hof café that opened in the Russian House more than a decade ago, told Meduza that many cultural and educational projects stopped almost immediately after Germany’s Foreign Ministry announced the closure. Commercial tenants were given until December to leave. Gimaeva said the closure would affect more than Russians:
People of all different nationalities come here, with all kinds of passports — including a lot of Ukrainians. […] So to me, this is about much more than just our café closing. A whole network of services that very different people have used for years is disappearing from one building all at once.
In Gimaeva’s view, the German authorities’ decision hurts “ordinary workers and private businesses” rather than Russian state institutions. Businesses may struggle to relocate on short notice, she said, and some may close, costing people their jobs:
People who have worked and supported themselves for years may now end up relying on German welfare. I feel like very few people are talking about those consequences right now.
The Russian House closed just before the September 20 election to Berlin’s state parliament, and the decision quickly became a campaign issue. Even before the closure was announced, Social Democratic mayoral candidate Steffen Krach stood outside the building with a sign reading, “Here’s something we can expropriate, friends in the Left Party! Are you with us?” He did not clearly state his position on the Russian House’s status; his gesture appeared to invoke the Left Party’s plans to nationalize housing. Krach did not respond to Meduza’s request for comment.
On September 4, after the foreign minister’s official announcement, two protests took place outside the Russian House — one supporting the closure and one opposing it. Reforum Space Berlin, a space for antiwar Russians created by the Free Russia Foundation, helped organize the protest in favor. Its coordinator, Yulia Abdullaeva, who has lived in Berlin since 2011, told Meduza that alternatives to the Russian House already exist in the city:
The question isn’t whether individual classes held there were good or bad. It’s whether the Russian state should still have a venue of its own in central Berlin today, using culture as a tool of its foreign policy and propaganda. […] All the community activities people genuinely need — Russian lessons for children, cultural events, a library, films, educational programs — can exist (and already do!) in independent organizations, without Russian state control.
Supporters of keeping the Russian House open held their own protest that day. One organizer was the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, a party that advocates better relations with Russia. Alexander King, co-chair of its Berlin branch, told Meduza that closing the Russian House and the Bonn consulate amounted to “far-reaching measures that could bring us closer to a possible military conflict.” In the September 20 election, the party failed to clear the 5% threshold for seats in parliament.
Samowar Hof owner Sabine Gimaeva also attended the protest in support of the Russian House. “To me, that’s a perfectly normal way to stand up for what matters to me — if a decision directly affects my family, our business, the people who work here, and cultural projects that have been here for years, of course I’m not going to pretend it doesn’t concern me,” she said.
Die Welt estimated that several hundred people attended the protest against the closure. Deutsche Welle gave more precise figures: about 250 people attended the rally supporting the closure, and about 500 opposed it. Reforum Space Berlin coordinator Olga Galkina, however, told Ekho that the two sides were roughly equal in number. In her view, those who wanted to keep the center included ethnic German immigrants known as “late resettlers” and Putinverstehers, or Putin sympathizers. Abdullaeva made a similar distinction:
I wouldn’t apply the label ‘Putinverstehers’ to everyone who went to the Russian House. It was mainly about the politics of defending the Russian House. For many people, it really was, above all, a place where they could hear Russian, go to a concert, or take their child to a class. I used to go there fairly often myself, but since the full-scale war began, I haven’t gone back — because the war changed what this institution means to me.
The Left Party, which won the Berlin election, had not publicly commented on the Russian House’s closure during the campaign. Earlier, however, the party’s deputy federal chair, Maximilian Schirmer, had called the center “a propaganda institution.”
The parties that finished second and third — the Christian Democratic Union and Alternative for Germany, respectively — differed in their positions. The Christian Democrats, Berlin’s current governing party, had consistently called for the Russian House to close. Alternative for Germany had not stated a position directly, though its Bundestag member Karsten Hilse attended the protest in support of the center.
As the Russian House closed, Rossotrudnichestvo announced plans to expand the network. On September 8, agency head Igor Chaika signed agreements to open 11 new Russian Houses in Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, Senegal, Mali, Sierra Leone, São Tomé and Príncipe, Togo, Madagascar, Armenia, and Thailand. The agency’s deputy head also said a new Russian House in Germany “will definitely open” and that the search for new partners was already underway.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
