articles.title: From the Cold War to post-Assad: 80 years of Syria-Turkey ties
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
From Cold War rivalry to post-Assad cordiality: 80 years of Turkey-Syria relations
In another sign of how swiftly relations have improved, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will soon visit Syria, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on 14 September after a two-day visit.
This year marks the 80th anniversary of the two neighbours establishing diplomatic relations in 1946, the same year Syria became independent.
A brief look at the history of Turkey-Syria relations suggests that the present moment may mark the closest the two countries have ever been.
Disquieting developments
Syria and Lebanon were under French mandate from the collapse of the Ottoman Empire until the aftermath of the Second World War, when both countries became independent. Turkey immediately established diplomatic relations. At the time, it was viewed as “a Turkish step towards a closer union with the Arab world”.
From those early years of relations, the two neighbours joined rival alliances and forged close ties with the two superpowers. Turkey joined the NATO alliance in 1952. After Turkey concluded a mutual defence treaty with Iraq, then under the pro-Western monarchy, Syria in 1955 recalled its envoy to Turkey for consultations.
Tensions reached an unprecedented high point in 1957 when regional fears spread of a communist takeover in Damascus following the appointment of leftist officers to the Syrian Army in August. Ankara deployed thousands of troops along its border. Damascus charged that Turkey massed its troops in a “manner which presages imminent attack”.
The crisis reached a breaking point by that October, with Damascus additionally charging that Turkish soldiers fired at Syrian border residents and Turkish warplanes flew over Syrian territory.
It even risked drawing in the superpowers, with the US warning the Soviet Union that it would honour its commitments to Turkey’s defence and Moscow declaring it would “inevitably” intervene if Turkey went to war. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev wasn’t so subtle when he remarked that “if war breaks out, we are near Turkey and you are not”.
The crisis showed signs of thaw and ultimately ended that month. In early October 1957, Syria’s new minister to Turkey clarified that Syria only feared an attack by Israel, adding: “I hope Turkish-Syrian relations become better for both of our countries have close ties in language, history and custom.”
Khrushchev seized the opportunity presented by Turkey’s National Day on 29 October to “unexpectedly” show up at the Turkish Embassy in Moscow and toast “peace,” crediting Soviet diplomacy with “cooling off” Turkey.
Syria entered into a brief political union with Gamal Abdel Nasser’s Egypt, then known as the United Arab Republic, in 1958. In January of that year, Turkey again warned its southern neighbour of communist infiltration, arguing that such danger “has introduced in our region disquieting developments”.
Damascus seceded from the UAR in 1961 following a coup. Nasser broke off diplomatic relations with Turkey for recognising the new provisional government in Damascus on the day it was formed, citing a “hostile attitude” toward the UAR.
Any hopes for warmer relations between Ankara and Damascus were short-lived. The 1963 coup brought the Ba’ath Party to power, and Syria entered a closer, lasting relationship with Moscow, which became its leading arms supplier for the rest of the Cold War.
Still, the neighbours avoided another crisis like 1957 until the end of the century.
Insurgency, territorial disputes, and water-sharing
The rule of the Assads in Syria began in 1970 when Hafez al-Assad seized power in yet another coup, invariably justifying his family’s long and brutal reign by citing the endless coups that preceded them.
Assad’s first decade in power coincided with Turkey beginning its damming of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, both of which originate in Turkey and flow downstream to Syria and Iraq. Ankara’s move would create recurring tensions in the relationship over the decades to come.
Another dispute Assad would raise was over Turkey’s Hatay Province. During the French Mandate over Syria, it was known as the Sanjak of Alexandretta. France supported its transfer to Turkish sovereignty in 1939, hoping to convince Ankara to join the Allies against Nazi Germany. It didn’t work. Alexandretta became Hatay.
The Hatay and water-sharing disputes persisted for years. Assad would host the Kurdistan Workers’ Party group, well-known by its Kurdish PKK acronym, and its leader Abdullah Öcalan for years after it launched its armed rebellion against Turkey in 1984. While the two sides signed a border security agreement in 1985, relations between them were strained in this period by Syria’s support of the PKK and the Armenian Secret Army for the Liberation of Armenia.
In 1989, two Syrian MiG-21 fighter jets flew 12 miles into Turkish airspace and shot down a civilian Turkish plane, killing all five people aboard. Syria offered condolences and ordered an inquiry.
By 1990, Turkey’s massive Ataturk Dam on the Euphrates neared completion, again raising objections downstream, with Syria fearing it could lose 40 percent of water it could hitherto rely upon.
Turkey’s state minister said his country had “no international obligations” to provide other countries with water but added that Ankara would do its “best not to harm our neighbours”.
In 1992, Turkey promised to honour past water-sharing agreements. Turkish Foreign Minister Hikmet Cetin said Ankara would respect a 1987 pact on water-sharing under which Turkey would allow at least 500 cubic meters of Euphrates water a second into Syria. The two signed an accord committing to reach a “final solution” on Euphrates water allocation by the end of 1993.
From brink to thaw
Exactly forty-one years after the end of the 1957 crisis, 10,000 Turkish troops amassed along the Turkish-Syrian border in October 1998. Turkey’s military threatened “economic, political and military sanctions” on Damascus. Ankara finally had enough of Syria providing its PKK arch-enemy sanctuary.
“I am not only warning Syria, I am warning the world – this cannot continue,” declared Turkish President Suleyman Demirel. In addition to expelling the PKK, Turkey demanded that Syria drop territorial claims to Hatay.
The crisis lasted less than a month. On 20 October, they signed the Adana Agreement, under which Syria would end its support of the PKK. Damascus expelled Ocalan, who Turkey captured the following year, and restricted the group’s activities on its soil.
Hafez Al-Assad passed away in 2000. Under his son and successor Bashar, Turkey-Syria relations experienced a notable thaw.
Bashar Al-Assad became the first Syrian head of state to visit Turkey in 2004, declaring that his visit coincided “with a period when Syrian-Turkish relations are reaching a peak”.
The following year, Turkish President Ahmet Necdet Sezer visited Syria for two days. In April 2008, Erdogan flew to Damascus, where he discussed the possibility of direct Syria-Israel talks with Assad. The following August, they would meet again when Assad visited the Turkish resort of Bodrum, where he was also vacationing that month.
In 2009, Turkey and Syria reached a deal allowing their citizens to travel to each other’s countries without visas. As Turkey-Israel relations sharply deteriorated following the deadly May 2010 Israeli raid on the Mavi Marmara flotilla, Turkey-Syria ties briefly blossomed as tens of thousands of Syrians visited Turkey’s southeastern Gaziantep monthly.
In a far cry from the 1957 and 1998 crises, Turkey and Syria even held joint military exercises along their shared border in 2009 and 2010.
Little could anyone at the time know that the lowest point in relations was just around the corner.
Lowest point
Assad would ultimately initiate the worst of the regional crackdowns that followed the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings, killing and torturing what were initially peaceful civil demonstrators.
Turkey sought to preserve relations and urge restraint. By August, Turkish Foreign Minister Ahmet Davutoglu went to Damascus to deliver Erdogan’s message that Ankara had “run out of patience” with the Assad regime’s unrelenting violence, which at that point had killed more than 2,000 people. Assad remained unmoved.
The war grew increasingly violent with larger numbers of Syrian refugees pouring over the border into Turkey. The Syrian refugee population peaked at up to 3.7 million over the next decade, more than any other country hosting refugees from that bloody conflict, which eventually left more than 500,000 dead.
Turkey closed its embassy in Damascus in March 2012, hosted the anti-Assad opposition, and banned all Syrian flights from its airspace. Aleppo University even withdrew an honorary doctorate in international relations it had awarded Erdogan in 2009. In December 2015, both states cancelled their 2009 visa agreement.
Syria shot down a Turkish RF-4E reconnaissance jet after it briefly violated its airspace on 22 June 2012, killing both crew members.
Turkey would later intervene directly in Syria in August 2016 with its cross-border Euphrates Shield operation that targeted both the Islamic State and the Kurdish YPG. Ankara avoided fighting Assad’s forces, who were ferociously bombarding east Aleppo with Russian support at the time.
Instead, Turkey remained largely focused on combating the Kurdish forces in a series of cross-border incursions that followed in 2018 and 2019. At the same time, it established an on-the-ground military presence in Syria’s northwestern Idlib province, where the Islamist armed opposition Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) had come to control and govern.
The deadliest clash ever between Turkey and Syria occurred in Idlib in early 2020. After an airstrike killed at least 33 Turkish soldiers, Turkey launched Operation Spring Shield, devastating Assad’s forces with heavy air, artillery, and drone strikes.
New leader, new thaw
After the deadly February 2023 earthquake, which affected both sides of the Turkey-Syria border, regional states offered the Assad regime a second chance in return for reforms and ending the Captagon drug trade. Syria was readmitted into the Arab League but made little tangible effort to implement any reforms or even basic policy changes.
By June 2024, Erdogan offered to restore diplomatic relations for the first time in over a decade. In reference to the 2008 vacation, the Turkish leader said, “In the same way that we kept our relations with Syria alive in the past - we had these meetings with Mr Assad that included family meetings – we cannot say that it will not happen again”.
It did not. Not under Assad anyway. In his final days, the Syrian leader was detached from any semblance of reality, reportedly spending a lot of his time playing Candy Crush on his phone.
By December, a victorious HTS burst out of Idlib, swiftly captured Aleppo and marched on Damascus. Assad fled into exile in Moscow. HTS leader Ahmed al-Sharaa has succeeded Assad as interim president, ending a half-century of that family’s rule.
Sharaa quickly forged close relations with Turkey, making his first visit in February 2025. Turkey reopened its embassy in Damascus mere days after the transitional government seized power, and Turkish Airlines resumed flights to Damascus for the first time in 13 years.
Turkey even seems poised to replace Moscow’s traditional role as Syria’s main military client. However, Sharaa has shown signs that he wants to diversify Syria’s relations to avoid over-reliance on any one country.
The new leadership in Damascus has heralded a new era in Turkey-Syria relations, which may prove much more resilient and long-lasting than past thaws.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.
Follow him on Twitter: @pauliddon
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Iran will defend itself against any threat or military attack: Pezeshkian
articles.body:
Iran will defend itself against any threat or military attack: Pezeshkian
TEHRAN— Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has reaffirmed Tehran’s readiness to pursue diplomacy with Washington over the nuclear issue and other outstanding disputes, while stressing that negotiations can succeed only if they are based on mutual commitments, respect for international law and tangible steps to rebuild trust.
In an interview with CBS News during his visit to New York for the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Pezeshkian said Iran does not seek war or confrontation, but would defend itself against any threat or military attack.
The president’s remarks came amid renewed diplomatic activity surrounding the Iranian nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran maintaining that any return to negotiations must be accompanied by practical guarantees that previous agreements will not again be disregarded.
Trust at the center of Iran-US diplomacy
Pezeshkian said Iran had previously reached understandings with the United States, but that the diplomatic process had been undermined by Washington’s failure to honor its commitments.
He pointed in particular to the US withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement and subsequent military actions against Iran, arguing that these developments had created a profound atmosphere of mistrust between the two countries.
For Tehran, he said, the issue is therefore not simply whether negotiations can resume, but whether agreements reached through diplomacy will be implemented in practice.
Pezeshkian said Iran was prepared to negotiate within the framework of international law and the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), including arrangements concerning nuclear monitoring and inspections.
His comments followed an Iranian proposal for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the resumption of negotiations, with Tehran presenting the two issues as part of a broader diplomatic framework for reducing tensions. CBS reported that Iran had offered to reopen the strategic
waterway within seven days and restart talks as an initial step toward a longer-term nuclear agreement.
Iran reiterates peaceful nature of nuclear program
Pezeshkian again rejected any suggestion that Iran seeks to develop nuclear weapons, saying the country has never pursued such a goal.
He also said disagreements over inspections could be resolved through negotiations and mutually agreed arrangements. Asked directly whether Iran would allow UN nuclear inspectors to return, he answered affirmatively, adding that the details of inspections could be addressed within a negotiated framework.
The Iranian president also criticized attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities, arguing that such sites had been subject to international monitoring and questioning the legal justification for targeting facilities associated with a program Tehran maintains is peaceful.
From Tehran’s perspective, the central issue is that verification and monitoring should take place through established international mechanisms rather than military action.
Iran has repeatedly maintained that it is prepared to provide assurances concerning the peaceful nature of its nuclear activities while insisting on its rights under the NPT. Iranian officials have also argued that military attacks on nuclear facilities undermine the very diplomatic mechanisms designed to resolve disputes over nuclear activities.
Direct Trump meeting requires more than a gesture
Asked about the possibility of a direct meeting with US President Donald Trump, Pezeshkian said the accumulated mistrust between Tehran and Washington could not be overcome merely through a face-to-face encounter.
He referred to the US withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement and military attacks that 'took place even as diplomatic channels were being pursued.'
Pezeshkian said Iran needs practical evidence that Washington is prepared to honor agreements and is not seeking to overthrow the Iranian government.
His position effectively places implementation and guarantees at the center of any future diplomatic process: Tehran, he indicated, is not opposed to negotiations, but does not consider negotiations meaningful if pressure, threats and military action continue alongside them.
CBS reported that US and Iranian officials had already held indirect discussions through mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, although no direct meeting between Trump and Pezeshkian took place.
Hormuz: Iran links reopening to implementation of arrangements
The Strait of Hormuz was another major focus of the interview.
Pezeshkian said Iran could return to an earlier framework concerning the strategic waterway if Washington accepted the arrangements previously discussed. He stressed that implementation should be based on reciprocal commitments and dialogue.
The issue has become one of the most sensitive dimensions of the broader Iran-US confrontation because the strait is a critical international energy corridor and lies at the heart of the security architecture of the Persian Gulf.
Iran has maintained that the security and navigation arrangements in the waterway cannot be separated from the wider military confrontation and the commitments contained in previously negotiated understandings.
The latest Iranian proposal, according to international reporting, calls for the reopening of the strait within seven days if the United States takes corresponding steps to reduce military pressure and lift its blockade of Iranian ports.
Pezeshkian’s comments indicate that Tehran views the issue not as a unilateral concession, but as part of a reciprocal diplomatic arrangement in which commitments by both sides would be implemented simultaneously.
Iran calls for regional dialogue
Turning to wider regional developments, Pezeshkian said Iran does not seek conflict with its neighbors and favors resolving regional disputes through dialogue, mutual respect and adherence to international rules.
He said neighboring countries could work together to develop the region and establish mechanisms that would strengthen collective security rather than relying on external military intervention.
The position reflects Tehran’s longstanding emphasis on regional arrangements involving neighboring states, particularly in the Persian Gulf, rather than security frameworks dominated by extra-regional military powers.
Pezeshkian also criticized economic sanctions, arguing that their consequences extend beyond governments and affect ordinary people, particularly patients, elderly citizens and low-income groups.
He called for an approach grounded in justice and respect for human rights, linking the humanitarian consequences of sanctions to the broader question of international responsibility.
Coordination with the Leader
Pezeshkian also provided an account of his recent contacts with Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, saying he had met with him twice, including a meeting lasting approximately seven hours.
The president described the Leader as being in good physical condition and said Iran’s diplomatic approach is coordinated with the Leader.
He further explained that a six-member team comprising representatives of the military, Parliament and government has been authorized to conduct consultations and discuss decisions related to the diplomatic process.
Rejecting claims about wartime shelters
Pezeshkian also rejected reports that he had been confined to a shelter during the war imposed on Iran by the United States and the Israeli regime.
He said government affairs had continued during the conflict, with the president holding meetings with ministers and other officials while taking precautions against possible attacks.
Asked about reports that Iranian officials had operated from shelters, he stressed that the government could not have continued functioning had its leadership simply remained confined underground. CBS quoted him as saying that “if we were in a shelter, nothing would have gotten done.”
US detainees and the question of trust
On the detention of two US citizens in Iran, Pezeshkian questioned whether releasing them alone would be sufficient to restore confidence between Tehran and Washington.
He referred to previous cases in which Iran fulfilled commitments without receiving reciprocal action from the United States.
His response again reflected the central theme of the interview: Tehran’s concern is not simply the making of commitments but their implementation by both sides.
Iran rejects threats against Trump
Pezeshkian was also asked about threats against Trump and members of his family.
The Iranian president rejected the suggestion that the Iranian government was pursuing such actions, arguing that if Tehran intended to act against the US president or his family, it would not be engaged in negotiations.
The statement was also framed as part of Iran’s broader position that disputes with Washington should be addressed through diplomatic channels rather than assassination threats or military confrontation.
Taken together, Pezeshkian’s remarks presented a consistent message: Iran remains open to diplomacy, including negotiations with the United States over its nuclear program, but does not view dialogue as compatible with continued military pressure, coercive demands or the unilateral abandonment of agreements.
For Tehran, the restoration of trust would require more than diplomatic declarations. It would require concrete action, reciprocal commitments and mechanisms capable of ensuring that agreements reached at the negotiating table are implemented in practice.
The president’s comments also placed the nuclear issue within a wider framework that includes regional security, the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions and Iran’s right to defend itself.

articles.title: Swimming in Dangerous Waters
articles.body:
While debates rumble on regarding a national pantheon and Poland’s threats to block Ukraine’s EU accession should the monument include the graves of the 20th-century Ukrainian nationalist leaders Stepan Bandera and Roman Shukhevych, plans are underway, in the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi district of Odesa region, for a different kind of memorial burial site.
It will be a pantheon for Black Sea dolphins and it is slated for construction within the Tuzlivski Lagoon National Reserve – a unique area comprising forests, steppe, and 13 lagoons, connected to the sea, which attract a vast array of wildlife, including dolphins.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The idea for this pantheon was suggested by Ivan Rusev, a prominent ecologist who works at the reserve. Since 2022, Russian drones have frequently sparked fires inside the protected area. However, the most severe impact of Russian aggression in the area has been on the Black Sea dolphin population, which has plummeted catastrophically.
Rusev estimates that over 50,000 dolphins have fallen victim to the war over the past four and a half years. In just the last couple of months, 89 dead dolphins have washed up on the shore.
Apart from falling victim to the hundreds of Russian drones that explode into the sea before reaching the Ukrainian coast, vast numbers of dolphins have succumbed to marine pollution caused by fuel oil, gasoline, sunflower oil, and other liquid commodities. These substances spill into the sea whenever Russian missiles and drones destroy storage facilities at Ukrainian sea and river ports.
Russia Must Answer for Crimes in Crimea, Zelensky Says
Furthermore, intensive underwater radio surveillance by Russian warships and submarines – and specifically the use of powerful sonar systems – disrupts the dolphins’ ability to navigate underwater. This, too, leads to the deaths of these Black Sea cetaceans.
The remains and skeletons of dead dolphins found along the shore have already formed mounds at several locations within the protected coastal area. Once the planned pantheon is built, some of these remains will be interred there in a mass grave dedicated to the animal victims of the Russo-Ukrainian War. It will be the first monument constructed within the vast nature reserve.
Murky political waters
Yet the war has made it difficult for many Ukrainians to dwell on environmental damage, however grave. Survival under constant shelling and developments at the front naturally come first. At the same time, another threat to the country’s resilience is drawing growing—and increasingly sarcastic—attention: corruption, and the struggle to contain it.
Recent events have served as a reminder that Ukrainian politics often bears a closer resemblance to unsophisticated TV entertainment than to a platform for ideological confrontation and debate over how best to organize the economy and public services.
The process of exposing corruption and dealing with suspected perpetrators also displays a show-business dynamic which overshadows the legal procedure. However, theatrical as the scandals may appear, their effect on the political environment is real and they stir up the waters of government, making them almost impossible to navigate safely.
The saga of Operation Carthage, which led to the arrest, on corruption charges, of a deputy prosecutor general, is being followed like a soap opera popular for its most obvious plot twists.
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko – who had denied involvement in his subordinates’ corrupt activities – promised to resign following a conversation with President Volodymyr Zelensky, but then he vanished from the media spotlight for a week, during which time no official charges were brought against him.
Kravchenko remained in his post and was not called in for official questioning. Then, having authorized, for himself, a business trip to Paris, as prosecutor general, he left the country using a VIP taxi service. That same night, his wife also departed Ukraine via the Shehyni border crossing.
Kravchenko did not arrive in Paris, and having spent four days in lively speculation as to whether Kravchenko would return home from his “business trip,” Ukrainians began asking themselves who would be the next top civil servant allowed to flee abroad before his/her actions were investigated by the proper authorities.
It is hard to imagine the now ex-prosecutor general turning up in Kyiv, but were he to do so, he would almost certainly stand trial. However, Ukraine’s judicial system is not accustomed to being harsh on corrupt former officials, and Kravchenko would be unlikely to face imprisonment. What is more, if he were tried by judges from Odesa or Odesa region, he would have absolutely nothing to worry about.
That judicial leniency has an especially Odesan variation. Since 2021, for minor, non-violent offences, judges in the region have regularly handed down suspended sentences that include a requirement to read a list of fiction books selected by the judge—usually classics. Two teenage thieves received such a sentence in 2021.
During their trial, the judge at the Malinovskyi District Court noted that the defendants were barely able to articulate their actions coherently and displayed a remarkably limited vocabulary. In view of this, the judge ordered them to read works by Mark Twain, Jack London, and the Ukrainian national poet Taras Shevchenko. Since then, the reading requirement has been expanded to include writing a 500-word essay on each assigned book.
The most recent sentence of this type was handed down just a few days ago at the Dobroslav District Court in Odesa. A Russian-speaking resident, who had used the internet to justify Russian aggression and to promote the idea of Russia occupying Odesa region, received a suspended sentence.
The ruling required her to read two adventure novels by the Ukrainian writer Ivan Bahrianyi (1906–1963) and to read and provide written commentary on the Budapest Memorandum – a document signed by the US, the UK, and Russia, under which Ukraine surrendered its nuclear arsenal to Russia in exchange for guarantees regarding its security and territorial integrity.
One wonders which titles the Odesa courts might include in the reading list for a wayward prosecutor general. But beyond these darkly comic courtroom remedies, the region remains exposed to the far more immediate dangers of war.
As the shipping industry mourns the death of the Ukrainian captain of a cargo vessel recently hit by a Russian missile off the Odesa coast, we can only hope that the dolphin community migrates away from these dangerous waters a little earlier than usual this autumn.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: From Russia with “Russophobia”: Kremlin propaganda accounts are posing as “angry Latvians” to influence the country’s Telegram communities
articles.body:
After Latvia banned broadcasts by Russian federal television channels, Telegram became a key platform for Kremlin propaganda in the country. The Insider estimates that around one-third of socio-political channels in Latvia’s Telegram ecosystem are controlled by Russian propagandists posing as “angry Latvians” — and the figure rises to upwards of 65% when only Russian-language channels are included in the count. The channels portray life in Latvia as getting worse, blaming anti-Russian sanctions for harming the Baltic states while calling for an end to support for Ukraine.
Methodology
The Insider collected data from 72 Latvian socio-political channels (353,000 posts from January 1, 2025) and analyzed the network of reposts from these channels. Of the 93,000 shares, 30.3% were reposts between the channels themselves, while 43.7% came from Russian state media, official government channels, military bloggers, and pro-war “Z-channels.” Together, these account for three-quarters of all shared content. For content analysis, a sample of up to 200 posts — stratified by month — was taken from each channel, totaling more than 12,000 posts. Each post was examined for pro-Kremlin and anti-Ukrainian narratives. These narratives were identified in 65 Telegram channels.
All of the channels analyzed by The Insider publish in Russian, and some operate anonymously. The largest are linked to the state-run media group Rossiya Segodnya, which includes RT. They are run by RT editorial staff, in-house RT journalists, or frequent contributors to the channel. At least one channel was previously part of the disinformation network overseen by the late Wagner Group co-founder Yevgeny Prigozhin.
None of the people behind the five largest channels have actually lived in Latvia in recent years. Some have left for Russia and others for Belarus. From abroad, they criticize Latvian government policies while presenting themselves as voices of the country’s “outraged citizens.”
The channels regularly repost one another’s content and amplify material from other Russian propagandists, including RT head Margarita Simonyan. They also promote pro-government Belarusian social media accounts.
The channels repeat a common set of narratives that closely mirror Kremlin messaging: that Russian speakers in Latvia are being persecuted, that Nazism is on the rise in the Baltic states, and that ordinary people in the country are becoming poorer. The channels blame these problems on Riga’s support for Ukraine, arguing that public money is being diverted to the war.
Aleksejs Rosļikovs’ channel
The largest channel, with about 30,000 subscribers, is run by Aleksejs Rosļikovs, a former member of Latvia’s parliament, the Saeima.
Rosļikovs, 42, is a controversial figure in Latvian politics. Before entering public life, he spent years in business, running a confectionery company and later owning several private security firms, a taxi dispatch service, and a car rental company. He went on to serve in the Saeima and later on the Riga City Council.
Latvian authorities have opened a criminal case against him on suspicion of inciting ethnic hatred. The case stems from a June 5, 2025, speech in parliament in which Rosļikovs made an obscene gesture toward fellow lawmakers and ended his remarks in Russian by saying, “There are more of us; Russian is our language.”
In the spring of 2026, Rosļikovs left Latvia for Belarus. From there, he continues to run his Telegram channel and says he plans to run again for the Saeima with his Stability! party. He has told potential voters that if elected, parliamentary immunity would allow him to return to Latvia and that he would seek to lift sanctions on Russia.
Over the past month, Rosļikovs’ Telegram channel gained several thousand subscribers, and in early September,he unexpectedly made the platform private, limiting access to subscribers only. Rosļikovs also runs personal accounts on Facebook (where he has about 16,000 followers) and Instagram (where he has around 109,000). Alongside political commentary, he posts videos of himself working out and taking ice plunges, a Russian Orthodox tradition in which participants immerse themselves in near-freezing water in January to mark the baptism of Jesus.
Baltnews
The second most significant channel, Baltnews (@baltnews), is run by the editorial staff of the “Russia Today” International Information Agency — as is explicitly stated on the publication’s website. The channel has 24,000 subscribers.
Its editorial team publishes dozens of posts a day, quotes Russian and Belarusian propaganda outlets, and reposts content from other channels in the network. In the past year alone, Baltnews reposted content from the BelVPO channel 149 times and from the “Belvestnik” channel 107 times.
The publication also claims that due to ongoing financial aid to Ukraine, the standard of living for Latvians has declined, and that Russophobia is so rampant in the country that it has forced Russian speakers to emigrate. Particular emphasis is placed on the idea that neighboring countries do not respect Latvia and openly mock it.
Even positive news, such as falling prices in stores, are presented in a negative light: “According to estimates by Latvian retail chains, a basket of groceries that used to cost 50 euros now costs 46.28 euros. Savings of 3.72 euros are hardly going to save the local poor or those rapidly approaching poverty.”
Even positive news, such as falling prices in stores, are presented in a negative light
The channel’s editor-in-chief is 34-year-old Riga native Andrejs Starikovs. After Latvian authorities banned the publication in 2018 and opened criminal cases against its staff, Starikovs moved to Moscow.
In addition to running his propaganda page, Starikovs also produces films commissioned by the Russian authorities.
The “Baltic Antifascists” page
The third most significant page in the pro-Russian network is the channel of the organization “Baltic Antifascists,” which has nearly 20,000 subscribers. The organization and the channel were created in November 2022 and are led by 62-year-old Sergejs Vasiļjevs, a native of Latvia.
The “Baltic Antifascists” page actively accuses the Latvian authorities of Nazism and Russophobia. Vasilyev refers to Latvia itself exclusively as a territory “temporarily occupied by NATO troops.”
Vasiļjevs refers to Latvia exclusively as a territory “temporarily occupied by NATO troops”
Criminal cases have now been opened against him and several others for gathering intelligence on behalf of the FSB.
Vasiļjevs himself does not deny gathering data for Russian security agencies, speaking openly about it during live broadcasts. For example, one of the organization’s tasks was to gather information on the bulldozer operators who demolished Soviet monuments.
“We launched a poll [via a Telegram channel] and a flood of opinions came in. We collected all these files and forwarded them to the Investigative Committee of Russia. Now we have a number of suspects in the vandalism case [on Russian territory],” Vasilyev openly boasted in an interview.
The administrators also used the “Baltic Antifascists” group to gather information about Russian opposition events, Latvian volunteers fighting on the side of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, as well as NATO equipment and facilities in the Baltic states.
Vasilyev also has a co-defendant in his criminal case over the collection of information for Russia’s security services: 26-year-old Latvian citizen and St. Petersburg State University student Tatiana Andriets. In 2022, Andriets traveled to Riga for vacation and participated in a protest against the demolition of Soviet monuments. Latvian authorities charged her with “aiding a foreign state” and forming a criminal group. She spent nine months in pretrial detention and is currently under house arrest while her trial is ongoing.
Although Andriets is not a Russian citizen, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has repeatedly commented on her case, calling the trial “political” in nature.
Alexei Stefanov, Ruslan Pankratov, and Nikolai Mezhevich
Three other major public pages are run by journalists and political analysts associated with Russia Today who appear as regular guests on Russian television programs such as Solovyov Live, Zvezda, and REN TV. These include the personal channel of “Russia Today” special correspondent Alexei Stefanov, with 16,000 subscribers; the channel of political scientist Ruslan Pankratov from the Institute of CIS Countries (12,000 subscribers); and the channel of Nikolai Mezhevich, a researcher at the Institute of Europe of the Russian Academy of Sciences (12,000 subscribers).
They regularly repost each other’s content. For example, over the past year, Mezhevich’s channel has mentioned Stefanov’s channel 200 times. Stefanov himself constantly cites the channel “Latviyskaya Kochka” (lit. “Latvian Bump”) which reposts content from Margarita Simonyan’s public pages and those of other Russian propagandists.
In addition to narratives about the oppression of Russians in Latvia, the channels offer advice on how to move to Russia, promote content about the “horrible Nazis in Kyiv,” and scare their audience by claiming that war will soon break out on Latvian territory if the country does not change its attitude towards Moscow.
The network also includes smaller public channels with notable backgrounds. One is “Zloi Pribalt” (@wagner_baltika), whose name and logo match channels from Yevgeny Prigozhin’s former Wagner-linked media network. It has only about 1,200 subscribers but is the most prolific channel in the network, publishing about 66,000 posts since Jan. 1, 2025.

articles.title: US intelligence says Saudi Arabia has not abandoned its nuclear weapons ambitions
articles.body:
US intelligence says Saudi Arabia has not abandoned its nuclear weapons ambitions
TEHRAN — Classified U.S. intelligence submitted to Congress reveals that Saudi Arabia has not abandoned plans to develop nuclear weapons, according to a Washington Post report citing American officials.
The assessment, published in the paper on September 25, arrived alongside State Department briefing documents reviewing the Trump administration’s 30-year “civil nuclear cooperation agreement” with Riyadh, exposing blatant double standards in American foreign policy.
The deal is undergoing a 90-day congressional review period, where House Democrats have already introduced a joint resolution of disapproval to block it.
The agreement signed under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act initially limits Saudi uranium enrichment below five percent, but permits an increase to 20 percent after further joint review.
Crucially, the agreement fails to require Riyadh to sign the IAEA’s Additional Protocol, depriving international inspectors of snap access to undeclared facilities.
20 nonproliferation experts, including former IAEA director general Hans Blix, warned Congress in a joint letter that omitting the Additional Protocol makes covert weapons development nearly impossible to detect.
Democratic senators Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley pressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio, writing that Washington is “caving to Saudi demands by agreeing to a process that is all but certain to allow Riyadh to acquire the means to enrich uranium and possibly develop nuclear weapons.”
Senator Merkley called claims of a purely civilian program bogus, noting that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman previously warned the kingdom would build a bomb “if Iran acquired one.”
The contrast with Iran highlights deep Western hypocrisy. The Islamic Republic has categorically ruled out non-conventional weapons, adhering to a binding religious decree issued by the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei.
Continuous IAEA inspections have consistently verified the peaceful character of Iran’s energy infrastructure. Nevertheless, Washington and Tel Aviv have bombed Iranian facilities under baseless pretexts.
Additionally, lucrative financial incentives appear to eclipse proliferation concerns.
The arrangement opens tens of billions of dollars in construction contracts for American nuclear vendors, notably Westinghouse Electric.
Lawmakers highlighted that Westinghouse’s majority owner shares close ties with Newmark, a real estate firm run by the sons of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The senators also pointed out that former White House envoy Jared Kushner secured a $2 billion investment from the Saudi sovereign wealth fund shortly after leaving office.
While Washington has subjected peaceful Iranian infrastructure to aggressive strikes and illegal sanctions, it has agreed to actively equip a dynastic rentier monarchy with the tools needed to construct a nuclear arsenal.

articles.title: China rejects 'Cold War' mentality; Germany's FM Wadephul meets Russian counterpart Lavrov. Follow DW's UN General Assembly updates.
articles.body:
Germany's FM Wadephul meets Lavrov on UNGA sidelines
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 27, 2026
What you need to know
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul meets Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on sidelines of the UN General Assembly debate
- Wadephul addressed the UN later on Saturday and urged regulation on AI
- India urges de-escalation in regards to Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
- Chinese VP Han Zheng slams 'unilateral military actions,' says big countries should follow rules
We are continuing our coverage of the 81st UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
We are pausing our coverage
The debate has closed for the day and will resume again for its final session on Monday.
Here's a recap of the main developments on Saturday:
Johann Wadephul used his speech to the General Assembly to warn of the threat of AI, highlight the need for urgent UN reforms, and slam Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.
His Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, for his part, accused Germany and other European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
But the biggest headlines today came from the foreign ministers' rare meeting away from the general debate.
Wadephul described the meeting, their first since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, as an "intense conversation" that again highlighted the deep divisions between them.
Lavrov said the meeting was unnecessary and that no progress had been made.
Away from the war in Ukraine, the foreign ministers from India and Saudi Arabia called for de-escalation in the conflict in the Middle East and for maritime navigation to be fully restored and protected.
The conflict is sure to feature heavily in the United Arab Emirates' appearance on Monday during the final session of the debate, while another speech worth watching could be that of Kim Son Gyong, North Korea's representative.
Lavrov meeting reinforces deep divisions over Ukraine war: Wadephul
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said his meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov had highlighted the deep divisions between their two nations over the war in Ukraine.
Wadephul said the pair's meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly — the first since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — was "intense" and that significant disagreements remain between the two sides.
"Of course, we did not agree on the key points," Wadephul told German public broadcaster ZDF.
He added that he had "offered to de-escalate, particularly with regard to the situation in Ukraine, but that has not yet found open ears."
Wadephul also said he had told Lavrov that Germany "does not accept" incidents like the drone attack in Leipzig, which Berlin has accused Moscow of being behind.
"That this is an escalation that is not acceptable," he said, adding that he had warned Russia against continuing on that path.
"We can defend ourselves, we can stand our ground, and we will do so," the minister said.
Lavrov, for his part, said the meeting with Wadephul had been unnecessary. The Russian diplomat told German news agency dpa that he had "heard nothing different" from Berlin's public stance on the conflict.
"You could have just called me and said, 'Read my statement,'" Lavrov told the German foreign minister.
Wadephul: Russia's war in Ukraine 'shows contempt' for UN charter
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia's war in Ukraine targets the lives of millions of innocent civilians, Ukraine and its culture, as well as the "European peace order."
"It puts vital grain deliveries for millions of people at risk, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East," Wadephul said in his speech to the UN General Assembly, adding that Russia's actions "show contempt" for the UN charter and for the "common order on which we stand."
The minister also said Germany's support with Ukraine was consistent with UN values.
"Today Germany is the largest supporter of Ukraine and its defense against Russian aggression. This aggression has been condemned consistently by an overwhelming majority here in the General Assembly," Wadephul said.
He said Germany would continue to call on Russia to come to the negotiation table.
"I call on every member state to join us in convincing Russia that the future is built at the negotiation table, not on dead bodies in cities and villages," he added.
Prior to his speech, Wadephul met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the UNGA, in the first of such meetings since 2022.
The talks come in the midst of tensions between Berlin and Moscow, after Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.
"Wadephul called on the Russian Federation to abandon its dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and NATO," a German diplomat said of the talks in comments to AFP news agency.
"He made it clear: incidents such as the recent attempted attack in Leipzig or further hybrid assaults would not shake Germany's resolve to support Ukraine, which has come under attack," the diplomat added.
"The German foreign minister condemned Russia's ongoing and increasingly targeted aggression against the Ukrainian civilian population. This attempt to increase pressure does nothing to change Russia's untenable situation: every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers die in a hopeless war of positions, while the Russian economy continues to collapse," the diplomat said.
Germany calls for AI regulation, urges 'profound' UN reform
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul opened his UN General Assembly speech by warning about the extraordinary power of artificial intelligence and its implications for the world. He also addressed the erosion of international institutions in a world of rising nationalism.
"When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, we need to ask who controls it, who sets the rules, who is accountable," Wadephul said, adding that AI has the potential to upend the economy and "endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running."
"AI holds extraordinary promise," Wadephul said. But he warned that a "critical tension" exists when the technology is concentrated in two countries and a few companies. Such power holds great responsibility to humanity, Wadephul said, saying that as power becomes global, so must the responsibilites.
"AI is not waiting for our institutions to catch up, our institutions have to catch up with AI" Wadephul said.
"We need to make sure that tech progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping," he added, calling effectively for global regulation of AI.
"Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable models," he said.
On the weakening of UN institutions, Wadephul warned of a UN "under pressure."
"There are great powers that believe that they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN charter,"
Wadephul said that "the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this assembly" are harmed when international institutions are under attack.
"If this erosion contitnues, we all stand to lose," he added.
Germany's foreign minister urged for the the new UN Secretary General to lead "a profound process of reform," as the world needs "a functioning UN that plays an active role in conflicts, rather than managing."
"Germany stands up for peace and security," Wadephul said, citing his country's commitment to support Ukraine.
A new nationalism is not the path for nations, Wadephul said, adding that "it would makes our lives narrower, poorer and less secure"
India urges de-escalation amid Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
India's Minister for External Affairs, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, addressed the UN General Assembly, urging de-escalation and restraint from those involved in conflicts that have caused disruption to world navigation, in reference to the current crises in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea.
"In a globalized world, the effects of war are felt worldwide," Jaishankar said.
"Countries far from conflicts are being penalized for no fault in this. Those most impacted often have the least say," he added.
Jaishankar also denounced the security of seafarers caught in conflicts.
"We must ensure that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers is never compromised," he said.
Saudi Arabia says international community 'absent' in Gulf crisis
At UN, the Foreign Minister of Saudi Arabia, Prince Faisal bin Farhan al Saud, called for the defense of freedom of navigation in all international waterways.
"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.
The Saudi foreign minister called for the restoration of the Strait of Hormuz to its "pre-28th February status." The US and Israel began their military operations against Iran on that date.
He condemned the fact that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf nations "have been subjected to flagrant Iranian attacks" targeting their security, resources, and civilians.
Saudi FM also denounced Israel's war in Gaza, saying it opposed the "continuing suffering of the Palestinian people."
"We stress that a just and lasting peace can only be achieved through the implementation of a two-state solution and the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital."
Russia offers to help with Strait of Hormuz crisis
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Moscow can help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov said in his speech to the UNGA.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region," he added.
Lavrov claims Europe 'thwarts' Ukraine talks
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the UNGA, shortly after meeting with his German counterpart Johann Wadephul.
In his speech to the general assembly, Lavrov accused European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
Russia's unprovoked invasion of its neighbor will soon mark its fifth anniversary next February.
"Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the (Donald) Trump administration is interested," he said, referring to the US government and the various rounds of talks it has held with the Russian and Ukrainian government, led by Trump's son in law Jared Kushner and adviser Steve Witkoff.
German FM Wadephul meets Russia's Lavrov during UN assembly
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
A correspondent for the Russian Interfax news agency reported Wadephul and Lavrov, followed by aides, shaking hands before the press was asked to leave.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the meeting took place at the German initiative.
Moscow has been sanctioned by the EU over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which the Kremlin launched in February 2022.
The last meeting between the countries at this level was held in January of that year, between veteran diplomat Lavrov and Germany's then-top diplomat, Annalena Baerbock, who was on a visit to Moscow.
Lavrov and Wadephul's meeting was held as tensions between Berlin and Moscow have been high in recent weeks.
Germany has accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulates.
Moldova PM offers his country as testing ground for AI rules
Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan used part of his time before the General Assembly to present a vision of small nations serving as "regulatory sandboxes" for new technologies.
"Technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere, and artificial intelligence is widening that gap," said Tofan, who worked as an investor and businessman before becoming the head of Moldovan government two months ago.
"We want Moldova to become a place where emergent technologies can be tested responsibly through regulatory sandboxes, where regulators learn alongside companies, rules adjust with evidence, and good ideas do not wait years to reach the real economy."
"When an entrepreneur arrives with a technology for which the law has not caught up yet, the answer should not simply be 'There is no rule for this.' It should be 'Let us find a safe way to test it'," he said.
China cast itself as source of stability in changing world
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng called for safeguarding the post-WWII order, saying the world wanted "peace, not war."
"We should turn into action the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, and reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation," Han said.
"Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding the rule of law, and doing what's right."
"No matter how international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development, in its dedication to safeguarding fairness and justice and in its commitment to multilateralism," said the Chinese vice president.
"China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity, and make the world a better place for all of us."
China takes indirect swipes at US over Iran
Speaking at the UN on Saturday, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng said the world should reject "unilateral military actions that violate the UN charter and circumvent the Security Council authorization," in an apparent reference to the US attack on Iran.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of the countries in the Middle east, including the Gulf, should be respected, international industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded," he said.
In his speech, Han also spoke out against the US blockade of Cuba, albeit without explicitly mentioning the US.
He said China called on "the relevant country" to lift its blockade against Cuba and stop using the threat of force against the island nation.
In regards to Israel and the Palestinians, the Chinese official urged bringing the two-state solution back "on the right track" and "at an early date."
Welcome back
Welcome back to DW's coverage of the UN General Assembly Debate in New York City.
On day 5, China and Germany are some of the major countries addressing the event.
Stay tuned for more.
We are pausing our coverage
As the fourth day of the 81st UN General Assembly comes to a halt, we are pausing this blog for the night.
Today was another address-packed day, with several small island nations stressing the urgent need to address climate change, as they are most vulnerable to its consequences.
Norway and Sweden stressed the importance of continuing to support the UN, including with funds, as well as making it more representative by giving Africa a permanent seat on the Security Council.
Meanwhile, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took aim at India, rehashing in his address a short-lived conflict between the two countries last year. Sharif said his country faced "external aggression from India under a false pretext," adding that his country's response was "its inherent right of self-defense."
Before the session wrapped, India used its right of reply to address Pakistan's "bizarre remarks," and accuse its neighbor of terrorism. Pakistan was quick to respond, accusing New Delhi of "export[ing] terrorism and violence."
We will be back again tomorrow, when addresses from India, Germany, Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Canada, and others are scheduled.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Drone War Is Changing Every Few Months as Military Warns 2027 Will Demand Faster Tech
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Drone War Is Changing Every Few Months as Military Warns 2027 Will Demand Faster Tech
Ukraine will need faster battlefield innovation, greater use of artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, and a more flexible defense industry to keep pace with Russia as drone warfare continues to transform the front.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a UNITED24 Media correspondent at the forum, military commanders, defense manufacturers, and technology experts discussed the challenges at the “Defense 2027. Army, Technology, Industry” event in Kyiv on September 25, organized by Radio NV and the National Association of Ukrainian Defense Industries (NAUDI).
Yurii Fedorenko, commander of Ukraine’s 429th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade “Achilles,” said improvements in batteries and communications could significantly extend drone range and endurance, while warning that Ukraine also needs alternatives to Starlink for battlefield connectivity.
“Communications are the foundation,” Fedorenko said. “If we do not work toward replacing the Starlink satellite communications system, at some point we could lose the effectiveness of a significant number of strike crews.”
Fedorenko said drones are currently the main tactical threat on the battlefield, with Ukrainian troops particularly vulnerable while moving to positions or operating in areas where personnel are concentrated. He also predicted that the next stage of warfare would expand “not only into the air and range, but also underground.”
He added that artificial intelligence will increasingly be needed to process the enormous volumes of battlefield information that human operators cannot analyze alone.
Maria Berlinska, co-founder of the Dignitas Foundation and head of the Victory Drones project, said the technological landscape at the front can now change within just several months.
“Whoever is faster is more likely to stay alive,” Berlinska said, arguing that Ukraine should focus on engineering forecasts capable of identifying Russian technological developments six months to a year in advance.
“We can start winning the war if we start listening to our engineers,” she said. “When the country’s leadership has analysis and recommendations on the table, state resources can be directed toward acting ahead of the threat.”
She also called for greater reliance on private defense companies, saying the state should define future battlefield requirements, provide clear rules and financing, and allow private manufacturers to develop the necessary solutions.
Military journalist Yurii Butusov described the current battlefield as a “war of startups,” saying individual Ukrainian units increasingly have to operate like technology companies because weapons and battlefield systems can change every month.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported that domestically produced systems accounted for 95% of all unmanned aerial vehicles procured for the country’s Defense Forces, underscoring the growing role of Ukraine’s defense industry in supplying frontline units.

Speaking at the UN on Saturday, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng said the world should reject "unilateral military actions that violate the UN charter and circumvent the Security Council authorization," in an apparent reference to the US attack on Iran.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of the countries in the Middle east, including the Gulf, should be respected, international industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded," he said.
In his speech, Han also spoke out against the US blockade of Cuba, albeit without explicitly mentioning the US.
He said China called on "the relevant country" to lift its blockade against Cuba and stop using the threat of force against the island nation.
In regards to Israel and the Palestinians, the Chinese official urged bringing the two-state solution back "on the right track" and "at an early date."
Welcome back
Welcome back to DW's coverage of the UN General Assembly Debate in New York City.
On day 5, China and Germany are some of the major countries addressing the event.
Stay tuned for more.
We are pausing our coverage
As the fourth day of the 81st UN General Assembly comes to a halt, we are pausing this blog for the night.
Today was another address-packed day, with several small island nations stressing the urgent need to address climate change, as they are most vulnerable to its consequences.
Norway and Sweden stressed the importance of continuing to support the UN, including with funds, as well as making it more representative by giving Africa a permanent seat on the Security Council.
Meanwhile, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took aim at India, rehashing in his address a short-lived conflict between the two countries last year. Sharif said his country faced "external aggression from India under a false pretext," adding that his country's response was "its inherent right of self-defense."
Before the session wrapped, India used its right of reply to address Pakistan's "bizarre remarks," and accuse its neighbor of terrorism. Pakistan was quick to respond, accusing New Delhi of "export[ing] terrorism and violence."
We will be back again tomorrow, when addresses from India, Germany, Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Canada, and others are scheduled.

articles.title: China reject 'Cold War mindset' at UN General Assembly
articles.body:
Germany's FM Wadephul meets Lavrov on UNGA sidelines
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 27, 2026
What you need to know
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul meets Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on sidelines of the UN General Assembly debate
- Wadephul addressed the UN later on Saturday and urged regulation on AI
- India urges de-escalation in regards to Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
- Chinese VP Han Zheng slams 'unilateral military actions,' says big countries should follow rules
We are continuing our coverage of the 81st UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
We are pausing our coverage
The debate has closed for the day and will resume again for its final session on Monday.
Here's a recap of the main developments on Saturday:
Johann Wadephul used his speech to the General Assembly to warn of the threat of AI, highlight the need for urgent UN reforms, and slam Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.
His Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, for his part, accused Germany and other European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
But the biggest headlines today came from the foreign ministers' rare meeting away from the general debate.
Wadephul described the meeting, their first since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, as an "intense conversation" that again highlighted the deep divisions between them.
Lavrov said the meeting was unnecessary and that no progress had been made.
Away from the war in Ukraine, the foreign ministers from India and Saudi Arabia called for de-escalation in the conflict in the Middle East and for maritime navigation to be fully restored and protected.
The conflict is sure to feature heavily in the United Arab Emirates' appearance on Monday during the final session of the debate, while another speech worth watching could be that of Kim Son Gyong, North Korea's representative.
Lavrov meeting reinforces deep divisions over Ukraine war: Wadephul
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said his meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov had highlighted the deep divisions between their two nations over the war in Ukraine.
Wadephul said the pair's meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly — the first since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — was "intense" and that significant disagreements remain between the two sides.
"Of course, we did not agree on the key points," Wadephul told German public broadcaster ZDF.
He added that he had "offered to de-escalate, particularly with regard to the situation in Ukraine, but that has not yet found open ears."
Wadephul also said he had told Lavrov that Germany "does not accept" incidents like the drone attack in Leipzig, which Berlin has accused Moscow of being behind.
"That this is an escalation that is not acceptable," he said, adding that he had warned Russia against continuing on that path.
"We can defend ourselves, we can stand our ground, and we will do so," the minister said.
Lavrov, for his part, said the meeting with Wadephul had been unnecessary. The Russian diplomat told German news agency dpa that he had "heard nothing different" from Berlin's public stance on the conflict.
"You could have just called me and said, 'Read my statement,'" Lavrov told the German foreign minister.
Wadephul: Russia's war in Ukraine 'shows contempt' for UN charter
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia's war in Ukraine targets the lives of millions of innocent civilians, Ukraine and its culture, as well as the "European peace order."
"It puts vital grain deliveries for millions of people at risk, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East," Wadephul said in his speech to the UN General Assembly, adding that Russia's actions "show contempt" for the UN charter and for the "common order on which we stand."
The minister also said Germany's support with Ukraine was consistent with UN values.
"Today Germany is the largest supporter of Ukraine and its defense against Russian aggression. This aggression has been condemned consistently by an overwhelming majority here in the General Assembly," Wadephul said.
He said Germany would continue to call on Russia to come to the negotiation table.
"I call on every member state to join us in convincing Russia that the future is built at the negotiation table, not on dead bodies in cities and villages," he added.
Prior to his speech, Wadephul met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the UNGA, in the first of such meetings since 2022.
The talks come in the midst of tensions between Berlin and Moscow, after Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.
"Wadephul called on the Russian Federation to abandon its dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and NATO," a German diplomat said of the talks in comments to AFP news agency.
"He made it clear: incidents such as the recent attempted attack in Leipzig or further hybrid assaults would not shake Germany's resolve to support Ukraine, which has come under attack," the diplomat added.
"The German foreign minister condemned Russia's ongoing and increasingly targeted aggression against the Ukrainian civilian population. This attempt to increase pressure does nothing to change Russia's untenable situation: every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers die in a hopeless war of positions, while the Russian economy continues to collapse," the diplomat said.
Germany calls for AI regulation, urges 'profound' UN reform
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul opened his UN General Assembly speech by warning about the extraordinary power of artificial intelligence and its implications for the world. He also addressed the erosion of international institutions in a world of rising nationalism.
"When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, we need to ask who controls it, who sets the rules, who is accountable," Wadephul said, adding that AI has the potential to upend the economy and "endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running."
"AI holds extraordinary promise," Wadephul said. But he warned that a "critical tension" exists when the technology is concentrated in two countries and a few companies. Such power holds great responsibility to humanity, Wadephul said, saying that as power becomes global, so must the responsibilites.
"AI is not waiting for our institutions to catch up, our institutions have to catch up with AI" Wadephul said.
"We need to make sure that tech progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping," he added, calling effectively for global regulation of AI.
"Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable models," he said.
On the weakening of UN institutions, Wadephul warned of a UN "under pressure."
"There are great powers that believe that they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN charter,"
Wadephul said that "the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this assembly" are harmed when international institutions are under attack.
"If this erosion contitnues, we all stand to lose," he added.
Germany's foreign minister urged for the the new UN Secretary General to lead "a profound process of reform," as the world needs "a functioning UN that plays an active role in conflicts, rather than managing."
"Germany stands up for peace and security," Wadephul said, citing his country's commitment to support Ukraine.
A new nationalism is not the path for nations, Wadephul said, adding that "it would makes our lives narrower, poorer and less secure"
India urges de-escalation amid Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
India's Minister for External Affairs, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, addressed the UN General Assembly, urging de-escalation and restraint from those involved in conflicts that have caused disruption to world navigation, in reference to the current crises in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea.
"In a globalized world, the effects of war are felt worldwide," Jaishankar said.
"Countries far from conflicts are being penalized for no fault in this. Those most impacted often have the least say," he added.
Jaishankar also denounced the security of seafarers caught in conflicts.
"We must ensure that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers is never compromised," he said.
Saudi Arabia says international community 'absent' in Gulf crisis
At UN, the Foreign Minister of Saudi Arabia, Prince Faisal bin Farhan al Saud, called for the defense of freedom of navigation in all international waterways.
"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.
The Saudi foreign minister called for the restoration of the Strait of Hormuz to its "pre-28th February status." The US and Israel began their military operations against Iran on that date.
He condemned the fact that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf nations "have been subjected to flagrant Iranian attacks" targeting their security, resources, and civilians.
Saudi FM also denounced Israel's war in Gaza, saying it opposed the "continuing suffering of the Palestinian people."
"We stress that a just and lasting peace can only be achieved through the implementation of a two-state solution and the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital."
Russia offers to help with Strait of Hormuz crisis
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Moscow can help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov said in his speech to the UNGA.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region," he added.
Lavrov claims Europe 'thwarts' Ukraine talks
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the UNGA, shortly after meeting with his German counterpart Johann Wadephul.
In his speech to the general assembly, Lavrov accused European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
Russia's unprovoked invasion of its neighbor will soon mark its fifth anniversary next February.
"Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the (Donald) Trump administration is interested," he said, referring to the US government and the various rounds of talks it has held with the Russian and Ukrainian government, led by Trump's son in law Jared Kushner and adviser Steve Witkoff.
German FM Wadephul meets Russia's Lavrov during UN assembly
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
A correspondent for the Russian Interfax news agency reported Wadephul and Lavrov, followed by aides, shaking hands before the press was asked to leave.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the meeting took place at the German initiative.
Moscow has been sanctioned by the EU over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which the Kremlin launched in February 2022.
The last meeting between the countries at this level was held in January of that year, between veteran diplomat Lavrov and Germany's then-top diplomat, Annalena Baerbock, who was on a visit to Moscow.
Lavrov and Wadephul's meeting was held as tensions between Berlin and Moscow have been high in recent weeks.
Germany has accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulates.
Moldova PM offers his country as testing ground for AI rules
Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan used part of his time before the General Assembly to present a vision of small nations serving as "regulatory sandboxes" for new technologies.
"Technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere, and artificial intelligence is widening that gap," said Tofan, who worked as an investor and businessman before becoming the head of Moldovan government two months ago.
"We want Moldova to become a place where emergent technologies can be tested responsibly through regulatory sandboxes, where regulators learn alongside companies, rules adjust with evidence, and good ideas do not wait years to reach the real economy."
"When an entrepreneur arrives with a technology for which the law has not caught up yet, the answer should not simply be 'There is no rule for this.' It should be 'Let us find a safe way to test it'," he said.
China cast itself as source of stability in changing world
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng called for safeguarding the post-WWII order, saying the world wanted "peace, not war."
"We should turn into action the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, and reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation," Han said.
"Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding the rule of law, and doing what's right."
"No matter how international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development, in its dedication to safeguarding fairness and justice and in its commitment to multilateralism," said the Chinese vice president.
"China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity, and make the world a better place for all of us."
