articles.title: Patriot, Starlink and Starshield: Budanov explained what Ukraine needs to counter Russian attacks
articles.body:
Patriot, Starlink and Starshield: Budanov explained what Ukraine needs to counter Russian attacks
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine critically needs missiles for Patriot systems amid Russian attacks. Budanov also called for expanding the satellite capabilities of Starlink and Starshield.
Ukraine has developed a critical need for missiles for Patriot air defense systems, which remain one of the key means of protection against Russian missile attacks. This was stated by the head of the Presidential Office, Kyrylo Budanov, in an interview with Newsforce, reports UNN.
Details
According to him, the issue of replenishing ammunition supplies for air defense systems remains relevant amid Russia's intensive use of various types of missiles.
In addition to air defense systems, according to Budanov, Ukraine is extremely interested in expanding access to Starlink and Starshield satellite capabilities. This concerns not only ensuring stable communications, but also a broader range of technologies necessary for conducting modern warfare.
At the same time, Budanov emphasized that Ukraine's existing satellite capabilities are insufficient to perform the full range of tasks that arise while countering Russian attacks.
As of now, the access we have is insufficient. We need expanded capabilities—we need more coverage
According to him, expanding these capabilities is necessary, in particular, to more effectively counter Russian strikes and destroy the missile systems from which Russia attacks Ukrainian territory.
Context
The supply of missiles for Patriot and other American air defense systems is carried out, in particular, within the framework of international mechanisms supporting Ukraine. At the beginning of 2026, the Verkhovna Rada reported that during 2025, Ukraine had received 23 long- and medium-range air defense systems and approximately 11,000 missiles for various systems from its partners, while Ukrainian air defense had been additionally reinforced with four Patriot systems.
Additionally
Starshield is a system developed by SpaceX for government and security needs, based on Starlink technologies. The company officially identifies secure global satellite communications, Earth observation, and the ability to place specialized payloads on satellites among its main areas. Starshield also provides additional cryptographic protection measures for working with sensitive data.
Ukraine already widely uses Starlink satellite communications for the needs of its security and defense forces. In May 2026, the government separately regulated the procurement of satellite broadband services for the defense sector, providing for the possibility of long-term payment for such services and centralized traffic administration by the Ministry of Defense.
We remind you
Somewhat earlier, global media reported that U.S. President Donald Trump had not confirmed Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy's statement that Ukraine had been allowed to produce missiles for Patriot.

articles.title: A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible
articles.body:
A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible
Oleshky (Alyoshki in Russian) is a city on the left bank of the Dnipro River, across from Kherson on the right bank. Only nine kilometers (about six miles) separate them in a straight line. People once crossed between them by bridge, but the bridge is now closed. The two cities are on opposite sides of the front: Ukraine controls Kherson, while Russia has controlled Oleshky since 2022. As in other cities near the front, life in Oleshky is difficult and dangerous. By September 2026, conditions had deteriorated so badly that people in both Ukraine and Russia were calling the situation critical. Those who remain are trying to survive without food, electricity, and adequate medical care. They cannot leave safely and often cannot even bury their loved ones. Here is what Meduza has been able to learn about conditions in the city.
The situation in Oleshky was already being called critical in Ukraine in the spring. By September, even the Kremlin agreed
“It’s a humanitarian catastrophe, people are driven to despair,” Tetiana Hasanenko, head of Oleshky’s evacuated Ukrainian administration, told The Kyiv Independent in April 2026. She tries to keep in touch with residents and tells Ukrainian media what is happening there.
“If the situation doesn’t improve, people will just die there from hunger. Because there’s no way out, no food supplies coming in,” Anna, an Oleshky resident who recently escaped to a Ukrainian-controlled area, told the outlet.
In the summer, the U.N. mission in Ukraine said Oleshky’s last store had closed in January 2026, and all food deliveries had stopped by late May. Medical care was available only for the most urgent cases. Ambulances no longer responded to calls, and patients with serious conditions could not be transferred to other hospitals. Anyone trying to enter or leave the city faced two dangers: drones overhead and mines on the ground.
In July, Human Rights Watch said shortages of food and medical care in Oleshky were compounded by the collapse of basic utilities. The city had no electricity or gas, and people had switched to wood-burning stoves. People who had managed to leave Oleshky said they were afraid even to go out for water because drones circled overhead and mines lay scattered along the streets. Human Rights Watch said it was impossible to say for certain whose weapons they were. Both Russian and Ukrainian forces had used drones and mines in the area during the war.
At the time, the Russian occupation authorities in the Kherson region still denied that there was a humanitarian catastrophe. By August, however, they acknowledged that Oleshky and nearby villages had no water or electricity, communications were unreliable, and utility crews could not make repairs because of shelling. On September 21, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the situation in the city critical. “The Kyiv regime is doing everything it can to obstruct deliveries [of food and medicine]. Russian troops are continuing to work to resolve the situation,” he said.
Oleshky is in its fifth year under occupation. Why is there talk of a humanitarian catastrophe now?
Continued fighting and the gradual deterioration of infrastructure appear to have made conditions worse.
In the fall of 2022, when Russian troops retreated from the right bank of the Dnipro and left Kherson, Oleshky became a frontline city. The destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant dam flooded Oleshky in the summer of 2023, badly damaging its infrastructure. The occupation administration says Ukrainian attacks have hampered repairs and deliveries of food and medicine.
As the use of FPV drones increased along the front, Oleshky — like Kherson across the Dnipro — became increasingly dangerous. Drone attacks killed civilians as well as soldiers. Mines added to the danger. The area around the city was so heavily mined that, by early 2026, getting in or out had become very difficult. That was when conditions in Oleshky began to deteriorate rapidly, Hasanenko said.
Gardens fed Oleshky’s residents through the summer. No one knows what winter will bring. Some are reportedly already eating dogs.
It is difficult to reach Oleshky’s residents now, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Some go months without making contact. Those who can charge a phone with a generator and occasionally call or send a message say food is scarce. “People have run out of food. They’re making soup with weeds, throwing in purslane, lamb’s quarters, and amaranth. I can’t even talk about the animals anymore — they have it worst of all. I just cry and don’t know what to do,” one Oleshky resident told Ukrainska Pravda.
Through the summer, residents survived mainly on what they grew in their gardens. Bartering is widespread in the city. “Anything you can still buy costs, say, a thousand rubles. A kilogram of sugar or salt is a thousand rubles; so is a pack of Citramon [painkillers]. But money is actually worth nothing, because no matter how much you have, no one is selling anything,” Hasanenko told Suspilne.
Some people risk traveling to Radensk for food. The village is 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) from Oleshky, farther from the front, and better supplied. But the trips are dangerous because of mines and drones. An Oleshky resident who recently returned from Radensk told Ukrainska Pravda that she brought back 85 kilograms (about 190 pounds) of food for three families. She rode a bicycle to Radensk but returned to Oleshky on foot.
Hasanenko told Ukrainska Pravda that people in the city had begun eating dogs: “A week ago, I was still denying the reports, but now someone there has confirmed it to me. There’s really nothing to eat. The situation isn’t just getting worse every day — it’s getting worse every hour.”
According to Ukrainian officials, Russian troops in Oleshky are also short of food, so they have been taking it from civilians. Some residents have begun putting signs on their fences saying things like “No food here” or “Elderly people live here.”
Oleshky’s hospital has been called the city’s last refuge. It stayed open after pharmacies and stores closed. But conditions there are dire, too.
Residents weakened by malnutrition used to be taken to the local hospital, where staff fed them as best they could. Recently, the hospital, already operating at limited capacity, has all but stopped functioning. Staff can still stop bleeding, but there are no medicines or equipment, and there is not enough fuel for the generator. According to Ukrainska Pravda’s sources, the hospital has begun turning away civilian patients.
“The hospital is asking local people to bring whatever grains or anything else they have, so it can at least give bedridden amputees breakfast. It’s the only place people can still come to spend the night, because it doesn’t get shelled, and get a hot meal if someone cooks it off the generator. But things are critical there,” said volunteer Kseniia Arkhypova, who is from Oleshky and remains in contact with people there.
According to Arkhypova, Russian troops do not allow residents to bury the dead themselves because they “want to take the bodies to Henichesk for examination and produce a report saying the Ukrainian Armed Forces shot them.” Bodies awaiting burial used to be taken to the morgue, but it has since been destroyed, so they are kept in the hospital basement. “Everything’s leaking, and it stinks,” Arkhypova said, and bodies have been piling up since May. Some people quietly bury loved ones in their yards or gardens.
“The occupiers won’t allow the bodies of people killed [in shelling] to be released. There are about 100 bodies in the hospital basements. […] We know of cases where bodies are simply left lying under the scorching sun and no one removes them. At best, if someone knew the person who died, they might cover the body with branches or a piece of cloth,” Hasanenko told Suspilne.
More than a thousand people remain in Oleshky, including dozens of children. Few manage to leave.
Ukrainian volunteers estimate that about 1,500 people, including 40 children, still live in Oleshky. Another 4,000 people, including 150 children, live in nearby villages. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, these communities had a combined population of 40,000.
People remain in the city for different reasons. Some are elderly or have limited mobility. Others feel they have nowhere to go. Some have no documents. To leave through occupied territory, they need a Russian passport, but getting one in Oleshky is impossible because the city is cut off by land and air. Russia refuses to open a humanitarian corridor to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Some men of draft age fear they will be sent into the Russian army if stopped at checkpoints. Some people cannot leave relatives behind in Oleshky. Others have no money or are simply afraid of being killed on the way out.
There is no organized evacuation from the city. Ukrainian officials say the Russian army does not want civilians to leave because their presence deters Ukrainian strikes. Meduza found no comments from the occupation authorities explaining why they have not arranged an evacuation.
In any case, under the Geneva Conventions, the occupying power is responsible for civilians in occupied territory. It is obliged to provide the population with food and medicine “to the fullest extent of the means available to it.”
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: At least 16 people killed as Russia and Ukraine trade deadly air strikes
articles.body:
At least 16 people killed as Russia and Ukraine trade deadly air strikes
At least 16 people were killed over the past 24 hours as Russia and Ukraine traded deadly drone and missile strikes, authorities from both countries said Saturday. The UN has warned of rising civilian deaths as Kyiv and Moscow ramp up long-range strikes on critical infrastructure.
Russian and Ukrainian strikes killed at least 16 people over the last 24 hours, both countries said Saturday, with the war still raging in its fifth year.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have stepped up attacks after the deadliest summer since 2022 – the year Russia launched its full-scale invasion, starting Europe's worst war since World War II.
US-led talks to end fighting have not led to a breakthrough and the Kremlin has repeatedly said it intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
Read moreRussia slams Kyiv with ballistic missiles as Ukrainians brace for harsh winter
Kyiv said Russian strikes had killed at least six people – in northeastern Sumy, in Zaporizhzhia and in the Dnipropetrovsk region, where a 17-year-old girl was among the victims.
And in Kyiv, several people were wounded a day after a day-time Russian attack killed seven people. Moscow has intensified strikes on the capital as the city prepares for another winter of war.
Russia said Ukrainian strikes had killed four people in its Krasnodar and Belgorod regions.
Vladimir Saldo, appointed by Moscow to lead occupational authorities in the Kherson region, said a Ukrainian drone had hit a cafe in the village of Askaniya-Nova, near Crimea, Friday evening.
"Under the rubble, rescuers found the bodies of two young girls – born in 2004 and 2006," he said on Telegram, adding that a man had also been killed in the same area.
Moscow-appointed official Yevgeny Balitsky said night-time Ukrainian strikes killed three more people in the occupied part of the Zaporizhzhia region.
United Nations officials have warned about the increasing numbers of civilian victims in the war.
At the UN General Assembly this week, US President Donald Trump once again said that a deal between Moscow and Kyiv to end the war was "going to happen".
For many observers however, that prospect appeared distant.
'Everything is burning'
Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday that Russia was "escalating every single day".
Ukrainian air defences are currently intercepting 55 percent of jet-powered drones launched by Russia, the Ukrainian president said in his evening address Saturday.
In Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, residents of a typical Soviet-era apartment block hit by a Russian drone were cleaning up their building – already worried about what might come next.
Oleksandr Gorlachov, 43, had gone to his allotment plot outside the city Friday night.
Early Saturday morning however, he was woken up by a video call from his elderly parents – who are both deaf – and rushed back to help.
"I watched as my mother is standing there in her nightgown, my father in his underwear, outside the building in tears ... and there are flames, everything is burning," he said.
"The apartment is completely smashed up."
His mother, he said, is a seamstress.
"Her sewing machine was there. She was in tears because it's broken now. So, well, it's a tragedy. But in my family everyone is alive and for that I thank God," he said.
With mounting Russian attacks on the capital, his family is in "constant stress" and he tries to distract himself by planting tomatoes.
"They don't have enough land," he said, mocking Russia – the world's largest country. "They want to simply wipe out our nation."
'Not going anywhere'
Despite Russia making life in Kyiv increasingly tough, Gorlachov said he "wasn't going anywhere".
But fellow resident Anastasiia Grygorovych – woken up when her window "fell on me" – had already fled her hometown of Gorlivka, now occupied by Russia.
Now she was considering leaving Ukraine altogether.
"In general, I’m already thinking that I need to leave," she said.
Russia's invasion has forced millions to flee their homes.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Kyiv also hit Russia with retaliatory strikes Saturday. Ukraine has struck deeper inside Russia this year, hitting as far as the Urals and Siberia.
Zelensky said Kyiv hit an oil refinery in the southern Russian Krasnodar region and a plant "supplying the occupiers" in the neighbouring Rostov region.
The Ukrainian leader called on allies to adopt more sanctions on Moscow.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Turkish anti-drone guns put on show for 12 countries
articles.body:
- ASELSAN demonstrated its KORKUT 35 air defense gun system shooting down several types of drones before delegations from 12 countries.
- Mounted on an 8×8 wheeled vehicle, the system also hit a moving ground target while both were in motion.
Turkish defense company ASELSAN has shown its KORKUT 35 air defense gun system shooting down drones and hitting a moving target while driving, in a live-fire demonstration watched by military delegations from 12 countries.
The company released video of the firing.
The demonstration focused on drones, and KORKUT 35 engaged fixed-wing, delta-wing and small mini and micro drones, with particular attention to kamikaze drones built to dive into their targets, ASELSAN said. In a separate scenario, the system, mounted on an 8×8 wheeled armored vehicle, fired at a moving ground target while both were in motion, to show its accuracy and how tightly its rounds grouped.
ASELSAN says the system can also engage fighter jets, helicopters, cruise missiles and air-to-ground missiles, and describes it as a cheaper way to defend troops and key sites against low-cost aerial threats.
KORKUT carries twin 35 mm cannons that together fire about 1,100 rounds a minute, with an effective range of roughly 4 km (2.5 miles). It uses ASELSAN’s ATOM programmable ammunition, which bursts in the air near a target and scatters tungsten fragments, raising the chance of hitting small drones that are hard to strike directly. A typical battery pairs a command vehicle that searches for and tracks targets with gun vehicles that each follow and fire at an assigned target.
The system entered Turkish service in a tracked configuration and has been exported. ASELSAN unveiled the 8×8 wheeled version at the Eurosatory defense show in Paris in 2024, giving it higher road speed to keep up with moving units. In January 2026, the company released footage of the wheeled KORKUT 140/35 shooting down a first-person-view drone while on the move.
The system is also heading to Europe. In February, ASELSAN and Czech defense group CSG formed a joint venture to produce KORKUT in the Czech Republic for European and global customers, and unveiled a version mounted on a Tatra 6×6 truck. In September, KORKUT was identified among air defense systems in a public reveal by the Pakistan Air Force, though the variant supplied has not been disclosed.

articles.title: The General Staff revealed the occupiers’ losses over the past day — how many servicemen and pieces of equipment were “written off”
articles.body:
The General Staff revealed the occupiers’ losses over the past day — how many servicemen and pieces of equipment were “written off”
Kyiv • UNN
The General Staff reported 1,690 Russian losses, the destruction of equipment, and 221 combat engagements. The enemy carried out 90 airstrikes and 2,729 attacks.
The General Staff reported that over the past day, the losses of the Russian invaders amounted to nearly 1,700 personnel; in addition, four air defense systems and 14 ground-based robotic systems were neutralized, UNN reports.

In addition, eight tanks, seven armored combat vehicles, 57 artillery systems, three multiple rocket launchers, four air defense systems, 14 ground-based robotic systems, 1,826 unmanned aerial vehicles, 517 vehicles and seven units of the enemy’s special equipment were neutralized
Details

Yesterday, the enemy launched 90 air strikes, dropping 289 guided aerial bombs. In addition, the invaders used 10,489 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,729 attacks on populated areas and the positions of our troops, 26 of them using multiple rocket launchers

articles.title: Russia launches third consecutive attack on Kyiv, injuring 1, setting off fires
articles.body:
Russia launches third consecutive attack on Kyiv, killing 1, injuring at least 4, setting off fires
Russia launched another drone attack on Kyiv on the night of Sept. 26-27, marking the third consecutive day of attacks on the Ukrainian capital, according to authorities.
Air defense units were operating over the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in an evening update. Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground also heard air defenses operating in the city.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, a Russian drone struck an uninhabited residential building at around 10 p.m. local time on Sept. 26, according to Klitschko.
A fire at the building was later brought under control, while emergency crews continued working at the site.
In the Solomianskyi district, a drone fell in an open area overnight. The resulting blast wave damaged a five-story residential building, breaking windows and damaging its facade, Klitschko said.
A fire also broke out at a warehouse in the district after the site was struck by a Russian drone, he added. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said that a car service center was on fire as a result of the attack.
A woman was injured in the attack and handed over to medics, and a man was killed, the State Emergency Service said.
In the morning of Sept. 27, Russia struck a non-residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district, Klitschko said at 9:26 a.m. local time. At least three people, a woman and two 16-year-old children, were injured in the area.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured three others, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said.
In Vyshneve, five cars were damaged, and a fire broke out after a drone struck the area. In Brovary, the attack caused fires in a warehouse and an office building, according to Tkachenko.
The latest attack follows a series of Russian drone strikes on Kyiv that began overnight on Sept. 24.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said on Sept. 27 that, as a result of the Russian drone attack on the capital, a car repair workshop and over 30 vehicles were destroyed, whilst a restaurant, a petrol station, office buildings and a school building were damaged.
It added that a pre-trial investigation was launched into the commission of a war crime by the Russian military, which resulted in the death of a man.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that on the morning of Sept. 27, Russian forces struck a data center in Kyiv twice.
Ukraine's largest mobile operator Kyivstar said that its headquarters was damaged during the drone attack on Sept. 27, as reported by the Ukrainian media outlet Suspilne.
Russian drones continued targeting Kyiv during the day on Sept. 26, with further damage and casualties reported. By the evening, Ukrainian officials said five people had been injured in attacks on the capital during the day.
In recent months, Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones, placing additional strain on Ukraine's air defenses.
One of Russia's newer jet-powered drone models, the Geran-5, can reportedly reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (373 mph), has an estimated range of up to 950 kilometers (590 miles), and can fly at altitudes of up to 6,000 meters (19,700 feet).
Ukraine is developing interceptor drones aimed at countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some systems having undergone successful tests, according to Ukrainian officials. The government has not announced plans for mass production.

articles.title: Japan races to fill its ammo stores after Ukraine lessons
articles.body:
- Japan will begin building at least 65 new ammunition depots from fiscal 2027 using a standardized design to speed up construction.
- Analysts say Japan's push to store more ammunition draws on lessons from the war in Ukraine.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense will start building at least 65 new ammunition depots for the Self-Defense Forces from fiscal 2027, using a single standardized design to get them into service faster, the Nikkei business daily reported Sept. 20. The push to store more ammunition follows lessons Tokyo has drawn from Russia’s war in Ukraine, where stockpiles, supply lines and the safety of military sites have shaped the fighting.
The ministry has so far designed each depot individually, and switching to a standard model is meant to shorten design work and speed up construction, the newspaper said. The Self-Defense Forces operate about 1,400 ammunition depots nationwide, and the ministry plans to add roughly 130 by fiscal 2032. Sites for 65 of those have been chosen, and three had been completed by August 2026. The Nikkei did not say where the next 65 will be built or what the program will cost.
Japan’s 2022 National Defense Strategy and Defense Buildup Program call for the Self-Defense Forces to secure the ammunition they need as early as possible so they can sustain a long fight. When those plans were drafted, Japan held only about 60% of the Patriot PAC-3 MSE and SM-3 interceptors it needed for missile defense, and its stocks of artillery shells and rockets would have lasted about two months in combat, Shephard reported. Then-Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said in October 2022 that the forces’ ability to keep fighting was inadequate.
A 2024 study by France’s Foundation for Strategic Research said Japan was trying to absorb lessons from the war in Ukraine on logistics, ammunition stocks, unmanned systems and the survivability of military bases. RAND researchers wrote in 2023 that Tokyo was increasing spending on munitions stocks and base hardening, and urged Japanese planners to prepare for a protracted conflict. Japan’s Ministry of Defense has not publicly linked the new depot design to any specific foreign example.
Czech police concluded in 2024 that officers from Russia’s GRU military intelligence carried out the 2014 explosions that destroyed ammunition warehouses at Vrbětice and killed two people, with the aim of stopping weapons from reaching Ukraine. In August 2026, explosions hit a Bulgarian plant run by EMCO, which makes 155 mm artillery ammunition for Ukraine, and a KNDS Ammo facility near Rome. Bulgarian and Italian officials have been reluctant to blame Russia, but Western intelligence officials have said the GRU now recruits criminal gangs to attack European arms sites while keeping Moscow’s hand hidden.
Kyodo News reported in 2023 that the ministry planned its first new depots at nine Ground Self-Defense Force sites in Hokkaido, Miyazaki, Kagoshima and Okinawa to store long-range missiles, including at Camp Ebino and the Okinawa Training Area. Japan is also buying 400 U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Japan spent about 48.2 billion yen ($308 million) on new depots from 2022 through March 2026, and its budget for the fiscal year that began in April includes about 56 billion yen ($358 million) more, Austrian magazine Militär Aktuell reported.

articles.title: Russia's finance ministry raises taxes to bolster Putin's military budget
articles.body:
More frequent long-range strikes by the Ukrainian armed forces on strategically important targets, as well as growing spending to counter these attacks, are further deepening Russia's budget deficit.
The Kremlin is seeking additional funds for the war in Ukraine by raising taxes, as the federal budget deficit reached 5.8479 trillion roubles (€60.4 billion) in the first half of the year, according to official data.
By the end of July, the budget deficit amounted to 2.8% of annual GDP, almost twice the initially planned annual figure.
The volume of funds in Russia's reserve fund has fallen to 1.6% of GDP, forcing the Kremlin to borrow from domestic banks.
At the same time, GDP growth has slowed compared with the peak rate of more than 4% year on year recorded in 2023–2024.
According to government forecasts, growth this year will be 0.6%, with the economy contracting in the first quarter and showing a modest rebound in the second.
Analysts cite a sharp increase in government spending as the main cause of the deficit – including massive outlays on the war and advance financing of state contracts – along with weaker revenues under sanctions pressure and volatile commodity markets.
More frequent and intensified long-range strikes by the Ukrainian armed forces on strategically important targets, above all oil refineries and depots, as well as growing spending to counter these attacks, are further deepening the deficit.
The still-low unemployment rate and generous state payments in poorer regions are helping to contain consumer discontent for now.
However, economists warn that long-term problems are eroding the foundations of the economy and could eventually trigger a crisis.
The Ministry of Finance has submitted a draft law to the Russian government on a new three-year budget with an annual deficit of around 2% of GDP, as well as a bill amending the Tax Code "to increase the resilience of the budget system."
The proposal states that "the strategic priority of the budget is the financial provision of defence and national security needs, and social support for participants in the special military operation (Russia's official term for the war against Ukraine) and their families."
Civilians and businesses will pay for the war
The Ministry of Finance has proposed taxing Russians' so‑called "passive" income at rates of 13%–22%. This includes interest on deposits, dividend income, securities transactions, property sales, as well as insurance and gift contracts. At present, passive income is taxed at 13%–15%.
Extending the progressive scale of personal income tax to income from deposits, dividends, investments and the sale of property could bring the budget an additional 500–700 billion roubles a year. That estimate was given by economist Dmitry Polevoy, quoted by the outlet Meduza.
Another initiative by the ministry is to introduce value added tax (VAT) on purchases from foreign online shops.
That would be applied immediately at the maximum rate of 22%, although there had previously been talk of a phased increase.
It is also proposed to introduce a fee of 100 roubles (about €1) for parcels from abroad worth up to €200, which are currently exempt from customs duty.
In parallel, Russian media say the Federation Council has proposed higher taxes for the self‑employed.
Andrei Yepishin, deputy chair of the committee on the budget and financial markets, said couriers and drivers who in practice work full time should pay tax at a rate starting from 13% instead of the 4%–6% self‑employment tax.
According to the ministry's estimates, the changes will affect about 4 million Russians, roughly 2.74% of the population. However, the Finance Ministry stressed in particular that the amendments should not affect the income of participants in the war.
For large businesses, a windfall tax is being introduced, according to the Finance Ministry's press release: for certain companies in the mining and metals sector the tax will be 30% of additional income. For gold producers the rate will be 20%.
The Russian Ministry of Finance openly states that "the resources envisaged will ensure that the armed forces are supplied with the necessary weapons and military equipment, the modernisation of defence‑industry enterprises, the payment of monetary allowances to servicemen and support for their families."
The ministry notes that priority funding will continue under the national projects "Machine tools" and "Unmanned aerial systems."
Their funding over three years will increase to 135.7 billion roubles (€1.4 billion) and 103.3 billion roubles respectively (€1.06 billion).
The Kremlin's forgotten promise
It is noteworthy that the Kremlin forgot its promise not to raise taxes on the fourth day after the State Duma elections.
"This is not under discussion," presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said 10 days before the vote, according to the Interfax news agency.
Earlier this year, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov insisted that tax increases for Russian citizens were not being considered.
"These are fake leaks," he said at the time.
Judging by the proposed amendments to the Russian Tax Code, the authorities are having to seek additional revenue at home to sustain the war machine.
The measures being proposed show that the Kremlin intends to shift the rising cost of the war not only onto better‑off citizens with income from savings and investments and onto big business, but also onto ordinary consumers.
It is hardly surprising that consumer confidence has been gradually falling since its peak in 2024–2025, when higher military spending was fuelling economic growth and wage increases.
Recently consumers have been confronted with rising petrol prices and shortages due to Ukrainian drone attacks that have knocked out oil refineries. Many small businesses have also suffered losses of inventories and customers because of strikes targeting the online retailers Wildberries and Ozon.
The consumer sentiment index calculated by the Levada Centre, an independent Russian polling organisation, fell in the summer to 94 points, compared with 116 points in the spring and summer of 2025. Readings below 100 indicate that consumer sentiment is more negative than positive.
Against this backdrop, talk continues of VPN blocks and of a possible new wave of mobilisation, repeatedly denied officially.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russian P-18 Terek Early-Warning Radar Watching Skies for 250 Km
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russian P-18 Terek Early-Warning Radar Watching Skies for 250 Km
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian P-18 Terek early-warning radar in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region and an ammunition depot in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region during a series of attacks on Russian military targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff on September 26, the strikes were carried out throughout September 25 and overnight into September 26. The P-18 radar was hit near Semenivske in the Donetsk region, while a separate strike targeted an ammunition depot in Sievierodonetsk.
The military did not specify which weapons were used in the attacks or provide an assessment of the damage to either target.
The P-18, also designated 1RL131 Terek and known by the NATO reporting name Spoon Rest D, is a Soviet-designed mobile two-dimensional early-warning radar operating in the VHF band. The system entered service in 1970 and remains in operation, with several modernization packages developed over the decades.
According to the General Staff, the radar can detect airborne targets at ranges of around 250 kilometers and at altitudes of up to 35 kilometers. It is used to detect and determine the coordinates of aircraft and other aerial targets before passing radar information to other elements of an air-defense network.
Unlike fire-control radars that directly guide surface-to-air missiles, the P-18 primarily serves as an early-warning and surveillance sensor. Its VHF operating band and long detection range allow it to contribute to the broader air picture available to air-defense units.
Czech defense electronics company RETIA, which offers modernization packages for the P-18, also identifies its long range and ability to detect low-observable targets as key characteristics of the system.
On September 21, Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian Kasta-2E2 radar in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region. The mobile system, valued at an estimated $60 million, can detect low-flying aircraft, missiles, and drones at ranges of up to 150 kilometers.

articles.title: The intelligence war is turning against the Houthis
articles.body:
The intelligence war is turning against the Houthis
Russian satellite intelligence and Iranian command integration helped the Houthis exploit weaknesses on Yemen’s western front. Now that system is itself under attack.
The collapse of Yemen’s western front was not primarily the result of sheer Houthi numbers. It resulted from a fused Russian-Iranian command system in which elements of Russia’s space-based geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) and signals intelligence (SIGINT) capabilities were integrated into an Iranian-led command-and-control (C2) system supporting Houthi operations. Human penetration of Tariq Saleh’s National Resistance Forces gave that system the access required to turn technical collection into a battlefield advantage.
Through Project AURORAH, the GEOINT and SIGINT fusion system I created, I identified and sequenced Russian military reconnaissance over Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, the UAE and Jordan during the Iran-US war. A compartmented special-access programme (SAP) within the project reconstructed Russian orbital collection as a single multisensor system, including the sequences that preceded Iran’s precision strikes on countries across the region and on US military assets. That work later considerably assisted a major CNN investigation into Russian military geospatial satellite support for Iranian precision targeting across the Middle East.
The underlying principle had already emerged over Iran: orbital intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) was no longer merely supporting operations, but helping construct the operational picture of the battlespace before strikes were carried out. That use of satellite intelligence was already visible during the Iran war. Russian GEOINT mapped how forces were deployed, their movement corridors, headquarters and logistical changes, while SIGINT mapped the sources of electronic signals, communications patterns and command relationships.
The advantage came from sequencing different forms of satellite collection over time, not from any single spacecraft. Different reconnaissance satellites provided complementary geographic and electromagnetic coverage, allowing changes in how forces moved and operated to be followed over time rather than captured as isolated snapshots. During the Iran war, this combination of different forms of satellite intelligence had already shown how Russian satellite intelligence could sharpen Iranian precision operations.
In Yemen, Iran provided the operational integration. Russian-derived intelligence was combined with Houthi tactical reporting and human access to build a detailed picture of how Tariq Saleh’s command actually functioned: which headquarters remained responsive, where reported positions diverged from reality, which formations were poorly coordinated, and where gaps existed in command, reporting and communications between the National Resistance Forces (NRF) and the Saudi-led Joint Forces Command (JFC). That picture made weaknesses along the western coastal front possible to exploit.
This is where the front broke. One command-and-control pathway connected JFC headquarters with elements of the NRF; another connected those forces with one another and with their own senior command. Once both became unreliable, inaccurate information flowed upwards while confused or manipulated instructions flowed downwards.
The consequences were specific. One NRF commander acknowledged an order to hold a blocking position and then withdrew. Another reported that a non-NRF Yemeni formation had vacated a military airfield when personnel were still there, giving commanders an inaccurate picture of where friendly forces were positioned and contributing to casualties after a strike. A Saudi special forces task force at Mokha was the first to recognise that reported force deployments no longer matched the reality on the ground.
Saudi strike missions had been prepared, but airpower could not be used freely when the locations of friendly forces could no longer be reliably confirmed. The problem was compounded when some NRF brigades discovered during activation that 50 to 60 percent of registered personnel had failed to report, despite months of JFC biometric registration, salary restoration and force consolidation. As coordination around the critical military hub of Jabal al-Nar deteriorated, NRF formations began leaving positions before the main Houthi forces had reached them.
That debacle has become the central learning event of the campaign. Combined Saudi-Yemeni and Saudi-Pakistani Joint Terminal Attack Controller (JTAC) teams are now being embedded with major northern formations, restoring an authenticated link between forces on the ground and the JFC’s strike system. Saudi Operational Mentoring and Liaison Teams (OMLT) are also providing direct links to the JFC and independently verifying the manpower, location and readiness of Yemeni formations. At the same time, positive authentication of commands, compartmented reporting and redundant encrypted communications are closing the vulnerabilities exposed at Mokha.
Saudi Arabia has used a similar approach before, against a different adversary. In January 2026, JFC military counterintelligence mapped and systematically degraded the Abu Dhabi command-and-control system supporting Southern Transitional Council (STC) operations in southern Yemen, while liaison and targeting mechanisms maintained a reliable picture of operations on the ground. Once that external layer was removed, UAE task forces and aligned formations rapidly lost their freedom of action and withdrew under pressure from the Saudi-led campaign.
The system now supporting the Houthis is far more sophisticated. Russia provides satellite-based intelligence and signals intelligence; Iran integrates that information into Houthi command and operations. But that sophistication also creates vulnerabilities: the system depends on secure communications, specialist personnel, intelligence-fusion nodes, technical advisers and continuous links between Sanaa and battlefield headquarters.
Those vulnerabilities are now being targeted. On the evening of September 19, the Iranian-led top-level command-and-control structure in Sanaa suffered a massive blow. Confirmed senior Houthi battlefield losses now include at least two major generals, seven brigadier generals and 32 colonels, many removed alongside their immediate aides, staff and communications elements. There are also strong indications that figures above the rank of major general have been neutralised within the highest levels of the Houthi command structure, together with associated foreign personnel, although those details remain deliberately withheld for now.
The effect is more important than the count. Front-line command is being systematically degraded while senior command nodes in Sanaa are simultaneously coming under precise JFC air strikes, disrupting the chain between intelligence collection, decision-making, targeting and execution. Headquarters forced to relocate, surviving commanders attempting to reconnect with subordinate units and remaining junior Iranian advisers establishing alternative pathways all generate fresh signatures that can be detected, correlated and geolocated.
This is why the Houthi advance is now struggling to reproduce the momentum of the West Coast breakthrough. The command links they exploited are being hardened, while their own externally supported command-and-control network is being progressively blinded and exposed. The failure on the West Coast has therefore become a lesson the Saudi-led forces are acting on, rather than a permanent weakness in their military structure.
The Saudi-led JFC’s broader transformation in C6ISR – the systems connecting command, communications, intelligence and combat capabilities – target development and faster sensor-to-shooter integration has changed the military equation since 2015. At the same time, sustained Houthi escalation has exhausted the restraint that governed Saudi policy for years. The major Saudi-led campaign now taking shape will therefore begin against an adversary whose external command support is already under sustained attack.
That is the decisive difference. The Russian-Iranian system sustaining and amplifying Houthi military power is being degraded before major Saudi-led air, land and naval operations are fully under way, while the tactical failures exposed at Mokha are being corrected within the Saudi-led JFC. The Houthis exploited a compromised command system once; they are now being forced to fight while the external system that magnified their own effectiveness is systematically dismantled.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons: report
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons: report
US intelligence agencies have assessed that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons programme, according to classified documents provided to Congress and described to The Washington Post by US officials.
The assessment is raising fresh questions about US President Donald Trump’s agreement to help Riyadh establish a civilian nuclear industry. Some US lawmakers fear the deal could give Saudi Arabia the means to produce nuclear material that might eventually be used as a weapon, although the intelligence finding does not say the kingdom has decided to build one.
The agreement, announced in July, would allow US companies to pursue nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia. The Trump administration says the partnership will strengthen ties with Riyadh, uphold non-proliferation standards, and reduce the prospect of the kingdom turning to Russia or China for nuclear technology.
But Democratic lawmakers say the deal's restrictions do not go far enough. Under the agreement, Saudi uranium enrichment would initially be limited to less than five percent. That ceiling could rise to 20% following a further study and written agreement, according to The Washington Post.
The agreement also does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which would give inspectors broader access to nuclear sites and information.
In a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday, senators led by Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley accused the administration of accepting weaker safeguards that could enable Riyadh to acquire uranium-enrichment capabilities.
Their concerns have been sharpened by the intelligence assessment, which officials said was among classified material sent to Congress last month. The State Department’s contribution to those documents appeared more confident in the deal’s safeguards and Saudi assurances, the officials told the newspaper.
Saudi Arabia did not answer the newspaper’s questions directly. Instead, it referred to an earlier statement by Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman saying its nuclear programme would be peaceful and pursued with responsibility and transparency. The State Department said the US "does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapon program".
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in 2018 that Saudi Arabia would seek a nuclear weapon if Iran developed one. That conditional statement has long fuelled concern that an Iranian bomb could trigger a regional arms race.
Congress is reviewing the agreement and could move to block it, though opponents would need sufficient votes to overcome a possible presidential veto.
Its future may also depend on diplomacy over Israel: a senior US administration official told The Washington Post that Saudi normalisation with Israel remains a condition of the deal, while analysts said Riyadh is unlikely to take that step as long as Israel rules out a Palestinian state.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: What we know about Russian special military operation’s course over day
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 27. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces struck transport and fuel, energy infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian military, as well as drone production facilities in the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has compiled the main information on the progress of the special military operation over the day.
Situation in Kharkov Region
Russia’s battlegroup North has established control over Khripuny in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry said. "The battlegroup North continues to tighten the encirclement of Ukrainian military units in the northeast of the Kharkov Region and expand the zone of control. As a result of active offensive operations, the settlement of Khripuny in the Kharkov Region came under [Russian] control," the statement said.
Moreover, Russian servicemen are fighting to liberate the settlements of Nesternoye, Lukashovo, and Grachovka in the Kharkov Region. "Fighting is underway to liberate the settlements of Nesternoye, Lukashovo, and Grachovka. Enemy forces are being eliminated near the settlements of Varvarovka and Rublenoye in the Kharkov Region," the mininstry noted.
At the same time, the battlegroup continues fighting for Prikolotnoye in the Kharkov Region. "As part of efforts to expand the zone of control, the battlegroup North continues fighting for the town of Prikolotnoye in the Kharkov Region," the statement said.
Meanwhile, the Russian Armed Forces thwarted two Ukrainian military attempts to break out of the Kharkov Region encirclement near the village of Nefedovka. "[Russian servicemen] thwarted two enemy attempts to break out of the encirclement near the village of Nefedovka in the Kharkov Region," the military pointed out, noting that Ukraine has lost up to 60 servicemen in the Kharkov Region encirclement over the past day. "Over the past 24 hours, the Ukrainian losses in the encirclement amounted to up to 60 servicemen, two armored fighting vehicles, a car, an ATV, and two ground-based robotic systems," the statement said.
Concurrently, Russia’s battlegroup Center liberated 94 buildings and eliminated more than 30 Ukrainian servicemen in Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry emphasized. "In the DPR town of Dobropolye, the Center conducted offensive operations in the northwestern direction, continuing to eliminate encircled Ukrainian military units in the western and eastern districts of the city. A total of 94 buildings were liberated and over 30 Ukrainian servicemen were eliminated. Over the past 24 hours, the enemy made no attempts to break out of the encirclement," the statement said.
Special military operation progress
The Russian Armed Forces struck transport and fuel, energy infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian military, as well as drone production facilities in the past 24 hours, the army stresed.
"Russian servicemen struck transport and fuel-energy infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian military, drone production facilities and their component manufacturing plants, as well as temporary deployment sites of Ukrainian militants and foreign mercenaries in 149 areas," the ministry said.
According to its statement, Ukraine has lost approximately 1,515 troops in the special military operation zone over the past 24 hours. In particular, Russia’s battlegroup North wiped out over 300 Ukrainian servicemen, the battlegroup West eliminated more than 230 enemy troops, the battlegroup South wiped out over 230 military, the battlegroup Center eliminated up to 420, the battlegroup East destroyed up to 290 troops, and the battlegroup Dnepr wiped out up to 45.
Meanwhile, Russian air defenses downed four guided aerial bombs, a US-made HIMARS MLRS rocket, and 505 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry concluded.

articles.title: US and China move to ease tensions with tariff cuts and new AI dialogue
articles.body:
China and the United States have agreed on $30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions and the opening of a dialogue on artificial intelligence as part of an eight-point agreement reached following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington. The announcement was issued by China’s Foreign Ministry shortly after Xi landed in Beijing at the end of a three-day visit to the United States.
According to the Chinese Foreign Ministry, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump agreed to build “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, based on mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity. The provision, the first of eight, is intended to establish a broad framework for relations between the world’s two largest economies following months of trade tensions and technological competition.
At the heart of the agreement is the $30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement, covering products defined as “non-sensitive” by both sides. U.S. tariff reductions will apply to agricultural products, seafood and medical equipment, while Chinese relief will apply to products including toys and small electrical appliances. The sides also approved the establishment and advancement of a joint trade council and an extension of the outcomes reached in previous trade talks in Kuala Lumpur.
The agreement follows directly from a decision made earlier this week to extend by another two months the trade “truce” between the two powers, which had been due to expire on Nov. 10, as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday
Will the agreement ease tensions between the two powers?
The current agreement builds on understandings reached at the Busan summit in South Korea in October last year, where the sides announced a basic agreement on trade, which continued to take shape in further talks held in Beijing in May. As part of the new deal, according to the White House, China committed to purchasing at least 10 million tons of U.S. coal in each of 2027 and 2028, while the two sides established joint working groups to address agricultural market access and stabilization of the global oil supply.
One of the most notable provisions of the current agreement concerns the establishment of a dedicated dialogue channel — also dubbed the “super intelligence” channel — through which the two sides will exchange views on the risks and benefits of artificial intelligence technology. The first round of discussions under the dialogue is scheduled for November, while a separate communication channel will be established to handle AI-related incidents. The move marks one of the first mutual acknowledgments by Washington and Beijing of the need for international coordination surrounding the sensitive technology.
On broader foreign policy, the leaders agreed that Iran must uphold its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons — with the White House using stronger language, stating that Iran “can never” possess a nuclear weapon — and that transit fees should not be imposed on international waterways. Another provision addresses cooperation between Chinese and U.S. law enforcement authorities in combating drug trafficking, which the sides said has already produced tangible results, including dozens of arrests.
The three-day visit produced no major public breakthroughs, but the agreements announced at its conclusion — chiefly the tariff arrangement and AI dialogue — represent another attempt by the world’s two largest economies to contain tensions and keep trade channels open amid a dispute that has expanded in recent months to include export controls, rare-earth minerals, technology and the shipping industry.

Over the past week, the Russian Federation launched more than 2,200 attack drones at Ukraine; today it attacked a data center in Kyiv twice — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Russia used more than 2,200 drones, 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles over the past week. Four people were killed in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and Kyiv.

articles.title: In Germany, intelligence services are searching for Russian “weapons caches”; there is a threat of sabotage at a defense company — media reports
articles.body:
In Germany, intelligence services are searching for Russian “weapons caches”; there is a threat of sabotage at a defense company — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
German intelligence services suspect that weapons for sabotage against a defense company have already been hidden in Bavaria. The investigation is classified.
According to German intelligence, Russian intelligence has created weapons caches in Germany. As BILD has learned, a search for these caches is currently under way, reports UNN.
Details
On the evening of June 11, 2026, Serbian police stopped two cars near Subotica that were heading toward the Hungarian border. In the Peugeot belonging to Danilo Bogdanović, a Serb with a Russian passport, they found drone components, while in the black Volvo belonging to Slobodan Dučić, they discovered a concealed compartment containing two tin cans packed with explosives. Investigators assessed that a flying bomb could have been assembled from these materials. Bogdanović and Dučić were arrested.
The next day, a friendly intelligence service passed information to its German counterparts about a suspicious truck traveling to Germany from Serbia. According to the Serbian authorities, the truck contained a compartment for smuggling weapons. However, Serbian police failed to intercept the vehicle.
On June 27, Bavarian border police detained the truck as it entered from Austria. The Serbian driver was detained, banned from entering Germany, and sent back to Austria. The truck was confiscated. Investigators did indeed find concealed compartments—but they were empty. The security authorities concluded that the delivery of the weapons about which the Serbs had warned may have reached its destination in Germany earlier. According to BILD, the weapons may have been intended for an attack on a defense company in Bavaria that is of major importance for military aid to Ukraine.
The search for the weapons is in full swing. According to the German government, several networks of saboteurs controlled by Russia are currently operating in Europe. They are believed to be coordinated by the GRU, which is apparently conducting covert operations in Europe with the help of a special-operations unit. German investigators suspect that the weapons from the truck are already in a cache in Germany and ready to be used for acts of sabotage.
In response to BILD's inquiry, all authorities involved in the case unanimously cited the need for secrecy. The pages of documents that BILD was able to see in connection with the investigation bear the words "officially classified" printed in red at the top.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine, with Odesa Oblast targeted in 'mass strike'
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine, with Odesa Oblast targeted in 'mass strike'
At least 14 people were killed and 57 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day as Odesa Oblast in particular came under mass attack, local authorities said on Sept. 26-27.
In southern Odesa Oblast, Russia launched "a mass strike," damaging a residential building, a medical facility, a hotel, a shop and a grain storage facility, local governor Oleh Kiper said. One person was killed while two others were injured, he added.
Overall, overnight on Sept. 27, Russian forces launched 170 Shahed-type attack drones, including 76 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 147 drones, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at eight locations, the Air Force said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 27 that residential buildings, energy infrastructure, and other civilian infrastructure were attacked in Odesa, Kharkiv, Sumy, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Zhytomyr, and Kyiv oblasts overnight.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, four people were killed, and five were injured in Russian attacks across the region, local authorities said. Over the past day, Russia carried out 989 attacks on 59 settlements of the region.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed, and five were injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In the northeastern city of Sumy, a Russian glide bomb attack hit a residential area, killing two people and injuring 28 others, including four children, regional authorities said.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed two people and injured six others over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Sept. 26 and Sept. 27.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and the surrounding regions, killing two people and injuring three others, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kyiv, Russian drones injured five people over the past day, damaging residential buildings and warehouses, local authorities reported.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day damaged 23 facilities, injuring two people, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks in the region injured one person, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. He added that, as a result of the attacks, a high-rise apartment building, nine houses, a shop, and vehicles were damaged.
In Poltava Oblast, power lines have been damaged following the crash of a Russian drone, local governor Vitalii Diakivnych said. Around 500 customers were temporarily left without power while power company staff worked to restore the electricity supply, he added.
Zelensky said that over the past week, Russian forces launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types.

articles.title: Iran insists on Hormuz conditions, Gaza death toll over 74,000
articles.body:
At least seven people were killed and 40 wounded in a strike on a market in Yemen's Taiz, the health ministry in Houthi-controlled areas of the country has said.
Breadcrumb
Iran stood firm Sunday on its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump's rejection of the proposal that had created some optimism for breaking the Mideast war stalemate.
Iran's plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and fulfilling conditions in the ceasefire deal that fell apart months ago.
That agreement, which dissolved during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Araghchi said on Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights."
In Gaza, the death toll from Israel's genocidal war on the enclave has surpassed 74,000, Gaza's Health Ministry said.
This includes 1,145 Palestinians killed by Israel since a 'ceasefire' came into force in October 2025.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday that they seized an American submarine drone in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has blockaded in the months-long Middle East war.
"Through a coordinated, complex operation involving intelligence oversight and electronic warfare, IRGC naval forces' personnel successfully captured an advanced unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) belonging to the terrorist US military," the IRGC naval forces said in a statement, according to state TV.
They added that the drone was "operating in the Strait of Hormuz for espionage purposes", identifying the model as a Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle that was "now in the hands of the force's specialists for data recovery".
Police have evacuated homes near a U.S. air base in England and arrested several men over suspected explosives offenses.
The Gloucestershire Police force says “a number of properties” are being evacuated in Whelford, western England. That is close to RAF Fairford, a base used by American forces during the war with Iran.
Police say several men have been detained on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, and army bomb-disposal experts are examining several vehicles.
Parents across Riyadh received emails from schools on Sunday announcing a last-minute plan to shift to remote learning for a week, according to messages seen by AFP.
"We have just been informed by Saudi authorities that schools must remain closed all week," read two separate messages seen by AFP.
There was no official reason given but the move comes amid heightened tensions in the Gulf and near-daily attacks aimed at Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that he had sent envoys around the world to pressure countries to economically isolate Iran, hailing new restrictions targeting the country's airlines and banks.
"At my direction, teams were dispatched across the globe to engage with countries and demand action against the Iranian regime," he said on X. "These efforts are delivering results."
Bessent noted that Turkey and Oman have halted incoming flights from private carrier Mahan Air, while the United Arab Emirates has stopped all flights by Iranian airlines.
Dubai, the UAE's commercial hub, is a major destination for Iran's carriers, with multiple daily flights, a large Iranian community and close business links.
Iran's ISNA news agency, citing officials, reported that five countries had revoked the Islamic republic's flight permits: Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iraq, Oman and the UAE.
But it said flights were still operating to China -- which is refusing to yield to US pressure -- and Russia via the two main airlines, national carrier Iran Air and Mahan.
Mahan had announced that it would no longer serve Turkey at the request of the Turkish authorities, but flights continue several times a day in both directions, via Iran Air or smaller Iranian carriers, according to the Tehran and Istanbul airport websites.
ISNA said Afghanistan, Armenia, Belarus, Malaysia, Pakistan and Tajikistan were still also being served.
Bessent had said on Monday that all Iranian airlines "will be shut down around the world".

articles.title: Lavrov blasts assassination of Iran Leader as ‘unacceptable'
articles.body:
Russia's Foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov, addressed the UN General Assembly on Saturday and accused Western countries of destabilising the world through “force and double standards”, vowing that Moscow's “special military operation” in Ukraine would be “carried through to the end,” the UN website reported.
Quoting President Vladimir Putin, Mr. Lavrov said “the dictatorship of a single hegemon has run amok and is simply dangerous for everyone around it,” arguing that a fairer, multipolar order was emerging as countries of the Global South and East asserted themselves as “sovereign centres of development.”
Mr. Lavrov condemned the United States' seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife earlier this year, and their “extrajudicial detention” in the US, calling for their immediate release.
In a sharp rebuke of the war on Iran, Lavrov characterized the targeting of Iran’s leadership as a profound violation of established diplomatic norms and a dangerous precedent that threatens global stability.
He also denounced the killing of Iran's Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, along with members of his family and military and political leadership, as “another unacceptable manifestation of coercive diktat.”
He said the wider US-Israeli campaign had also struck Iranian nuclear facilities under the IAEA safeguards, causing “irreparable damage” to the non-proliferation system overseen by the UN-backed nuclear energy watchdog.

articles.title: Russian Attacks on Kharkiv Region Kill 2, Injure 7, Including 4 Children
articles.body:
Two people were killed and at least seven injured, including four children, as Russian forces struck the city of Kharkiv and 21 settlements across the Kharkiv region over Saturday.
Oleh Synehubov, the head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration reported the casualties in the morning of Sunday, Sept. 27. He said Russia used a missile, three multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS) and 41 drones against the region.

Both people killed were 50-year-old men. One died near the village of Pytomnyk in the Derhachi community, and the other between the villages of Shuby and Sinne.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) recorded a total of 221 combat clashes in total since Saturday.
In total, Russian forces launched 289 guided aerial bombs (KABs) on Ukraine nationwide. They also used 10,489 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,729 attacks.
Children among the injured
The village of Lebiazhe in the Prolisne community was among the hardest hit.
A 13-year-old boy was injured there, while a 56-year-old man, a 32-year-old woman and two boys aged 12 and 5 suffered acute stress reactions, according to Synehubov.
A 73-year-old woman was injured in the attack near Pytomnyk, while a 16-year-old boy was wounded in the strike between Shuby and Sinne.
In the village of Nyzhche Solone in the Borova community, a 60-year-old man was injured when an unidentified device exploded.
Drones target several Kharkiv districts
Russian forces attacked Kharkiv’s Shevchenkivskyi and Slobidskyi districts with drones, damaging an abandoned building and a stadium in the city.

Of the 41 drones used against the region, one was a Geran-2, the Russian version of the Iranian-designed Shahed.
Two were Molniya drones and 15 were first-person-view (FPV) drones.
The type of the remaining 23 is still being determined.
Civilian infrastructure targeted again
Civilian infrastructure was damaged across six districts of the region, according to the regional military administration.
In Kupiansk district, Russian attacks damaged an ambulance in the village of Prosianka, a residential care facility and a garage in Shevchenkove, an outbuilding in Velykyi Burluk, a private house in Kotivka and a civilian enterprise in Novoselivka.
In Chuhuiv district, an apartment building and 15 private vehicles were damaged in Lebiazhe, while power lines were hit in the village of Zarichne.
In Bohodukhiv district, strikes damaged four private houses in Zolochiv, private homes in Riasne and Kalynove, and private vehicles in Skovorodynivka and Sinne.
In Lozova district, a private house and a civilian enterprise were damaged in Lozova, an administrative building and four cars in Zlatopil, and a private house in Dobropillia.
A residential building and a hangar were hit in the city of Izium.
In Kharkiv district, the attacks damaged cars in Pytomnyk and Ruska Lozova, a private house in Tsyrkuny and a shop in Derhachi.
Evacuations continue as Russian strikes persist
The transit evacuation center in Lozova received 185 people over the past day, Syniehubov said, adding that it has registered a total of 62,012 people since it opened.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify the figures.
Citing the General Staff of the AFU, Synehubov said Ukrainian units repelled four Russian attacks near the settlements of Ternova, Kozacha Lopan and Lyman in the Southern Slobozhanskyi axis.
In the Kupiansk axis, Russian forces made three attempts to improve their positions, launching assaults toward Kupiansk, Radkivka and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Calls On Trump To Enact Russia Sanctions After Deadly Attacks Across Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on US President Donald Trump to enact sanctions against Russia amid its deadly attacks across Ukraine, which have become increasingly frequent as cold weather starts to set in.
"Russia is escalating every single day," Zelenskyy wrote on social media on September 26. "We ask President Trump to implement the Lindsey Graham Act against Russia and everyone who props up its war financially."
The law, signed by Trump a week ago, gives the president sweeping new authority to impose sanctions and tariffs on Russia, its energy sector, and foreign governments and entities that help Moscow evade existing restrictions.
Zelenskyy said that Russia's latest strikes on Ukraine killed at least four people in the Zaporizhzhya and Sumy regions, partly occupied by Russian forces, and left more than a dozen more injured across the country.
Civilian and energy infrastructure was damaged in at least eight Ukrainian regions, including a kindergarden in the capital, Kyiv, and a university in the country's second-largest city, Kharkiv, he added.
In Zaporizhzhya, fire swept through the city's central market following the attack, local resident Olena told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service -- the place where she had worked for more than 25 years is now covered in charred debris.
"The people won't come here anymore, that's for sure.... All the goods reeked of smoke," Olena said at the scene, adding that she would now have to relocate and search for a new place to work.
With a fifth wartime winter approaching, Russian strikes on Ukraine have become a daily occurrence.
Over the past four years, Moscow has sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by pounding the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Since this summer, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia.
The campaign has left Russia with nationwide fuel shortages and has stoked discontent among its citizens, who were largely disconnected from the war in Ukraine.
In the latest such strike on September 26, Ukrainian forces said they had hit the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region, describing the facility as helping fuel Moscow's war effort.
US Seeking Diplomatic Settlement
The developments came amid what appears to be renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war, with the White House reportedly seeking to find a solution before winter.
At their latest meeting in New York this week, Zelenskyy told Trump he "hoped" that Washington would help to end the war "as soon as possible."
The Ukrainian president had told journalists that Washington had proposed holding what would be the first Ukraine-Russia-US meeting in many months at a relatively low "technical level," with the United Arab Emirates serving as host.
While there was no immediate confirmation from the United States, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that all peace proposals were "on the table" but added that Moscow had to weigh its interests.
Control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region has been a central sticking point since US-led peace efforts began under the Trump administration in 2025.
Russia has vowed to seize the territory by force if Ukraine refuses to cede the areas it still holds, making Donetsk a major military priority.

articles.title: Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them?
articles.body:
Last winter, eight Ukrainian companies told the defense minister that their interceptors were ready to knock Russia's jet-powered drones out of the sky. They were not. A fast-flying drone is the easy part of the design, while combat testing exposed what the interceptors lacked in key features to chase an evading jet-powered Geran, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, said in an interview with NV.
Ukraine's answer to Russia's fast, hard-to-stop jet drones was supposed to be cheap interceptors, and last winter, their makers said they had them. But a jet Geran flies 450 to 500 kilometers an hour, up from the Geran-3's 320, varies its speed to slip past defenses, and will dodge harder once interceptors appear.
Catching one takes maneuverability, machine-vision target-lock, and fuel to loiter and search, not just speed, Flash said. Ukraine's cheap interceptors have already downed about half of Russia's slower drones, but the jet-powered systems have stayed a step ahead.
Eight makers said "ready"
At a meeting last winter called by Mykhailo Fedorov, then-defense minister, all eight interceptor makers reported the same thing: "everything's ready, the solution exists, it flies, we tested it, speed is sufficient," Flash recalled.
The mistake, he said, was that no one checked on them week to week. There were also too few jet Gerans in the skies then to test against.
"On the range, they showed: it flies. That was the problem," explained Flash.
Speed is the easy part
The engines are not the obstacle, Flash continues, since they can be bought abroad, and neither is a plane that flies fast in a straight line. The hard part is a machine agile enough to chase a jet-powered Geran, which is far more maneuverable than the propeller kind and will start changing altitude and throwing evasive maneuvers once interceptors appear.
Because an operator's aim frays at such speeds, he said, the decisive pieces are automatic target capture by machine vision and automatic terminal guidance.
"Building a construction that just flies fast is the easiest part," he added.
Mass orders must wait
That is why Ukraine cannot simply order thousands to blanket the country, Flash said: it first needs a proven design that works for any crew, from Security Service specialists to territorial defense soldiers, and is simple to launch, operate, and maintain.
Once such a sample exists, he said, scaling up is only a question of money. Meanwhile, the work is moving: a Ukrainian interceptor recently notched its first kills against jet Gerans and is heading toward mass production.
