articles.title: Germany’s Wadephul meets Russia’s Lavrov amid tensions over ‘escalation’
articles.body:
NEW YORK — German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul held a surprise meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the U.N. on Saturday, just one day after he welcomed the U.S. invite for Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit.
"It was an intense conversation", Wadephul told German public television ZDF after the meeting, which lasted about 30 minutes. "Of course, we did not reach agreement on key points. It was important to me to make it clear that Germany does not accept incidents such as the drone attack in Leipzig, and that this is an escalation that is unacceptable. And I clearly warned Russia not to continue down this path. We can defend ourselves, we can fight back. And that's exactly what we'll do."
“Wadephul called on the Russian Federation to abandon its dangerous path of escalation toward Germany, Europe, and NATO,” a German official said after the meeting. The official was granted anonymity to discuss the meeting.
Advertisement
The minister also “condemned Russia’s ongoing and increasingly targeted aggression against the Ukrainian civilian population” and highlighted that, “every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers die in a hopeless war of attrition, while the Russian economy continues to collapse,” the official said.
The meeting of the German and the Russian ministers — the first of that kind since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — comes amid high tensions between Berlin and Moscow.
Earlier this month, the German government accused Russian intelligence services of having orchestrated the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at the Leipzig airport in Eastern Germany. In reaction, Germany imposed sanctions, including the closure of Russia's consulate in Bonn, to which Moscow responded with similar measures against Germany, notably the closure of Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg.
Germany and Russia also clashed during a U.N. Security Council meeting earlier this week, during which Wadephul slammed “Russia's reckless and dangerous escalation in Europe,” while Lavrov accused Europe of “criminal methods.”
The German official said that Wadephul “made clear” during Saturday's meeting “that incidents such as the recent attempted attack in Leipzig or other hybrid attacks would not shake Germany’s determination to support Ukraine, which is under attack. However, they would further damage bilateral relations with Germany, which have already been severely strained by Russia.”
The Russian side did not immediately provide a detailed readout of Saturday's meeting. Moscow's foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, instead referred to a polemic Russian report that calls into question the authenticity of the Bucha massacre, and that appears to have been put on the table during the ministers' meeting.
Advertisement
The meeting was also immediately overshadowed by different explanations over who had requested it.
Zakharova claimed that Wadephul had asked to meet Lavrov. Yet Wadephul told ZDF that he had agreed to meet Lavrov after the Russian foreign minister, through third-party intermediaries, signaled a willingness to engage in talks.
The reunion of Wadephul and Lavrov was held against the backdrop of renewed efforts by the U.S. and its Western allies to jumpstart peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this week, the U.S. government issued an invitation to Putin for the G20 summit in Miami in December, raising the possibility of potential negotiations between the Russian president and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Florida.
While some other European leaders criticized that invitation, Wadephul said he welcomed the initiative, calling it "a litmus test for Putin."
“Opportunities like this must be seized,” Wadephul said on Friday.
Wadephul had added a caveat, however, saying that, “in my view, a ceasefire is also necessary in order to be able to negotiate in earnest.”
This article was updated with Wadephul's comments to ZDF.

articles.title: Pentagon brings in Ukrainian jamming maker to do to its candidate drones what Russia does to Ukraine’s, and see which survives
articles.body:
A Ukrainian jamming-systems maker went to a US Army base to do to candidate drones what Russia does to Ukraine's: flood them with electronic warfare (EW) and see which survives. Unwave company has tested four of its EW systems at Fort Carson in Colorado as part of the Pentagon's Drone Dominance program and has been asked to continue supporting it.
The Pentagon is using Drone Dominance to choose the drones it will buy at scale, more than 200,000 by 2027, and it needs to know they work under jamming, the condition that decides most drone fights in Ukraine.
So it brought in a Ukrainian electronic-warfare maker to supply that jamming, turning Ukraine's hard-won counter-drone experience into the test bench for American hardware. It follows a pattern in which US defense efforts adopt Ukrainian battlefield models.
Ukraine brings the jamming
From 24 August to 2 September, Unwave's team worked at the base, running scenarios that pitted its jammers against drones tasked with protecting fixed positions, moving vehicles, and infrastructure.
The crews operated from three separate positionsat short and long range to compare how drones from different manufacturers held up.
"Our mission was to create conditions as close to the real battlefield as possible," the company said, adding that it judged the tasks successfully completed but could not detail the scenarios for security reasons.
In all, 14 drone makers and three electronic-warfare firms took part.
Four systems on show
Unwave brought four:
- VIHA, which it calls Ukraine's first tactical-operational jammer for directed suppression of drones
- BOOMBOX, built to shield troops and positions from FPV and drop-drones
- SHATRO, for vehicles
- CHOVEN-2, a multi-frequency amplifier for cars.
Its participation was organized by Revenant Technologies, a US firm that specializes in bringing combat-proven defense tech to the American market, and helped design the scenarios using its ties to Ukraine and frontline experience.
A foothold in the US market
For Unwave, the value is a door into the alliance's security architecture. The event showed the importance of Ukrainian, American, and European specialists testing together, the company said, and "such interaction will help integrate Ukrainian technologies into the security architecture of our allies."
Read also
- 
						
							Ukraine’s jet-drone kill rate just hit 55%. Russia’s answer: $12 billion to make more of them
- 
						
							Ukraine destroys record 76 Russian air-defense systems this month, losses analyst says Russia “will never be able to restore”
- 
						
							Asked if Ukraine would send troops to defend NATO, Zelenskyy offered something else: know-how to stop drones now reaching its neighbors

articles.title: "Only a Matter of Time": Budanov Warns of Threat to the Korean Region from Pyongyang
articles.body:
"Only a Matter of Time": Budanov Warns of Threat to the Korean Region from Pyongyang
Kyiv • UNN
The head of the Office of the President said that North Korea is learning from the war against Ukraine and has established mass production of one-way attack drones. He warned of the threat of an escalation in the region.
North Korea is using the experience of the war against Ukraine to improve its weapons and has already established mass production of single-use attack drones. Kyrylo Budanov said this in an interview with Newsforce, reports UNN.
Details
According to Budanov, North Korea supplies Russia with weapons and materials and sends its military personnel to fight directly against Ukraine. At the same time, Pyongyang is improving its own weapons based on combat experience and is adopting new types of weapons, some of which are Russian-made.
North Korea is learning from our war and arming itself. The world must see this connection while there is still time
He said that North Korea had already established mass production of single-use attack drones. In his view, the country's rapid militarization primarily indicates preparations for possible active hostilities in its own region. Budanov also mentioned a recent incident on the demarcation line between the Republic of Korea and North Korea, without specifying the circumstances.
The situation is worsening with each passing day. And it is only a matter of time before a trigger event occurs that leads to uncontrollable consequences
We remind you
A few days earlier, Pyongyang launched a short-range ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea. In response, South Korea convened an emergency meeting.

articles.title: Iran to punish Trump, Netanyahu even after war ends
articles.body:
Iran's senior armed forces spokesman, General Abolfazl Shekarchi, said the Strait of Hormuz remains under Iranian control despite American provocations, warning that no vessel can guarantee safe passage without Tehran's approval.
Speaking in a televised interview, Shekarchi reviewed the history of the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, which he said was imposed on Iran under US leadership. He said the war, despite heavy losses, helped build the capabilities of Iran's armed forces from its early days, citing popular mobilization through the Basij as a key achievement.
Shekarchi said Iran's post-revolution military shifted its doctrine from conventional to asymmetric warfare, which he described as relying on lower-cost, simpler but effective equipment to counter the enemy's expensive heavy weaponry.
He said Iran had once been unable to buy basic medical supplies for wounded troops during the Iran-Iraq war, but has since become self-sufficient in producing modern defense equipment.
Shekarchi said Iran's armed forces are now significantly stronger than at the start of previous wars, adding that Iran's missiles and drones have become more advanced and that the country holds surprises for any future act of aggression using new military technology. He said Iran has not attacked the sovereignty of neighboring Muslim countries and that its responses have targeted American interests and facilities within those countries.
He warned neighboring Muslim states to reconsider their positions, saying reliance on the United States would not serve them, and said Iran would not make the slightest retreat in the face of the enemy.
On the Strait of Hormuz, Shekarchi said any vessel attempting passage outside Iran's designated routes would not be secure, and warned Washington against any interference in the strait, saying such a move would be met with force. He said Iran, as a global power, would never allow the United States to regain its former position in the international order, adding that American forces have no path to safety other than withdrawing from West Asia, and that the sooner they leave, the smaller their losses would be.
Referring to US President Donald Trump and Israeli regime’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Shekarchi said Iran would continue to pursue the killers of the country's martyred Leader and the Iranian people even after the end of the war, adding that they would be punished for their actions.
MNA

articles.title: Energy, shipping, and ending the war — Budanov spoke about preparations for the trilateral talks in October
articles.body:
Energy, shipping, and ending the war — Budanov spoke about preparations for the trilateral talks in October
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is planning a meeting with the United States and Russia in October. They will discuss ending the war, strikes on energy infrastructure, and shipping security.
Ukraine plans to hold a trilateral meeting with the United States and Russia next month. The issues expected to be discussed include a possible end to the war, reducing strikes on energy infrastructure, and the safety of shipping, Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov said in a comment to Novyny.LIVE, as reported by UNN.
According to Budanov, the Ukrainian side is preparing for a meeting at which a number of security and technical issues are to be considered.
"First, we are planning such a meeting. Second, reducing strikes on the energy sector. Well, terrorism is abnormal in principle. Security, shipping, and so on. We have many technical issues," the Head of the Office of the President said.
He named next month—October—as the tentative timeframe for the talks. At the same time, Budanov did not specify the exact date, location of the meeting, or composition of the delegations.
The Head of the Office of the President had previously also spoken about preparations for the October round of talks. In particular, on September 12, on the sidelines of the Yalta European Strategy (YES) forum in Kyiv, he confirmed to the media that Ukraine was preparing for talks in October in a trilateral format. At the time, he did not comment on a potential location for the meeting.
The United States proposed a technical meeting in the UAE
On September 25, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the American side had proposed preparing a meeting of representatives of Ukraine, the United States, and Russia at the technical level. Washington proposed the United Arab Emirates as a possible venue. At the time of the statement, Kyiv was awaiting proposals from the United States regarding the date. According to the president, the Ukrainian and American negotiating groups had also agreed to hold consultations with the European side. After that, the United States was to establish contacts with Russia, and approximately ten days later the parties planned to return to discussing the results. This timeframe concerned the consultations, not an announced date for trilateral talks.
That same day, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that the possibility of such a meeting had been discussed during a phone call between Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. He allowed for it to take place in the near future, but did not provide any specific parameters.
What is being discussed regarding energy and shipping
The issue of a mutual cessation of strikes on energy infrastructure had already been raised during diplomatic contacts in September.
On September 14, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to support de-escalation if its American partners could ensure Russia's genuine and long-term readiness to stop the strikes. This position was voiced after Trump's statement that the parties had allegedly reached an agreement not to attack energy facilities. At the same time, as Reuters reported, neither Ukraine nor Russia confirmed that such an agreement had been concluded at the time.
A separate area is the safety of maritime transport. On September 23, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to do its part to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea, provided that Russia took genuine steps toward de-escalation.
According to the president, Egypt, India, and Turkey proposed their own options for ensuring maritime security. Ukraine supported measures capable of ensuring safe shipping and was awaiting a response from the Russian side.
Context
On September 6, American representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Zelenskyy in Kyiv after visiting Moscow. Following the meeting, the president confirmed Ukraine's readiness for trilateral talks. The parties also discussed the supply of air defense systems and support for Ukraine's energy sector ahead of winter.
We remind you
Earlier, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was looking for excuses not to meet and not to end the war.

articles.title: ‘Russian sleeper cell’: Can Germany’s far-right AfD be barred from sensitive intel?
articles.body:
‘Russian sleeper cell’: Can Germany’s far-right AfD be barred from sensitive intel?
The prospect of an AfD-led government in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt has exacerbated long-standing fears that the far-right Russia-friendly party may gain access to sensitive information of interest to the Kremlin, fuelling debate as to whether and how it can be barred from classified intelligence.
What happens when Germany’s domestic intelligence service is monitored by the very people it is meant to spy on?
The once speculative question has acquired sudden urgency – for both Germany and its allies – in the wake of a regional election that has put the German far right on the cusp of power for the first time since 1945.
The Alternative for Democracy (AfD) party scored a resounding election win in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month and is trying to form a coalition government in the small eastern state, one of 16 that enjoy broad powers under Germany’s federal system.
If it succeeds, the Moscow-friendly party could notably gain access to intelligence gathered by agencies tracking both domestic and external threats, a prospect that has spooked officials amid escalating tensions over the war in Ukraine and a surge in hybrid attacks attributed to Russia.
Watch moreOnly the beginning? German far right's breakthrough shakes Europe to its core
According to French investigative and satirical weekly Canard Enchaîné, such concerns were enough for France’s domestic intelligence agency to notify its German counterpart last week of its plans to withhold sensitive information about far-right extremists and Russia should the AfD govern in Saxony-Anhalt.
Unmasking spy cops
Germany’s domestic intelligence service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), has consistently ranked right-wing extremists as the greatest threat to German democracy. Its latest annual report, published in June, said their number had increased significantly to 58,700 last year, fuelled by a surge in support for the AfD.
The BfV stirred controversy last year when it designated the AfD as a right-wing “extremist group”, though the classification was suspended in February after a legal challenge from the party.
While the national party is now designated as “suspected extremist”, pending a court ruling, its local chapter in Saxony-Anhalt has a “confirmed extremist” label that means it is under surveillance by federal intelligence, including undercover agents.
German officials fear that an AfD government in the eastern state could use routine intelligence sharing to find those agents and scupper efforts to monitor it, said Jacob Ross, a Senior Research Fellow at the German Council on Foreign Relations.
“If the AfD gets hold of the interior minister job in charge of police forces and intelligence, they would potentially have access to files about their own surveillance,” Ross explained. “One of the big fears in the intelligence community, and more widely in German politics, is that they would then very rapidly try to find out who within their own ranks is spying on them.”
An asset for Russia
A greater concern for Germany and its allies is the possibility that sensitive information regarding German, European and NATO security arrangements might end up in Russian hands.
Before the election in Saxony-Anhalt, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius told German newspaper Bild that he opposed sharing classified information with AfD officials should they enter regional governments, stressing that their “close ties to (Russian President Vladimir) Putin are undeniable”.
The far-right party has repeatedly sparked alarm in Berlin by requesting information on vulnerabilities in German and NATO defences that would be of interest to Russia. In a heated debate at the Bundestag last November, a lawyer for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling conservatives accused the AfD of harbouring a Russian “sleeper cell” intent on investigating Germany’s critical infrastructure.
Fears of sensitive information falling in Russian hands are well founded, according to Anton Shekhovtsov, director of the Austria-based Centre for Democratic Integrity and an expert on the European far right and its links to Russia.
With Hungary’s Viktor Orban out of power, “The AfD is now the largest and strongest pro-Russian party in the entire European Union,” Shekhovtsov argued, citing “extensive links with Russia that have been built over many years”. He added: “Obviously this is a weak spot for Germany and for the EU when it comes to dealing with Moscow and the political warfare that it is waging in Europe.”
Read moreFive takeaways from Germany's regional elections after far-right gains
According to a New York Times report published on Tuesday, the German federal government has moved swiftly to allay concerns among EU allies, drafting plans to block an AfD-led state government from reviewing sensitive intelligence.
One notable measure involves denying AfD officials access to a secret war plan drafted in 2024, a 1,000-page blueprint detailing how Germany and its allies would respond to a Russian attack similar to the invasion of Ukraine. Other possible steps include withholding intelligence concerning Russian subterfuge and investigations into far-right extremists.
The Austrian precedent
There are precedents for European countries restricting access to intelligence when dealing with far-right parties that are seen as cozying up to Russia. One notable example is Orban’s Hungary, which France accused of “betraying” the EU by leaking information to Moscow, just weeks before the longtime nationalist leader was voted out of power.
Austria also came under intense scrutiny after the far-right Freedom Party joined a coalition government in 2017 and secured the interior ministry portfolio, leading some European partners to place limits on intelligence sharing.
“The perception at the time was that Austrian security and intelligence services were deeply penetrated by Russia,” said Ross. “Those in Germany who argue in favour of excluding AfD from information flows often point to the Austrian case, warning that Germany could also lose its reputation as a trustworthy ally when it comes to intelligence-sharing mechanisms.”
Placing caveats on intelligence sharing is relatively commonplace, including between close allies, said Dan Lomas, an assistant professor in International Relations at the University of Nottingham specialising in intelligence and security-related issues.
“Intelligence services that cooperate on, say, counterterrorism might seek to limit the flow of other intel when they think it could be leaked,” he explained. “They might also seek to bypass specific figures in government, sharing information with other domestic services but with the caveat that it mustn’t be passed on to certain officials.”
Such limitations could pose logistical challenges should AfD continue its ascent at the regional level, warned Ross, pointing to the specificities of Germany’s federal system. Just days after triumphing in Saxony-Anhalt, the party also topped elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, underscoring its dominance in swaths of the country.
In the event of a major crisis, “keeping AfD-run states in the dark could create holes in operational plans”, he said. “Because while the army and the defence of German territory are within the purview of the federal government, the police forces needed to secure roads, convoys and power stations are the responsibility of individual states.”
Breach of trust
Another long-term problem, added Lomas, is that such limitations breed mistrust between security services, elected officials and the broader public, while also posing problems of democracy.
“Even if you find a practical way to work around the AfD, doing this is corrosive at a time when public trust in liberal Western democracies is already under threat,” he said.
Read moreHow far-right AfD breakthrough may ‘cause absolute chaos’ in Germany
Efforts to restrict far-right access to state secrets could lead to legal challenges from AfD, which argues that the country’s mainstream parties are undermining democracy by thwarting the will of voters.
Jork Herrmann, an AfD spokesman, told the New York Times, “It would be utterly undemocratic and impossible to justify to voters to withhold intelligence information from the party based on unsubstantiated and unprovable allegations.”
If the courts agree with Germany’s domestic intelligence agency and confirm AfD as an “extremist” organisation that poses a danger to the constitution, that would give the federal government “legitimate grounds not to share sensitive information”, said Shekhovtsov. But if they don’t, he added, “it’s hard to see on what grounds they could be kept in the dark.”
The conundrum facing German officials underscores the limitations of the “firewall” strategy aimed at keeping the far right out of power, argued Ross. He contrasted that approach with French President Emmanuel Macron’s decision last week to convene all major parties – including Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party, which is polling well ahead of rivals ahead of elections next year – for an intelligence briefing on the threat of hybrid attacks from Russia.
“Macron seems to think it’s best to brief the National Rally rather than have pro-Russian experts do so,” he said. “In Germany, we’re counting on the firewall to hold firm. But if it doesn’t, then we have a huge problem.”

articles.title: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
articles.body:
Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”.
“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”
Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”
Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically admonish that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”.
“There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures.
Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale.
His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods.
Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI.
Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday.
The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote.
Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later.
An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014.
Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity.
In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’”
Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’
“So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”

articles.title: Lavrov slams Germany despite meeting counterpart
articles.body:
AP Photo
Russia’s top diplomat rejected German calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” toward the country, instead accusing Germany of being Ukraine’s main sponsor and seeking to be a leading military power in Europe.
“Does Berlin understand what this could lead to?’ Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov asked in his speech at the U.N. General Assembly’s annual gathering of world leaders. “Didn’t they not learn the lessons of World War II?”
Lavrov was dismissive after the German and Russian foreign ministers met on Sept. 26 on the sidelines of the meeting, holding what’s believed to be the first such tête-à-tête since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“He simply reiterated his official public position condemning Russia,” Lavrov said. “You can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not.”
The meeting, at German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s request, came just before Lavrov addressed world leaders, where he also criticized the militarization of Japan. He made clear that Russia will veto any attempt by Germany and Japan for permanent seats on the Security Council, the U.N.’s most powerful body. The two nations fought Russia, Britain and the United States in World War II.
A German delegation official said that during their meeting, Wadephul called on Russia to abandon its “dangerous path of escalation” toward Germany, Europe and the NATO alliance. Ties between Russia and Germany have soured in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack last month at Leipzig airport, Germany has blamed the incident on Russia, and tit-for-tat responses that followed it.
Wadephul expressed openness to a better relationship but said it required a genuine willingness from Russia’s leadership to end the war in Ukraine, according to the official.
Later, Lavrov told a U.N. news conference that “nothing new came from that initiative of the foreign minister.”
He challenged Germany to name one commercial vessel in the Black Sea that was damaged or targeted by Russian strikes, asserting that “there are no such cases.” As for the claimed attempted drone strike at Leipzig Airport, he called it “an unclaimed drone” that Germany immediately said was Russian.
Lavrov denounced the West in his speech and at the press conference, saying it “aspires to inflict strategic defeat on Russia, but these aspirations will result in the war mongers being led into a strategic dead end.”
He recalled last year’s 80th anniversary of the Allied victory “over German Nazism and Japanese militarism” in World War II. And he made a point of blasting the notion of Germany or Japan gaining a permanent seat on the powerful U.N. Security Council. The United States has long supported permanent seats for those countries and India.
In his attacks on the West, Lavrov also said, “the U.S. has destroyed the European security system and created a Russophobic regime in Kiev.”
Russia believes an agreement on ending the Ukraine war was reached at the August 2025 meeting in Alaska between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Lavrov said, “and we continue to remain ready to return to it.”
“A fairer, multipolar world order is emerging before our very eyes,” said Lavrov, whose country is part of the BRICS group of leading developing nations and other organizations that he portrays as more forward-looking and constructive.

articles.title: Swiss neutrality and food security initiatives suffer hefty defeat
articles.body:
Swiss neutrality and food security initiatives suffer hefty defeat
Swiss voters want no big overhaul of neutrality policy: a proposal for a stricter constitutional definition is heading for resounding defeat. An initiative to boost domestic food production has also been soundly rejected. Final results will follow later this afternoon.
Is Switzerland neutral enough? For most citizens, the answer is clearly yes: after polls closed Sunday, projections by the gfs.bern research institute indicated that around 70% are set to reject the “neutrality initiative”, which proposed a strict constitutional definition of it. The extent of the rejection is even heftier than opinion polls had predicted.
Lukas Golder, co-director of gfs.bern, told Swiss public broadcaster SRF on Sunday that voters had not rejected neutrality, but opted for a more “nuanced” version of it – including sanctions, concretely against Russia. A majority clearly believe neutrality should leave “room for manoeuvre to politicians and the government”, rather than being permanently pinned down, he added.
The initiative, launched by the pro-sovereignty association Pro Schweiz, crystallised debates about neutrality sparked by Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine – and, in particular, Bern’s subsequent mirroring of European Union (EU) sanctions on Moscow.
Claiming this watered down the country’s traditional stance, and served neither Swiss interests nor international peace, the proposal wanted no more such sanctions in future – unless approved by the UN Security Council. Its definition of a “perpetual and armed” neutrality would also have reduced cooperation with military alliances like NATO, except in case of imminent war.
>> Less flexibility, more clarity? Read more about what the neutrality initiative aimed to achieve:
More
Should Swiss neutrality be stricter? Voters will decide
How much cooperation is too much?
On Sunday, Centre Party Senator Marianne Binder-Keller told SRF that the initiative would have led Switzerland into “total isolation” at a time of new security challenges. The result is a signal that the country is “part of the Western, rules-based security architecture, is a partner for cooperation, and participates in sanctions” in cases where international law is breached. Such a stance also serves Swiss security interests, she claimed.
But for Stephan Rietiker, president of Pro Schweiz, the key question is how far such “cooperation” stretches. “Does it mean integration into the military structures of NATO, or does it mean preparations in case of a possible attack?” he told SRF. The initiative would still have allowed room for the latter, he claimed – but it struggled to get this message across.
Indeed, despite ample funding – including from billionaire and former government minister Christoph Blocher – polls early in the campaign made it clear the initiative was fighting an uphill battle. While it had some backers on the pacifist left, just one big political group, the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, was in favour. All other parties and the government rallied around the status quo: a neutrality that respects the Hague ConventionsExternal link while allowing flexible responses to geopolitical changes – including sanctions. They also denied the country had shifted course. “Switzerland was neutral, is neutral, and will remain neutral”, Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said several times in the campaign.
The initiative also struggled to attract support with imagery based around a dove and the “give peace a chance” slogan – Switzerland, its argument claimed, could do more good with its diplomatic mediation than with sanctions against warring states. Opponents countered that the initiative was “pro-Putin”, and that ultra-strict neutrality can end up helping the aggressor – an argument helped when the Kremlin itself spoke out in favour of the proposal.
Ultimately, if defeat for the initiative doesn’t mean an end to Swiss neutrality, it doesn’t mean an end to debates about it either. Bern will remain out of conflicts – and out of military alliances – but still faces questions about its place at the heart of a rearming Europe, and how much cooperation it wants with NATO and its neighbours. Swiss voters will soon tackle similar questions: in November, a referendum is scheduled on a proposed easing of the country’s weapons’ export rules.
More
Food security fares even worse
As predicted by the polls, the food security initiative – which aims to boost Switzerland’s self-sufficiency in food production – is also heading for clear rejection. According to latest gfs.bern projections, around 72% of voters came out against it on Sunday, with a very clear “no” vote across the whole country.
Although the issues raised could certainly have garnered majority support, Golder told SRF that the initiative had sought to achieve too much too quickly. For her part, Franziska Herren, who led the initiative, told SRF that “we did nothing wrong”. She added that it had been “surreal”, to say the least, to see how the entire political establishment had opposed the initiative. Herren warned that despite the result the problems relating to water resources and agriculture in the context of climate change still remain as before.
“The public did not want to be deprived of the freedom to choose for themselves what they ate,” said Petra Gössi, a representative of the opposing camp. According to Gössi, a centre-right politician from the Radical Liberal Party, Swiss agricultural policy still remained an issue, but the market also played a part in determining it and condemning meat was not a viable option.
Anne Challandes, vice-president of the powerful Swiss Farmers’ Union, was pleased with the clear result. “This is a show of support for farming families,” she said.
Largely overshadowed by the debates around the neutrality initiative, the proposal failed to gather any steam during the campaign. In theory, it should have received more support from farmers as it aimed to boost Swiss self-sufficiency in food production from 46% to 70% in a decade by promoting the domestic cultivation and consumption of plant-based food. Instead, the farming community perceived it as an existential threat due to fears that it would affect meat and dairy consumption.
With a campaign budget of CHF1.63 million ($1.96 million), the ‘no’ camp comprising associations representing the meat and dairy industries, as well as the Swiss Farmers’ Union, attempted to take the wind out of the sails of the food security initiative (budget CHF720,000) quite early in the campaign. They framed the issue as a “vegan diktat” telling people what they should eat, even though the initiative text does not prescribe a specific diet or call for any restrictions on meat production. To make matters worse, no political party besides the Young Greens backed the initiative and even environmental organisations like Greenpeace and WWF did not endorse it.
>> Switzerland may not be ready for more plant-based fare but other places are:
More
Dutch cities are banning meat advertising – will Switzerland follow?
The result proves that the farming lobby is still a formidable opponent in Swiss politics, especially without the support of the political left and Greens. Like previous attempts to make Swiss farming more sustainable, the food security initiative faced an uphill task to win over voters. Most of all, it had a fatal flaw that sank similar initiatives like the pesticide ban initiative and the drinking water initiative in 2021, as well as the biodiversity initiative of 2024: good intentions but too ambitious.

articles.title: Men arrested in major incident at UK air base used by US
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Men arrested on explosives offences in major incident at UK air base used by US
British police said on Sunday they had arrested several men on suspicion of explosives offences and Army bomb disposal experts were examining a number of vehicles in a "major incident" near an air base used by the US in southwest England.
Police said nearby residents had been evacuated from their homes.
The British government gave authorisation to the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned in July that any base used in strikes would be a legitimate target.
A Reuters eyewitness said armed police had blocked access to the main gate of the base, while equipment had been positioned in front of access points and residents of a nearby village were evacuated to a leisure centre.
Around 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were stationed in the village of Fairford near the base.
"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident. It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act," Gloucestershire police said in a statement, referring to a village near the air base.
"The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles."
Police said they believed the incident was now contained.
A spokesperson for the US Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families," the spokesperson said.
"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families."
Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned the UK not to allow US bombers to fly from Fairford.
British ministers have also briefed providers of critical infrastructure on the threat posed by Russia, with the government increasingly concerned about possible sabotage operations and cyberattacks. Russia denies mounting hybrid attacks on Western nations.
(Reuters)

articles.title: Latvia moves to buy American long-range strike missiles
articles.body:
Latvia is moving to acquire Anduril Industries’ Barracuda family of long-range cruise missiles, a purchase that would make it the first Baltic state to field a strike weapon of that reach, following a visit by President Edgars Rinkēvičs to the American company’s California facilities on 25 September, the president stated in a post published after the visit.
Writing on X, Mr Rinkēvičs said: “It was great to visit Anduril to meet with Palmer Luckey and to witness signing of memoranda of cooperation with MOD of Latvia and Origin Robotics. Looking forward to complete acquisition of Barracuda long-range missiles and Latvian-US defense industry cooperation.”
Neither Latvia nor Anduril has disclosed which variant is wanted, how many missiles would be bought, the price or a delivery date.
The Barracuda-500M, the long-range member of the family, has a range of more than 500 nautical miles, or around 926 kilometres, which is roughly three times the reach of the ATACMS rounds Latvia has ordered for its HIMARS launchers. Given that the country operates no fast jets and has a limited helicopter fleet, a ground-launched configuration would be the obvious route for it to take.
Anduril offers the family as an answer to a shortfall in affordable, producible long-range precision weapons, claiming it requires half the production time, 95 per cent fewer tools and half the parts of comparable weapons. The variants can operate autonomously and collaboratively with one another, acting as decoys as well as conducting strikes, and can be launched from fighters, helicopters, cargo aircraft, ships and ground launchers.
Production is already being scaled up on both sides of the Atlantic. The American Department of War signed a framework agreement in May for at least 1,000 surface-launched Barracuda-500Ms a year over three years for the United States Army, starting in 2027, and in July the Polish state group PGZ agreed to assemble and later produce the same variant at its Military Aviation Works No. 2 plant at Bydgoszcz. PGZ has said European production could make the missile eligible for purchase by other EU member states under the bloc’s SAFE defence loan programme.
The second agreement signed during the visit concerns counter-drone work, and under it Origin Robotics, based in Riga, is to integrate its BLAZE autonomous interceptor into Anduril’s Lattice command and control system, giving a layered counter-uncrewed aircraft capability for Latvia and NATO’s eastern flank. BLAZE is a briefcase-sized interceptor using radar and camera guidance, while the company’s BEAK drone is already in service with Ukrainian forces.
Latvia has not said whether any Barracuda production, assembly or other industrial work would be carried out in the country however, though its Investment and Development Agency says the defence technology delegation now in the United States is seeking opportunities covering joint development, testing, manufacturing, system integration and supply chains.

articles.title: Poland wants a Patriot plant and a permanent U.S. military base - media
articles.body:
Poland wants a Patriot plant and a permanent U.S. military base - media
Kyiv • UNN
Poland has proposed establishing a U.S.-licensed Patriot missile plant. The country is also preparing legislation to accelerate the construction of a U.S. base.
Poland has proposed locating on its territory a plant producing missiles for Patriot air defense systems, if Ukraine receives the relevant license from the United States. This is reported by rmf24.pl, according to UNN.
Details
Deputy Minister of National Defense Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka noted that a special law would be adopted to accelerate the construction of a permanent U.S. military base in Poland.
She added that such a base could be located in western Poland, and that two possible locations are being considered.
Everything indicates that the Americans will not make a decision before the completion of the so-called strategic review initiated by Pete Hegseth. A report on the presence of Americans in Europe is currently being prepared. This report is to reach Secretary Hegseth's desk on November 1, and then President Trump's desk on December 1, and it is likely that only after that date can we expect a final decision
Responding to a question about the location of the base, she said that there are currently two proposals and that negotiations with the Americans are ongoing.
The American side has reviewed the locations we proposed and shared its assessment of these sites with us in Washington, and on this basis we will continue our work
The deputy minister also noted that the base could be located in western Poland, as this region "is considered by the Americans to be a safer place."
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka added that Poland's efforts to establish a service center and, subsequently, produce "Patriot" missiles are a process independent of Ukraine.
My interlocutors in Washington confirmed that even if such a decision is made regarding Ukraine, this will not change our efforts and will not cancel the approval for Poland
We remind you
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski stated that Ukraine had destroyed 30–40% of Russia's oil-refining capacity.

articles.title: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
articles.body:
The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages.
“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.
Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”
Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.
This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians.
The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted.
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.
In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.
He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.”
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.
Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.
Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.
In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.
“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”
On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.
Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.
Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far.
“Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation.
“Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.”
He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.”
According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.
“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.
“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”
Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.
“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.
Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.
Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.”
She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”
In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”
Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.
“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”

articles.title: Andriy Rizol on How Cultural Diplomacy Advances Ukraine’s Interests
articles.body:
The Watch Ukrainian Association has organized more than 800 cultural events in 268 cities across 55 countries since March 2022, according to the organization. Its activities range from film screenings and photo exhibitions to concerts, lectures and international tours by Ukrainian artists.
The association says its projects, organized with partners and without state funding, have raised about Hr. 16 million for Ukraine’s armed forces, military intelligence and the rehabilitation of service members. It has held events at the Council of Europe, European Parliament, European External Action Service, UNESCO, US Congress, UN, UK Parliament and OSCE headquarters.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Its key initiatives include the CinemAid Film Marathon, Culture vs War, The Will to Win and Empowered. In 2024, Culture vs War became the umbrella brand for its cultural diplomacy projects.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Andriy Rizol, a producer and chairman of the association’s board, spoke to Kyiv Post about how culture can communicate Ukraine’s experience of war and build support abroad. Rizol is also CEO of Babylon and an honorary ambassador of Ukraine for cultural diplomacy.
What Germany’s Wingcopter 262 Means for Ukraine’s Drone War
“Be free to create”
Kyiv Post: How did Watch Ukrainian begin focusing on international cultural diplomacy?
Andriy Rizol: When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, we realized immediately that we had to act. On the fifth day of the war, we launched the CinemAid Charity Film Marathon. It brought together more than 70 events in 15 countries and helped us build a network of coordinators around the world while raising funds for the Armed Forces.
In April 2022, we launched the Culture vs War multimedia project. It combined documentaries, photo exhibitions and art books, with Ukrainian artists as protagonists.
We believed that international trust in artists was often higher than trust in politicians or the military — especially when artists were directly involved in the war. We wanted to tell the world about Russia’s war through their personal stories of resistance and their experiences.
What is the main message you want international audiences to take away?
Our slogan is “Be Free to Create.”
Ukrainians want victory, but we also need to explain why. We are fighting to preserve our freedom to create and to shape our own future.
The stories of our protagonists demonstrate this in different ways: members of the band Antytila through their service in a medical unit; Taras Kompanichenko through his moral support for the Armed Forces; Serhii Zhadan through his ability to inspire; and the first artists who volunteered to defend Ukraine, including Akhtem Seitablaiev, Serhii Mykhalchuk, Yaroslav Pilunskyi and Dmytro Linartovych.
How do you choose the protagonists?
The first criterion is a shared worldview. We look for prominent people who are known in Ukraine and internationally and who can serve as moral reference points.
But they cannot simply be made to speak from a script. Their stories have to reflect their genuine personal experience of the war.
This approach resulted in four feature-length documentaries, “Culture vs War,” “Palyanytsia,” “Empowered” and “Veterans’ Theater,” as well as seven short films focusing on individual artists.
Working with the government
How do you cooperate with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?
We began our dialogue with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs early in the full-scale war. It has always been based on equal partnership, and in some cases representatives of our organization also assist the MFA.
I have known Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha since his time as ambassador to Turkey, when we organized Ukrainian Film Days there. We have warm professional relations, and he understands the role culture can play in diplomacy.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Tetiana Sybiha has revitalized and brought together the Association of Wives of Ukrainian Diplomats, supporting humanitarian, cultural and charitable projects involving diplomatic and civic communities.
We also cooperate with the Diplomatic Academy of Ukraine and its head, Ihor Ostash, who has extensive diplomatic experience and a strong interest in culture and art. Together, we work with young diplomats on public and cultural diplomacy.
In August, we launched the School of Cultural Diplomacy together with the Institute for National Resilience and Security and the Diplomatic Academy. Its purpose is to strengthen joint efforts by increasing the expertise of professional diplomats.
We are gradually building an ecosystem that includes the MFA, diplomatic missions, the Association of Wives of Ukrainian Diplomats, the Diplomatic Academy and independent cultural institutions. The goal is to move from parallel efforts toward a coordinated system.
At the same time, Ukraine needs broader consolidation of cultural figures, specialized institutions, government and business to develop a comprehensive global cultural diplomacy strategy.
In 2024, the MFA granted me the status of Honorary Ambassador of Ukraine for Cultural Diplomacy. This has led to invitations to conferences, working meetings and panels where I can share our experience and develop joint initiatives.
Our goal is to make cultural diplomacy a priority and culture a national security priority.
For us, cultural diplomacy is not soft power. It is an effective tool for advancing Ukraine’s national interests and strengthening Ukraine’s ability to act internationally. In principle, it is an effective weapon.
That is why we focus on major political platforms and authoritative institutions capable of influencing decisions on support for Ukraine.
Why has the Veterans’ Theater resonated so strongly?
                                                                                                                                                                         
The idea emerged during a creative session of the Watch Ukrainian Association in April 2024. It was proposed by director, actor and civic activist Akhtem Seitablaiev.
We saw the project as a possible form of therapy through culture. At the same time, communicating the reality of the war to international audiences was becoming increasingly difficult as war fatigue grew.
We therefore created an art project that combined a stage production with a documentary featuring veterans as protagonists. It speaks about the war and its real consequences without necessarily putting the war itself “in the frame.”
The flagship production is “Eneida,” directed by Olha Semyoshkina, with Akhtem Seitablaiev as artistic director. It has attracted significant interest both in Ukraine and abroad.
The documentary “Veterans’ Theater” was screened in 19 countries as part of the Empowered UA film marathon.
For us, however, the motivation goes beyond the success of a particular project. We want to create trends, influence public discussion and help address real challenges.
Cultural diplomacy is essential to Ukraine’s future
What should Ukraine’s cultural presence in the world look like by 2030?
There are still remnants of an inferiority complex in Ukrainian society, but the situation has changed fundamentally.
Ukraine now has unique experience and significant achievements in military technologies, unmanned systems, IT, medicine, banking, logistics, e-document management, public services and volunteer practices, as well as in creative industries, documentary filmmaking, contemporary music and art. No other country has exactly the same experience.
Our next film is titled “Novators,” or “Innovators.”
By 2030, I want Ukraine to be respected and understood as a reliable and desirable partner of the democratic world. Cultural diplomacy can contribute to this.
We also need to change our perspective. We should not only learn from the world; we should also show what the world can learn from Ukraine.
That is the idea behind Empowered. We should no longer portray Ukrainians only as people who are poor, deprived or exhausted. We should show Ukrainians creating solutions, products, technologies, ideas and cultural phenomena that can be useful and interesting to the world.
The Empowered project was initiated by Watch Ukrainian with the support of the European Union and the MHP-Hromadi Foundation. It continues and develops the Culture vs War approach, seeking to strengthen the image of modern Ukraine as a strong country of talented people capable of enriching civilization across different areas of life.
We communicate this message through the personal stories of our protagonists.
I believe in large, ambitious, systemic and consolidated projects that produce concrete results. We simply do not have time for hesitation or delay.
