articles.title: Russia's strike near Poland put Ukraine's railway lifeline in focus. But the bigger threat lies elsewhere
articles.body:
Russia's strike near Poland put Ukraine's railway lifeline in focus. But the bigger threat lies elsewhere
Passengers board their train after being evacuated due to an air raid alert near the border with Poland in Ukraine on Sept. 18, 2026. (Ania Tsoukanova / AFP via Getty Images)
On Sept. 13, a Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers from the Polish border. The attack near Yahodyn caused no casualties, but it drew attention to one of Ukraine's most important links to the outside world amid the pressures of Russia's war — the railway.
Ukrainian state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said its monitoring team detected the threat early enough to evacuate the crew before the strike on the locomotive.
Russia has targeted Ukraine's railway throughout the full-scale invasion, but the intensity of attacks has risen sharply over 2026. At the same time, Ukraine increasingly depends on the railway for passengers, trade, diplomacy, and wartime logistics.
"The first goal is to disrupt logistics, both passenger traffic and the movement of goods," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told the Kyiv Independent.
"The second follows from that — weakening the economy, disrupting transport links with neighboring countries. Intimidating our partners may also be one of their goals."
While Moscow is unlikely to erode international support for Ukraine, he said, the immediate impact on transportation and trade is more serious.
read also
A lifeline
Ukraine historically developed around an extensive railway network, making it far more heavily dependent on rail than most European countries. Its road infrastructure, meanwhile, remains less developed.
Around 60% of the country's freight is transported by rail, and trains account for about 37% of domestic and international passenger transportation, according to Serhiy Vovk, director of the Centre for Transport Strategies.
In many European countries, he said, rail typically accounts for around 10% to 20% of passenger and freight transport.
"A passenger train may arrive six hours late after an attack, while five or six freight trains behind it can remain waiting for hours for capacity to reopen."
The dependence is even greater in foreign trade. About half of Ukrainian exports move by rail, Vovk estimates. For products such as iron ore, metals, and some agricultural goods, moving comparable volumes by road would be prohibitively expensive and place enormous pressure on highways.
Pressure on the railway could grow further if stable operations at Ukraine's Black Sea ports are not restored after another sustained Russian bombing campaign.
"If the issue of stable port operations is not resolved by November or December, domestic storage facilities may remain filled with grain and processed agricultural products that need to be exported," Vovk said.
The railway also became the backbone of Ukraine's "iron diplomacy," carrying foreign leaders and officials between the western border and Kyiv after the airspace closed in 2022.
Passengers increasingly feel the growing pressure on the railway. An attack hundreds of kilometers away can disrupt schedules for hours, and Russia's growing use of drones against trains and railway infrastructure means evacuations or emergency stops can become necessary along the route at any time.
But these visible delays are only one part of a wider disruption that can ripple through the network. Passenger trains operate on fixed schedules and are generally prioritized, while freight trains only move when capacity becomes available.
"A passenger train may arrive six hours late after an attack, while five or six freight trains behind it can remain waiting for hours for capacity to reopen. So the passenger sees the delay. But the larger hidden impact is felt by businesses and the economy," Vovk said.
read also
Real bottlenecks
Vovk does not see attacks on border crossings alone as a strategy capable of cutting Ukraine off from Europe. Western Ukraine has a relatively extensive railway network, so traffic can be rerouted when a route or junction is damaged.
But since the start of the full-scale invasion, Russian attacks have damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives, according to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. More than half were hit this year alone.
"Without enough locomotives, the entire system can … grind to a halt."
Replacing the locomotives is difficult. Ukraine uses a 1,520-millimeter rail gauge, meaning most European locomotives cannot simply be transferred into service, and available compatible stocks abroad are limited.
"Without enough locomotives, the entire system can … grind to a halt," Vovk said.
Amid migration, mobilization, and losses among railway workers, Ukraine is also short of about 10% of the locomotive crews it needs, he said. Unlike a damaged track, that shortage cannot be fixed quickly.
"You cannot train a qualified driver in a year," Vovk said.
read also
A winter stress test
New rules allowing trains to continue operating under lower-level air threats rather than automatically stopping came into effect on Sept. 18. Under the highest threat level, boarding and disembarkation are suspended while passengers and staff move to shelters.
Decisions on trains already in motion are made on a case by case basis, using information from Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring teams.
The company is also dispersing rolling stock and passenger flows, developing protected facilities for workers and passengers at major junctions, and exploring greater use of electronic warfare systems.
With winter approaching, preparedness becomes more urgent.
"A train that stops for hours in an open area in summer is an inconvenience. In freezing temperatures, particularly with children or elderly passengers on board, it can become a safety problem," Vovk said.
Protocols may increasingly need to ensure that trains stop near stations or populated areas where passengers can access shelter, electricity, and heat, he said.
Besides protecting tracks and stations under constant Russian threat across the country, Ukraine also needs to restore and procure locomotives, train new personnel, and build reserves.
"Otherwise, when passenger and freight volumes increase, the problem may no longer be whether the tracks are available, but whether there are enough locomotives — and enough people — to keep trains moving," Vovk said.

articles.title: Saudi mufti tells troops prepare to give lives in Yemen war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi grand mufti tells troops to prepare to give lives in fight against Houthis
Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti Saleh bin Fawzan al-Fawzan has exhorted the coalition forces fighting against Yemen's Houthis to be ready to sacrifice their lives in the conflict, the Saudi Press Agency reported on Friday.
Addressing soldiers on the frontlines of the conflict and in stationed along the country's borders, the mufti's statement comes as Yemen slides further back into civil war, with the Houthis advancing on government-held territory.
The Iran-backed group have also launched barrages of drones and missiles towards Saudi Arabia.
Al-Fawzan cited verses of the Quran and the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad praising the status of those who stand watch on the borders, and said that protecting the land housing Islam's two holiest sites is "among the greatest duties and the best acts of devotion, for which lives and souls are sacrificed in pursuit of God's pleasure".
The mufti also slammed the Houthis - a predominantly Zaydi Shia movement - as having founded their cause on "corruption of belief and corruption of methodology".
"They rebelled against their rulers, engaging in successive acts of sedition for many years. They have divided the land and its people, so stand united against this misguided sect and deviant group that declares the Prophet's companions to be infidels, deems the blood of Muslims permissible to shed, and violates their mosques by demolishing annd destroying them," al-Fawzan said.
Fighting has reignited between Yemen's internationally recognised government, backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Houthis, after four years of relative calm.
Earlier this month, the Houthis seized Yemen's key port city of Mokha and the islands on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, improving their surveillance of passing ships.
On Saturday, Saudi military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said that a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed group was intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Maliki said the missile was fired toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
The Gulf Cooperation Council, condemned the latest Houthi attacks as a “grave escalation and threat to regional security” and urged the international community to respond.

articles.title: Iran Army spokesperson claims United States could attack again due to bad regional situation
articles.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Sunday it had seized a US Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle operating in the Strait of Hormuz, which it said was conducting espionage, according to state media.
The IRGC said the vehicle had been captured using intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities and was being examined by Iranian specialists to recover its data.
The US could launch a renewed attack on Iran due to its bad regional situation, Iran's Army Spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia also said on Sunday, according to state media, adding that his country is ready for confrontation and to inflict greater damage on the US.
Akraminia said Iran's armed forces were fully prepared for confrontation and warned that the US would suffer greater damage if it launched another attack on his country.
Iran Commander-in-Chief says war at decisive stage
Separately, Iranian Army Commander-in-Chief Amir Hatami said the war was at a critical and decisive stage, adding that Tehran would not accept a situation in which it was unable to trade while foreign powers used the region's strategic waterways.
"If Iran cannot trade, if Iran cannot live, no one will be able to trade or live. The Strait of Hormuz is the strait of our dignity and honor, and it will not be allowed for the country's enemies to use this major logistical chokepoint while the Iranian people are deprived.”

articles.title: Netanyahu faces his nightmare at UN: The Soleimani portrait in Iran’s empty seat
articles.body:
Netanyahu faces his nightmare at UN: The Soleimani portrait in Iran’s empty seat
TEHRAN — Benjamin Netanyahu arrived at the United Nations determined to turn the General Assembly into a stage for Israel’s military narrative.
But behind the speeches and threats was a more striking image: the portrait of Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani sitting on the desk of the absent Iranian delegation.
Netanyahu, the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, was permitted to enter the United States and address the world’s foremost international body without arrest. The war criminal spoke as if international accountability were a concept reserved for others.
As he began speaking, dozens of delegations rose from their seats and walked out. Israeli officials counted 77 delegations as absent or having walked out — nearly 40 percent of the UN’s 193 member states.
Netanyahu brought a pager to the UN podium—a device now associated with Israel’s September 2024 operation, when thousands of pagers exploded in Lebanon, killing many and wounding more than 3,000, including civilians.
And the symbolism did not stop there. Netanyahu had also presented Donald Trump with a pager, turning a device associated with the deadly operation into a political prop shared with the U.S. president. Then, standing before the world, Netanyahu raised one at the UN and issued threats. The message was stark: a device associated with bloodshed had been transformed into a symbol of defiance on the world’s diplomatic stage.
At the institution created in the name of international peace, the Israeli leader chose to display technology associated with a mass-casualty operation as a symbol of military achievement.
He insulted delegations that had walked out, calling them “moral cowards.” He celebrated Israel’s military actions, repeated lies about the war in Gaza, defended the occupation of Palestinian and Syrian territories, and labeled human rights defenders as “antisemites.”
He also claimed the bombardment of Iran’s nuclear facilities was one of the easiest decisions he had made as prime minister.
But there was another object in the room.
On the Iranian delegation’s desk, where diplomats should have been seated, a portrait sat quietly: the face of Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani — Iran’s commander assassinated in a U.S. drone attack in Baghdad in January 2020 — watching over the empty chairs.
That photograph carried a message of its own.
Netanyahu displayed the weaponized technology associated with Israel’s war of atrocities. Iran left behind the face of a commander whose death was supposed to demonstrate the reach of American power.
Washington and Tel Aviv believed that assassinating Soleimani would eliminate a major figure of the resistance. They believed that removing a man from the battlefield would weaken the cause he represented. Years later, his portrait remains capable of transforming an empty diplomatic desk into a political statement.
For Iran, Soleimani remains an embodiment of the resistance strategy that challenged American and Israeli influence across West Asia. For Israel and the United States, he represented a major adversary. His assassination did not eliminate an individual; it became another chapter in the confrontation between Iran and the American-Israeli security order in the region.
The legal dimension of Netanyahu’s appearance was equally difficult to ignore.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former war minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024. The ICC said there were reasonable grounds to believe they bore criminal responsibility for acts including starvation as a method of warfare, murder, persecution, other inhumane acts and intentionally directing attacks against civilians.
The United States, which presents itself as a guardian of a rules-based international order, has meanwhile challenged the authority of the very institution that issued the warrants.
Trump called on ICC member states to withdraw from the court during his UN address, while his administration has pursued measures against the ICC. Washington’s campaign has targeted an institution that has acted against Israeli officials and investigated U.S. conduct in Afghanistan.
This is the contradiction at the heart of the so-called rules-based order: when an international court takes action against a close American ally, Washington moves against the court itself. When Israel faces allegations of war crimes, the United States provides diplomatic and political protection. When Iran defends its sovereignty, it is portrayed as the aggressor.
Iran’s representative, Nasser Asadi, delivered a forceful response at the UN, criticizing the decision to give Netanyahu a platform while Palestinians are denied one. He condemned Israel’s actions, criticized U.S. support for Israel and rejected the narrative presented by Netanyahu.
He closed with a direct warning: “Any further act of aggression against our sovereignty, territorial integrity, or national interests will be met with a decisive and devastating response.”
This is where the Soleimani portrait acquires its deeper meaning.
Washington and Tel Aviv repeatedly kill commanders, destroy infrastructure and launch attacks beyond their own borders. But military superiority does not automatically produce political surrender. The continued resonance of Soleimani’s image illustrates the limits of that assumption.
Netanyahu can stand at the UN podium and declare victory. He can display a pager and recount battlefield achievements. But he cannot decide what the region remembers.
Washington can pressure international institutions, deliver advanced weapons to Israel and blindly provide political and diplomatic protection for it. But Iran continues to deliver its own message. General Soleimani remains a powerful symbol of resistance to Israel and the U.S. His portrait remained while Netanyahu spoke to empty seats.
That is perhaps the most striking image of Netanyahu’s UN appearance: while the war criminal spoke, General Soleimani — the immortalized and unforgettable figure— was still sitting in the room.
Israel cannot kill an idea. America cannot bomb a memory. The resistance runs in our blood, and no pager, drone or speech at the United Nations can extinguish it.
The Zionists have weapons. The Americans have their veto. But Iran has its martyrs — and martyrs never die.

articles.title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to end war and reopen Hormuz
Tehran says it is awaiting an official response through mediators and that it will not back down from its conditions.
Araghchi ignores Trump, waits for mediators’ response on Hormuz
United States President Donald Trump has rejected a plan submitted by Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, as Tehran continued to insist that only diplomacy can solve the conflict between the two countries.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said on Saturday that Iran wants to make a deal to open the vital maritime corridor immediately only “because they are losing so badly”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Pezeshkian says Iran ‘no longer trusts talks with Washington’
- list 2 of 3US official claims Trump holds all the cards in Iran talks
- list 3 of 3Trump ‘rejects’ Iran’s seven-day ceasefire proposal. What’s next?
“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine. I’d like to make a deal, too,” he said. But the proposal put forth by Iran “would not be acceptable,” he said.
The plan by Iran, announced on Friday at the United Nations General Assembly, calls for the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift oil sanctions and end its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, said at the time that those steps could be completed within four or five days, clearing the way for the strait to reopen and for negotiations on a final agreement to begin by the seventh day.
Araghchi responded to Trump’s rejection in a post on his Telegram channel on Saturday, saying Iran “will not back down” on its conditions.
“We have seen the first reaction from the US president, but nothing has been conveyed to us from the mediators yet,” Araghchi wrote, adding that Trump had a history of making “contradictory” statements.
He said Iran was “waiting for the definitive opinions to be conveyed to us by the mediators” and would “make a decision based on that”. He added that “only a negotiated solution” can get the US “out of this deadlock”.
‘Never-ending war’
US officials had signalled on Friday that Trump would reject the proposal. The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed US officials, reported that Trump was “privately sceptical” that Tehran would meet his demands. He reportedly told aides that he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the US midterm elections in November.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said the Iranian proposal appears “dead in the water”. But he noted Trump has offered no alternative.
“The one thing that has been made clear by President Trump is that he is content to stay in the status of limbo,” Hanna said, “despite concerns from much of the American public that the Iran conflict is turning into another ‘never-ending war’.”
Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway critical to global oil supplies, shortly after the US and Israel launched their war on February 28. Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway have since sharply curtailed shipping.
The US has responded with an economic blockade on Iran and threats of secondary sanctions against airports and companies doing business with Iranian airlines – measures that have already prompted the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Oman to cancel flights.
Earlier in the week, Araghchi met with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, to lay out conditions for ending the war, which would also include waiving oil sanctions and establishing a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.
‘No trust in the American side’
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was also in New York for the UNGA, said on Saturday that Tehran no longer trusted negotiations with Washington, citing past rounds of talks that were followed by military strikes and new sanctions.
“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera.
He denied that Iran bore responsibility for the closure of the strait, saying the US had “closed the routes before us”. He said the waterway would reopen to commercial shipping if negotiations succeeded in ending the war.
Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said Iran’s proposal was intended chiefly as a gesture of goodwill.
“I think they are trying to show the willingness to talk and negotiate,” he told Al Jazeera. “That’s what’s important for their home audience back in Iran, and it’s also important for the American public.”
Harrison said Iran’s leaders likely anticipated Trump’s rejection, since the proposal closely mirrored the now failed memorandum of understanding signed in June that Tehran believes Washington had undermined.
“I don’t think they were surprised at all” by Trump’s move, he said.

articles.title: Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
Russia plans to spend $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 26, citing Ukrainian military intelligence.
Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence had obtained Russian internal documents showing the volumes of weapons Russia is preparing to produce next year and the funding allocated for them.
In recent months, Russia has increasingly relied on jet-powered drones in attacks on Ukrainian cities. In some attacks on Kyiv, jet-powered drones have accounted for around two-thirds of all drones launched.
"Next year, just for the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, Russia plans to spend $12 billion on this one category of weapons," Zelensky said.
Zelensky said Ukraine is scaling up production of interceptor drones to counter Russia's increasingly widespread use of jet-powered drones. Several interceptor prototypes are already being tested in combat, he said, with some identified as potential primary means of defense against the weapons.
"We are scaling up production and components. There will be a response," Zelensky said.
The remarks come as Russia has intensified its attacks against Ukraine in recent days, despite renewed international efforts to secure a ceasefire. U.S. President Donald Trump called for an end to the war during his address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, while Zelensky said following their meeting that Ukraine was ready to accept a ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure if Russia agreed to the same terms.
Zelensky said Russia's planned spending on attack drones shows that Moscow is not preparing to halt the war "at least for now."
He also said Ukraine's partners need to increase pressure on Russia through sanctions and strengthen joint efforts to defend against drones.
Ukraine currently intercepts about 55% of Russia's jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to Zelensky. More than 2,730 jet-powered Shaheds were launched against Ukraine in September, he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine aims to raise the interception rate to the level achieved against conventional Shahed drones, which he said is above 90%.
Ukraine has already signed 11 drone deals, according to Zelensky. The 11th, with Finland, was signed this week in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
He said Ukraine is preparing a 12th agreement, which it expects to sign with another country in the coming weeks.
"For Ukraine, this means more production capacity, more funding, and more technological advantages," Zelensky said.
Zelensky also said Russia is conducting a campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers, infrastructure, and communications. He said the goal is to leave Ukrainians without internet access, communications, and digital services.
Earlier, Russia's attacks on Kyiv on Sept. 26 caused internet outages across the capital and disrupted access to some online services.

articles.title: Ukraine used combat robots against the Russian army in Donbas for the first time
articles.body:
Ukraine used combat robots against the Russian army in Donbas for the first time
Kyiv • UNN
The Armed Forces of Ukraine delivered ground-based kamikaze robots by drones more than 10 km behind enemy lines in Donetsk region. The tactic was used in Operation “Vivaldi.”
Ukrainian troops have announced the first use of a new tactic in which kamikaze ground robotic systems are delivered by drones directly into the enemy's rear. The robots were deployed more than 10 km deep into territory in Donetsk Oblast controlled by Russian forces as part of Operation "Vivaldi," the 3rd Army Corps of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports, according to UNN.
Details
The corps called this a "new stage in the war involving the deployment of ground robots." After being delivered by drones, the ground systems moved independently in the area of Russian positions, searched for targets and attacked them.
The new tactic was called "Gryphon" — in honor of the call sign of a Ukrainian serviceman who went missing.
The robots were delivered more than 10 km into the enemy's rear
Where the enemy did not expect it, Russian soldiers appeared among the dead and wounded. The unique deep-strike tactic was created from scratch by fighters of the strike UGV unit
The importance of the new tactic is that ground robots do not need to cover dozens of kilometers to the target on their own or break through the front line. They are delivered by air deep into Russian positions, after which the UGVs can operate without directly endangering Ukrainian troops.
According to the commander of the 3rd Army Corps, Andrii Biletskyi, during Operation "Vivaldi," drones and ground robotic systems are being used ahead of the infantry.
Biletskyi also stated that over the past few weeks, the Defense Forces had liberated more than 125 sq km of territory, including the settlements of Serednie, Derylove and Shandryholove in the Lyman sector. According to his claim, the total losses of Russian forces during the operation exceeded 3,000 personnel.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Retaliatory Drone Strikes Hit Russian Oil Refinery Supplying Moscow’s Forces
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Retaliatory Drone Strikes Hit Russian Oil Refinery Supplying Moscow’s Forces
Ukrainian forces struck the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region overnight on September 26 as part of retaliatory strikes in response to Russian aggression, triggering a fire at the facility.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed the strike on September 26, saying the refinery is involved in receiving, storing, and processing crude oil and producing petroleum products used to support the Russian Armed Forces.
The Ilsky refinery has an annual processing capacity of approximately 6.6 million metric tons of crude oil. The General Staff said strikes against facilities of this type are intended to reduce Russia’s military and economic capacity.
Reports of the attack began emerging around midnight, when residents in the area reported explosions and Russian air defense activity. Footage subsequently circulated by the Exilenova+ monitoring channel showed a fire at the refinery. ASTRA later geolocated eyewitness footage to the Ilsky facility in the Seversky district of Krasnodar region.
Krasnodar region Governor Veniamin Kondratyev confirmed that drones had targeted the Seversky district and said fires had broken out on the territory of two enterprises, though he did not identify the facilities.
The Ilsky refinery, located roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) from Krasnodar, has been targeted by Ukrainian drones multiple times. The previous reported strike occurred on August 8.
The Ilsky strike came one day after Russia’s Perm oil refinery halted operations following a Ukrainian drone attack. According to Reuters, it became the fourth Russian refinery to suspend operations in less than a week amid Ukraine’s continued strikes on Russia’s oil-processing infrastructure.

Russian foreign minister again talks of Anchorage "understanding", says Russia ready to return to it
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has said that Russia is ready to return to the "understanding" that Moscow claims was reached in Anchorage between US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Source: Lavrov at a press conference following the UN General Assembly High-level Week, as reported by TASS, a Kremlin-aligned Russian news outlet
Details: Lavrov said Russia believes an understanding was reached in Anchorage and is ready to return to it.
Lavrov claimed that Russia was not suffering from a "lack of trust" and was ready to continue negotiations on a settlement of the war in Ukraine, but said that agreements must be honoured.
He also claimed that Europeans are preparing for war with Russia. Lavrov said that "metastases of Nazism" are evident among EU and NATO member states, particularly in Germany.
Previously: On 15 September, Lavrov claimed that Russia "would have already been living without war for a year" if the US had not "backed away from the agreements" supposedly reached in Alaska in August 2025.
Background:
- US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin met at a military base in Anchorage, Alaska, on 15 August 2025. The meeting ended without an agreement or the announcement of a ceasefire in Ukraine.
- Bloomberg reported that during a subsequent conversation with European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said Putin continued to demand the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the entirety of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts but was prepared to freeze the front line in Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts.
- On 15 June 2026, Lavrov said Russia was expecting another visit from the US president's special envoys and wanted to hear how Washington planned to implement what Moscow described as agreements on ending Russia's war against Ukraine reached between Putin and Trump in Anchorage.
- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently told journalists that no agreements on Ukraine had been reached at the Trump-Putin summit the previous year. He later said that the approach proposed by Russia in Anchorage had failed because it was unacceptable to Ukraine.

articles.title: No public mentions of Taiwan at official Xi and Trump meeting
articles.body:
Taiwan not openly discussed at Xi and Trump meeting
September 27, 2026
US President Donald Trump picked his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping up directly from the airport and in his welcoming remarks he praised the strong friendship between their two nations, as well as recalling how China and the US fought together as allies during World War II.
"Look at the greatness that we had together fighting in World War II," he said. "Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country," he said at the White House, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that fought alongside China against the Japanese between 1941 and 1942.
However, these pilots did not actually volunteer to fight with the People's Republic of China, whose leader was visiting Washington and which was not founded until 1949. The Americans were risking their lives for the former Republic of China, whose government relocated to Taiwan after communist victory in the Chinese Civil War in 1949.
"China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen," Trump said at a state dinner for Xi on Thursday evening. Sun Yat-sen was the founder of the Republic of China in 1912 and the Kuomintang, or KMT, which remains a major political party in Taiwan today.
Taiwan a major problem between US and China
Ever since the end of World War II, Taiwan has been a point of contention between Beijing and Washington. For decades, the US government ignored the communist regime in the People's Republic of China. But since 1972, Washington has acknowledged the "one China principle," according to which there is only one China, whose legal government is in Beijing and Taiwan belongs to it. Diplomatic relations between the US and China were only established in 1979.
The Taiwan Relations Act came into effect in 1979 too. The US law legalized arms exports to Taiwan. It also allowed the US government to take military action to prevent changes to the status quo in the Taiwan Strait.
A potential war between China and Taiwan would not only jeopardize stability in the Asia-Pacific region but also plunge the global economy into a prolonged recession, as supply chains would be severely disrupted.
During their high-profile meeting, Xi did not openly urge the US to respect the "one China" principle as he has done in the past, and Trump did not mention Taiwan in public either. In May, he put on hold a $14-billion arms deal that the US had concluded with the Taiwanese government late last year. The arms sales deal remains under review.
"Given the US' production capacity and its own military needs, it will take some time before approved arms can be delivered," said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist and professor at the National University of Singapore. "It remains unclear what else the US can currently offer Taiwan."
Ahead of crucial midterm elections in November, Trump urgently needs some positive headlines. He and his Republican party rely on farmers for support so they need China to import US agricultural goods. In 2023, before their current trade war, China imported $43 billion worth of soy, beef, wood and other goods from the US. However Beijing has drastically reduced its imports since.
Taiwan mentioned behind closed doors
China used the meeting "to make clear to Trump its opposition to any US military support for Taiwan," said William Yang, an analyst with the International Crisis Group. "Xi wants to convey this message personally and behind closed doors, thereby influencing Trump's decision on arms sales to Taiwan."
China's Xinhua news agency said that Xi had addressed the issue behind closed doors. It reported that Xi had expressed hope that the US would take strong action against Taiwanese independence and said that China's position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was clear. He reportedly added that "building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability is neither an expedient measure nor something that can be achieved overnight."
It will not have pleased Taiwanese politicians that the US president openly considered treating Taiwan as a bargaining chip in its negotiations with China, German sinologist Eberhard Sandschneider of the consultancy Berlin Global Advisers suggested during a political chatshow on German public television. "People living on the island of Taiwan do not take this lightly. This is an existential issue for Taiwan."
He added that he did not think China would take military action against Taiwan. That would be a move just as illogical as the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US attack on Iran, he argued.
Nobody is playing poker in China, Sandschneider continued. "Clear strategic interests are pursued there. National sovereignty and winning back Taiwan are key concerns. At the same time, it is well known that any military attack on Taiwan would not only lead to a military disaster but also to an economic collapse. The resulting setback for the global economy would call into question the Communist Party's legitimacy," the expert said.
De Zheng contributed to this article, which has been translated from German.

articles.title: Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open
articles.body:
With a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today’s politicians: the swearing.
“All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before,” said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. “Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language.
“Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It’s not OK. It’s a decline in respect and honor, period.”
Over the past decade, Donald Trump has been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language.
Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he was memorably reported to have complained that US was admitting immigrants from “shithole countries” – Trump has let rip during his second.
He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally.
A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. “They don’t know what they fuck they’re doing,” he told reporters on the White House lawn.
Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025, when asked about Venezuela’s then president, Nicolas Maduro. “He’s offered everything,” claimed Trump. “You know why? Because he doesn’t want to fuck around with the United States.” (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.)
Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump’s decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH,” he posted on his Truth Social platform in April.
“President Trump doesn’t have a very strong sense of decorum,” said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing’s place in society. “The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn’t care.”
Civility in politics
Trump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies.
In Nixon’s case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase “expletive deleted”.
Trump’s increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush’s mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, a live mic picked up his description of a New York Times journalist as a “major-league asshole”.
A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced “regret” that his remark was heard.
These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through.
Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem.
“The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession,” Phillips said. “The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians.
“Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing.”
In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word “shit”, in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics.
Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were “full of shit”.
Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: “We’re done with that shit.”
Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity.
Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey told Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents to “get the fuck out” of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January.
Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois, told a Washington thinktank she was “tired of fixing shit that Republicans break”. Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections, she said: “Fuck that shit.”
A rhetorical maneuver
While the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care.
“The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election,” argued Phillips. “It wouldn’t be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain.”
Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking “covert prestige” in descending into coarse language.
“There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people,” he said. “People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you’re really like them enough that you would be a good president for them.
“It’s comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: ‘Would you want to have a beer with them?’ It wasn’t a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver.”
Benjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of “WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves,” suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that “we are in a very strident time of political disagreement”.
The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses.
“I don’t see any reason why there’s anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that,” said Bergen. “I think the language norms are just changing.”
But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. “If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely.”
In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics.
“We’re dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries,” he said. “However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that’s in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands.
“Politicians’ fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn’t quite as high.”

articles.title: Poland eyes spending up to $4.4 billion on ‘Fort Trump’
articles.body:
Poland’s ‘Fort Trump’ could cost up to $4.4bn – National Security Bureau
Poland could pay up to 17 billion zloty ($4.4 billion)to house a permanent US military base on its territory, the presidential National Security Bureau (BBN) has said. The project, which is currently being discussed with Washington, involves a facility that could house 5,000 troops, the agency told the newspaper Rzeczpospolita this week.
Warsaw offered to host a permanent US base during President Donald Trump’s first term in 2018, proposing to name the facility ‘Fort Trump.’ Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski confirmed this week that a deal on the base was nearing completion.
Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who traveled to the US this week for the talks on the base among other things, stated that the final decision rests with Trump and that she did not expect it to be made before the review of the posture of US forces, which is expected to be finalized in November or December. According to the BBN, the base could be completed in 2029 under “optimal conditions.”
Under Trump, Washington has pressed European NATO members to boost defense spending and take on more responsibility for arming Ukraine while the US concentrates resources on competing with China. The US is also widely expected to scale back its military presence in Europe as part of this strategy shift.
America still considers Poland a “model ally,” according to US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, the man behind the US policy shift that has since become known as ‘NATO 3.0.’ Sobkowiak-Czarnecka also told journalists this week she had heard “many warm words from the American side acknowledging our preparedness and motivation.”
The US already has a permanent Army garrison and command headquarters in the city of Poznan, although most of the 10,000 US troops stationed in the country serve on a rotational basis. According to Deputy Defense Minister Stanislaw Wziatek, this number could grow to 15,000, with 5,000 stationed permanently at the new base.
Warsaw has been one of Kiev’s most ardent supporters in its ongoing conflict with Moscow. It also serves as a key logistics hub for delivering Western military aid to Ukraine while also bordering the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to the northeast.
Tensions between Moscow and Warsaw recently flared as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski vowed to inflict a swift defeat upon Russia in case of a direct clash with NATO. “If Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly,” he stated in mid-September, prompting Nikolay Patrushev, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to warn that Poland could “cease to exist” within days if it undertakes military action against Russia and forces Moscow to use its full arsenal.

articles.title: The Cold War’s strangest diplomatic tool is back on the ice
articles.body:
Did you know that the Irish gifted ice hockey to the world? Well, it’s between ourselves and the Scots, but everywhere I went in Canada, hockey experts and fans would regale me with how Irish soldiers, serving with the British Army, kept their hurling, Ireland’s ancient sport, going in the winter by converting ice-covered ponds and fields for play. Unable to use a hide bound small ball, they eventually settled on using lumps of coal that would be visible against the white playing surface. Vladislav Tretiak, the greatest goalkeeper of all time, reminded me of the Irish contribution to his beloved game every time we’ve met.
“Irish gave a lot of players to hockey,” he told me in Ulyanovsk, “and they’re proud of their roots.”
I would like that in giving the sport to the world, we Irish have therefore contributed to one of the most important processes in this increasingly divided world of ours – sports diplomacy. And, as always, ice hockey is leading the way.
In 1972, Canada and the Soviet Union played an eight-game series, which Tretiak starred in, with the Canucks winning 4-3, with one game tied. Soviet mastery and surprising grit stood up to Canadian violence and rock ‘em, sock ‘em hockey. It was a watershed moment at a time when sport built a bridge, with Ottawa even establishing an International Sports Relations Desk.
“The Canadians were tough, my God, they were also very good players. We thought they were born in skates,” Tretiak noted in an interview with Capital Sports in 2018.
Phil Esposito, who scored on Tretiak for the triumphant Canadians, told me in 2024 that “it opened up a direct dialogue that continues to today.” He added that “sport has a unique way of bringing people together.”
Brendan Shanahan, born to Irish parents and who would win an Olympic Gold in 2002 for Canada, as well as three Stanley Cups with Detroit Red Wings, told Capital Sports in 2019 that “it [Summit Series] was a wake up call to Canada, one we listened to.” Shanahan played alongside Russia’s Viacheslav Fetisov for two of his Stanley Cup wins, a player who led the way for Soviet players to cross to the NHL.
“He was nearly forty when he was with us [at Detroit] but he was just special. And we had [Igor] Larionov, another of those early pioneers. And then the younger guys like [Vladimir] Konstantinov, Slava Kozlov, and Sergei Federov. They all grew up inspired by it [Summit Series].”
Sports diplomacy led to the influx of Russian players to the NHL and today, it’s still working, but in reverse.
When I first went to top level ice hockey in Russia, in November 2007, it was the final season of the Russian Super League. I ventured out to the Sokolniki Arena in Moscow to watch Spartak, a club just back after a year out of hockey due to financial issues. It was a far cry from the NHL games I watched in Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa, and New York. In fact, it wasn’t even close to the 2nd tier American Hockey League games I attended in 1996-7 in such Canadian hotspots as…St. John or Fredericton, New Brunswick. In fact, the attendance, presentation, atmosphere, and overall vibe wasn’t a patch on the now-defunct Junior League Charlottetown Abbies with whom I worked.
It didn’t get much better once the Kontintental Hockey League (KHL) came into being in 2008. In 2011, working a CSKA Moscow game at their old home in the now demolished CSKA Ice Palace, I felt like I was in a time warp. I wandered from the ‘press area’ to find something to eat and drink, and there were a couple of tables with women behind them selling plastic cups of tea and ‘butter brot’ [a piece of bread with some form of meat on it].
“On the ice there was product, but so much around it was chaos,” Julius Supler told Capital Sports in 2016. The Slovak coached CSKA from 2011-12 and had tales to tell about how the KHL was only going to succeed when all clubs had modern arenas. And boy was he right.
Working the KHL beat from 2017-2022 for Capital Sports, I witnessed the birth of a product that sat comfortably between the OTT NHL and the delightful DEL [German Ice Hockey League]. The KHL has come on so much that it’s not only unwanted or over the hill North Americans or Europeans coming in for a pay day, it’s an alternative, and right now that is a boon for sports diplomacy.
Julius Hudacek arrived at Sibir Novosibirsk from Sweden as a highly rated, but eccentric goalie. The Slovak performed a ‘HudaShow’ after each game, win, lose, or tie. He was pretty handy between the pipes, though. A triple Slovak champ, World Championship silver medalist, and best keeper in both Slovakia and Sweden, it was in 2018 that I first got to interview him as part of a special series of Capital Sports shows hosted at Moscow’s Jewish Museum and Tolerance Center called Champ Talks.
“I don’t think of politics, just people,” he told the audience during our live show, “hockey is more important and a connection.”
He would join us a couple more times on our radio show before leaving Spartak in 2021. He returned to the KHL in 2022-23 to play for Kazakh club Barys Astana. I asked him if he was worried about falling foul of sanctions? “For what, being a normal person and not a politician?” Was his response.
In 2024, when Irish-Canadian defenseman Trevor Murphy, then with Sibir Novosibirsk, was asked if he was worried about playing in Russia? He shook his head and told my colleague from Capital Sports, “Why should I be? I’m playing hockey. Just playing hockey.” Now with SKA St. Petersburg, Murphy has maintained that attitude as he enters his eighth season in the league.
“It’s important,” Phil Esposito said in 2024, “to not lose sight that these are humans. Nobody wants it [war], but we don’t blame all for it.”
According to a leading New York-based hockey player agent, no player or coach he’s spoken with has thought twice about repercussions of playing in Russia. While the 2026-27 season is still young, between 48-52 North American players are currently on club rosters. In terms of coaches, Canadians Guy Boucher and Mitch Love and American Scott Gordon are all at KHL clubs Avangard Omsk, Traktor Chelyabinsk, and Shanghai Dragons respectively.
The player agent, who also represents coaches, says that there is an issue for coaches coming from North America. “I’ve had clients who wanted to come to Russia, but were warned by figures in Canada and the US not to. Players, they’ll go, but coaches, it’s a bit tougher.”
Ilya (38) is a fan of Traktor Chelyabinsk who lives in the Chelyabinsk Region town of Kasli. Hockey is what “helps survive life.” He works night shifts as a security guard and during his days off as a taxi driver. His vehicle has enough Traktor merchandise to let you know he’s a supporter of the hockey club.
“I was born in Chelyabinsk and it’s my team. People say we don’t have much to hope for [in the region], so hockey is most important thing. I go to games, every year ten, and bring my son. I don’t see him most of the day as he’s in school, I work, but the drives to hockey, then games, then coming home, we [bond].”
I felt a tinge of sadness as he spoke, remembering my dad and I doing the same, but with our traditional sports in Ireland, and it brought home how important it is for kids and fathers to do things together. I told Ilya this and he brought up the “foreigners.”
“My father worked in a factory and he got me to hockey. Now I do the same. And my son, he’s twelve, and he sees online what people think of us [Russians] and then in our jersey we see Canadians and Americans. And I tell him, see, we’re not so bad, not all people hate us.”
While sports fans know that players and coaches are at their clubs for money, there is also a two-way respect. This has increased in Russia as genuine talent like Canada’s Nathan Legare arrived this summer to the Urals-based club. One local journalist likened the signing to “Father Frost coming early.”
Speaking with KHL fans in Russia and Belarus, they don’t see the North Americans or Europeans plying their trade in the league as outcasts, mercenaries, or anything other than regular hockey players coming to do a job. In itself, that is a major compliment.
The KHL media department weren’t keen on speculating, though they did say that interest in the league abroad has remained stable. KHL beat reporters from Russian sports sites and newspapers have confirmed this and that contacts with colleagues in North America, especially, has not dimmed since 2022.
The New York-based agent, when I asked about the coming years, was equally positive.
“There are a limited number of places in the NHL and if you’re an ambitious player, you won’t drop down to Germany, or Sweden, or even the AHL, if you’re released, you’ll look at Russia and think, man, the salaries are good, the level is really high, and if I perform well enough, I can stay there and not be pumped and dumped like I would with an NHL organization.”
This is what Jordan Weal, a Canadian now with Dynamo Moscow, told us in 2022. “It’s more stable, because you can develop and play in one place, not get moved around the franchise or traded in a few minutes. There are more rights for players in a [contract] sense.”
As vital as the pipeline of quality foreign imports is for the future of the KHL and Russian hockey, the bigger picture is that bridges built in 1972 are being maintained. If sport diplomacy helped open opportunities for dialogue between nations at a time when nuclear Armageddon was never more than a few minutes away, then hockey can offer us a new avenue for the meeting of peoples.
And once it all works out, you can thank the Irish for giving the world a winter sport that melted the old Cold War and put the new one on ice.

articles.title: American warship sunk by missiles off Scotland in live fire
articles.body:
The decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring has been sunk off the Hebrides during the joint US-UK live-fire exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026, in an engagement that drew in warships and aircraft from both navies, according to US Naval Forces Europe and Africa, which has released footage of the strike.
The video shows the American destroyer USS Paul Ignatius launching a missile and the frigate being hit. Other attackers took part alongside her, among them aircraft and further surface vessels, and the full order of battle has yet to be set out.
We will be bringing you an in-depth look tomorrow at what happened off the Hebrides, how the engagement was put together and which units and weapons were involved.
Paul Ignatius is an Arleigh Burke-class Flight IIA destroyer, hull number DDG-117, commissioned in July 2019 and named for the former Secretary of the Navy who held the post under Lyndon Johnson. She has been forward-deployed to Naval Station Rota in southern Spain since June 2022, one of the American destroyers held in Europe for ballistic missile defence and wider tasking across the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
Klakring was an Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigate, decommissioned in 2013 and laid up at the Philadelphia Naval Inactive Ship Maintenance Facility until she was towed down the Delaware River on 12 August ahead of the Atlantic crossing, making first for Campbeltown. The exercise itself was originally planned for a window in May before moving to the second half of September at the QinetiQ Hebrides range in north-west Scotland.
A Request for Information issued by the Ministry of Defence in August 2025, inviting industry to take part, described Atlantic Thunder 26 as “a US-UK multi-domain exercise designed to validate SUW kill chains, build resilient kill webs and deliver strategic messaging through kinetic demonstration.”
The strike was only one part of the exercise though, Klakring is expected to now settle at a depth of around 6,000 feet, where uncrewed underwater vehicles are to carry out battle damage assessment and seabed survey work, a phase the Ministry of Defence treated as central when it approached industry last year.
The precedent is Atlantic Thunder 22, held off the same range in September 2022, which ended with the sinking of the former USS Boone by HMS Diamond, USS Arleigh Burke, RAF Typhoons and US Navy P-8 Poseidons, and was billed at the time as the most complex multinational sinking exercise staged in UK waters.

articles.title: ADF neutralizes 147 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
ADF neutralizes 147 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on September 26, the enemy attacked with 170 Shahed-type attack UAVs, 76 of them jet-powered, as well as Gerbera drones and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from the areas of Oryol, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk and Shatalovo in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by Ukrainian combat aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 07:30 on September 27, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 147 drones.
Hits were recorded at 18 locations, while falling debris from downed targets was reported at eight locations.
As Ukrinform reported, seven people were injured in Russian attacks on Kyiv on September 26.

articles.title: Saudi strike on Yemen's Taiz kills seven
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi strike on Yemen's Taiz kills seven
A Saudi airstrike on Taiz in southwest Yemen killed seven people and wounded dozens more, Houthi media reported on Sunday.
The Iran-backed Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel said the strike killed seven and wounded 40 in a central marketplace in Taiz, minutes after reporting that a Saudi fighter jet had targeted the area.
Following years of relative calm, Yemen's war reignited in July, against the backdrop of the widening Middle East war.
Fighting intensified in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping lane.
The Houthis have in parallel launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports, already choked off by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted two Houthi drones that were heading in the direction of the capital Riyadh.
Schools in Riyadh announced on Sunday that they would be shifting to remote learning for a week, without giving a reason, according to messages emailed to parents and seen by AFP.
Taiz, a major city controlled by the internationally recognised government, has been thrust to the frontlines of fighting between the Houthis and government forces.
Yemen's war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of vast swathes of the country's north.
Despite Saudi backing, Yemen's government forces have been unable to repel the latest Houthi offensive.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree nonetheless reported on Saturday that Saudi air forces launched 27 strikes targeting Taiz, Marib, Saada, Amran, Ibb and Hajjah provinces.

articles.title: China opposes 'unilateral military actions' amid US-Iran war, calls for 2-state Palestine solution track
articles.body:
Saadet Gökce
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
 China’s vice president on Saturday voiced Beijing's opposition to "unilateral military actions" amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict, also using his address to the UN General Assembly to urge a two-state solution to the Palestinian issue.
"We should settle differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation, and oppose unilateral military actions that violate the UN Charter and circumvent Security Council authorization," Han Zheng said, urging major countries to shoulder "special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security," and take the lead in "complying with the rules, upholding rule of law, and doing what's right."
He also said China believes the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern countries, including Gulf states, should be respected.
"International industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded," said Han.
He called for advancing governance in the West Bank and post-conflict reconstruction in Gaza in line with the principle of Palestinians governing Palestine.
China also calls for "bringing the Palestinian question back onto the right track of the two-state solution at an early date," he said.
On Ukraine, he said China plays a continued "constructive role in its own way" to achieve a political settlement of the crisis, also urging "the relevant country to immediately stop using the threat of force against Cuba and immediately and completely lift the blockade and sanctions against Cuba."
On tech advances, he said the world should take a people-centered approach and ensure positive AI development amid the rapid development of new technologies and industrial transformation, while narrowing the digital divide and promoting development that is universally beneficial.

articles.title: Trump and the chain of setbacks in Iran, China and Russia
articles.body:
Contrary to the image Donald Trump has tried to project of American power and influence in the world, recent days have been marked, for him, by a series of setbacks—setbacks that this time appear not in a single file, but simultaneously across several important arenas of US foreign policy. Reuters, in a report, addressed this very issue, citing Trump's speech at the United Nations, his meeting with China's president, the war against Iran, and the unsuccessful efforts to end the war in Ukraine as signs of the limits of his ability to advance Washington's demands.
In his speech at the UN General Assembly, Trump tried once again to present an image of American power. While defending his administration's conduct in the war with Iran, he threatened Tehran that if an agreement was not reached, it might face harsher military measures. Trump even spoke of the possibility of Iran's annihilation and emphasized that Washington remains ready to use its military power to achieve its objectives.
But raising the level of threats does not necessarily mean an increase in America's ability to achieve its political goals. The war with Iran—which Trump has from the outset tried to frame within the context of American military power—continues, and has become one of the most complicated files of his administration's foreign policy. Iran's resistance to American military and economic pressures has meant that Washington has been unable to convert these pressures into a clear and lasting political outcome.
Developments in recent days also show that the path to an agreement remains difficult. On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Iran put forward proposals to end the conflicts and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but Trump did not accept these proposals. Under these circumstances, the continuation of the conflict shows that American pressures have still not been able to force Tehran to accept Washington's core demands.
On the other hand, many of America's European and Asian allies have not gone along with Washington's requests for greater participation in confronting Iran. This matters from another angle as well; because American power does not depend solely on this country's military strength—the ability to build coalitions and bring allies along is also an important part of Washington's global power.
The China file shows a similar picture. In his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump tried to use the summit as a sign of his ability to manage one of the world's most important geopolitical rivalries. However, according to Reuters, the tangible result of this meeting remained largely confined to maintaining the trade truce and preventing an escalation of economic tensions between the two countries.
While important files such as Taiwan, trade, artificial intelligence, and China's role in international developments remain points of disagreement between Washington and Beijing, no concrete achievement was reached that could be said to resolve these disputes. This shows that even when Trump enters direct negotiations with China's leader, the gap between a display of power and the achievement of a real agreement remains considerable.
Of course, this does not mean America is empty-handed against China, or that Trump lacks tools of pressure. Washington still possesses considerable economic, technological, military, and diplomatic leverage. But the main issue is the extent to which these tools can be converted into a political outcome. Indeed, the ability to exert pressure is different from the ability to impose a final result.
On the Ukraine file as well, Trump faces a similar challenge. He had repeatedly promised that he could end the war between Russia and Ukraine, and in recent months has made efforts to bring Moscow and Kyiv closer to an agreement. However, Washington's efforts to reach a ceasefire—including in the energy sector—have so far not led to a stable and significant outcome.
The continuation of the fighting between Russia and Ukraine shows that American influence, even in a file where Washington plays an important role, is not sufficient to impose a final solution. Russia and Ukraine both have their own particular interests and calculations, and Trump cannot simply force them to accept a demand merely by announcing it.
These three files reveal an important point about the Trump administration's foreign policy. America remains one of the most powerful actors in the world, and its president has extensive economic, military, and diplomatic tools at his disposal; but there is a gap between the "ability to create pressure" and the "ability to convert pressure into a political outcome."
In the Iran file, the war continues; regarding China, fundamental disagreements remain unresolved; and in Ukraine, Trump's efforts to end the war have not yet led to a final agreement. For this reason, this set of developments can be seen as a sign of the difficulty of converting American power into political outcomes.
Trump can still threaten, exert pressure, and make decisions that affect global equations; but developments in recent weeks show that in international politics, a display of power is not the same as achieving the desired result. The important question now facing the American president is to what extent Washington can convert its power into results—not just in a single file, but simultaneously across several major global crises.
MNA

articles.title: Russian propaganda intensifies social media campaign urging Ukrainians to join protests
articles.body:
Russian propaganda intensifies social media campaign urging Ukrainians to join protests
According to Ukrinform, this was stated by Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation under the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) on Facebook.
"The Center is recording a large-scale information campaign orchestrated by Russia on social media, calling on Ukrainians to take part in protests and destabilize the situation," the Center for Countering Disinformation said.
Calls to take to the Maidan and demand that the authorities "immediately conclude peace," "cancel mobilization," hold "immediate elections," and so on are being actively circulated in Ukraine's information space. Alleged Ukrainian servicemen are presented as the "leaders of the protests."
The Center said that, according to intelligence it had received, Russia is attempting in this way to involve Ukrainian military personnel in protests in order to cause internal destabilization and undermine Ukraine's defense capabilities.
"Do not fall for enemy manipulation and rely only on verified sources of information," the Center urged.
As Ukrinform reported, Russian propaganda has been circulating AI-generated videos allegedly showing Ukrainian military personnel disguising themselves as civilians on the front line.
Photo: Freepik

articles.title: Group of 14 Bipartisan US Senators Urge Trump to Block Putin From G20 Summit in Miami
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Group of 14 Bipartisan US Senators Urge Trump to Block Putin From G20 Summit in Miami
A bipartisan group of 14 US senators sent a letter calling on President Donald Trump to rescind his invitation to Russian leader Vladimir Putin for the upcoming G20 summit scheduled for December in Miami, as reported by The Washington Post.
The initiative was spearheaded by Republican Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the lead Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, alongside six other Democrats and six other Republicans.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Putin alone bears responsibility for Russia’s full-scale aggressive war against Ukraine. Allowing his participation in the G20 summit in the United States raises serious concerns about legitimizing and normalizing a government that continues to launch daily strikes on civilian targets in Ukraine every day," the senators stated in the letter, according to The Washington Post.
The lawmakers also highlighted that Putin, Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, and other members of the Russian delegation remain under US sanctions for actions Washington considers a threat to national security.
According to the signatories, failing to isolate Putin from the international community leaves him with far less motivation to end Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Washington Post noted that Siluanov’s previous attendance at a G20 finance ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, last month drew sharp pushback from several nations.
European Union representatives specifically requested that the Russian minister be excluded from the official group photograph.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio previously announced that the United States had formally invited Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit scheduled for December in Miami.
Speaking after a meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Rubio expressed hope that Putin would attend, noting the summit could provide an opportunity for talks with US President Donald Trump and other global leaders.
Rubio also highlighted that Washington was open to playing a constructive role in facilitating a limited ceasefire involving energy and grain, stating that while such a step would not solve Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it could help alleviate broader global pressures.
